II

William J. Bray III

Grand Master – 2010-2011
Most Worshipful William J. Bray III is a past master of North Hollywood
Lodge No. 542, having served as its Master in 1979. Brother Bill is also a member
of Hollywood Lodge No. 355 and San Benito Lodge No. 211 of California and
Kodiak Lodge No. 9 of Kodiak, Alaska.
Brother Bill is married and lives with Linda, his lovely wife of 50 years
in Chatsworth. They have one son, Bill, a Master Mason, a lovely daughter-in-law
and two fantastic grandsons, all living in Minnesota.
Brother Bill served his country in the United States Navy and was
medically retired. He then joined the family business as Vice President and
General Manager, and retired in 2006.
Brother Bill’s Masonic career and affiliations are as follows: He was
Inspector from 1990 through 1999, with brief interruptions to serve as Grand
Sword Bearer, Grand Marshal, and Grand Orator. In addition to these three terms
as a Grand Lodge Officer and his services as an Inspector, Brother Bill has served
on numerous Grand Lodge committees.
Brother Bill was elected Junior Grand Warden in 2007.
rd

In the Scottish Rite he holds the rank of 33 degree, Inspector General
Honorary in the San Fernando Bodies. He is a member of all three of the York
Rite Bodies, and a member of Al Malaikah Shriners in Los Angeles and is a
Past President of Old West Shrine Club. Other Masonic memberships include
the Royal Order of Scotland, the Robert the Bruce Association, and St. Croix
Conclave, Red Cross of Constantine.
Bill was named Knight Commander of the Temple by the Grand
Encampment of Knights Templar. He is also a member of the Allied Masonic
Degrees Council No. 105, the National Sojourners, Los Angeles No. 26, he is a
Hero of ’76 and has received the Honorary Legion of Honor from the Order of
DeMolay. Additionally, he was made an Honorary DeMolay by both the Northern
and Southern Jurisdictions of DeMolay in California. San Benito Lodge No. 211
honored Brother Bill with the Hiram Award.
He and his wife, Linda, have been very active in the Order of the Eastern
Star. In 2001 he served the Grand Chapter of California as Worthy Grand Patron,
and served the General Grand Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star as Worthy Grand
Chaplain from 2003-2006.
Brother Bill has also served his community as a Scoutmaster for Boy
Scout Troop 226 in Chatsworth. His son is an Eagle Scout and both are members
of the Order of the Arrow. Brother Bill has served as an usher in his church, is a
member of the Canoga Park Elks, and many other military service organizations.
Brother Bill received the Man of the Year Award for Chatsworth in 1981.

One Hundred Sixty-Second
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, September 23, 2011
The 162nd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
William J. Bray III on Friday, September 23, 2011.
Brother William J. Bray IV, son of the Grand Master and member of
North Star Lodge No. 23 in Minnesota, raised the opening session of Grand Lodge.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at
the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following
which the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our
Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters
were then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master
then directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the
usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number was present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Leonard B. Froomin,
Grand Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren.
“Eternal Judge among the stars, our thoughts are directed to You at this
time. Each of us is sending a message. We are remembering loved ones, Masonic
Brothers, friends well known and some not yet met. We are forever joined to them
by our vows taken at the altar, dedicated to worthy principles, workers for the
betterment of our fellowmen and ourselves. We seek to make a better world, one
worthy of Your act of creation.
At this very moment we recall Your faithful servants who, having
toiled in this life to live by Your values, have been called to Your side to reap
the rewards of their labors and to await our arrival. The day we see them once
more will be joyous beyond our imagination and they will delight in showing us
God’s kingdom.
We must today rededicate ourselves to qualify to stride beside them
through the hallways of heaven.
I speak now to each individual seated before me: in your mind’s eye
do you see that Brother who passed from this life this year at a time you shared
with him in the past? Was it at a degree? Did he welcome the candidate with a
positive message about beginning the path of a better life? Did he actually coach
that Brother and be his guide along the way? Are you seeing his smiling face as he
danced at a Lodge’s event, ate watermelon at the Lodge’s annual picnic, greeted
children and their families at the Child I.D. location, took a basket of food to a
needy family, or helped in a cleanup around the Lodge building? Did you ask
yourself why he was smiling? I’ll tell you: he was happy doing the Lord’s and
Masonry’s work. Don’t be sad now: he has achieved his reward. We salute all
of our Brothers with the silent battery of three times three in recognition of the
fact that our Brothers formed their cubical stone perfectly and are now placing
it in heaven where the Great Architect will smile in approval of their job well
done. Amen.”
Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Master, Stanley M. Cazneaux.

16

Proceedings of the

Eulogy
Stanley Meeker Cazneaux
I was once asked how to measure a Grand Master’s legacy. I responded
by asking whether my response was to be limited by his twelve months in office
or the influence the man had on the craft during his entire Masonic career. My
question in response to this question clearly shows my view of how to measure
the man, and my take on Stan Cazneaux’s legacy is the subject of this eulogy.
Even a casual reader of our recent Grand Lodge Proceedings will
conclude that now is indeed an exciting time to be a Mason. The statistics are
impressive: the number of applications received, the number of degrees conferred,
complete lines in lodges with no Past Masters repeating, and the list goes on. Many
Masonic jurisdictions without much effort are reaping the benefits of a renewed
interest among young men in what Masonry has to offer. Yet, in this renaissance,
California stands at the forefront because of the foresight demonstrated by
California’s Masonic leadership long before this renaissance first was reflected in
our membership statistics.
There are hinges of history, formative moments which have an impact on
what follows. I can identify what in my view is the hinge for our present success.
I can even pin point the date and place when that hinge moved. It occurred at Stan
and Gloria Cazneaux’s home on Saturday, August 17, 1991, when Stan gathered
the men who would be on his Executive Committee to plan for the upcoming
Grand Lodge year. The meeting was complete with reports and charts, and the
four line officers as a team developed important plans and made equally important
commitments not just for Stan’s term as Grand Master but also for the three
years following.
Financial reforms were the first important changes implemented as a
result of that August 1991 weekend meeting. The four of us agreed that under
our collective watch Grand Lodge would live within its means, no more budget
overruns, and that we would recommend changes in our Grand Lodge law and
procedures to make this fiscal responsibility permanent. In our system, the Grand
Master is really the only person with the power to control Grand Lodge expenses.
Starting with Stan’s term, the Deputy Grand Master assumed responsibility
for preparing the Grand Lodge budget which he must administer the following
fiscal year as the Grand Master. As a result of this reform, the Grand Master is
now intimately aware of every item in his budget and by presenting it himself
to Grand Lodge for adoption commits himself to stay within that budget. This
important reform has remained in effect for every Grand Lodge budget adopted
since Stan’s term of office. Our Grand Lodge’s financial health today is due in no
small part to this change. Stan also changed the Grand Lodge fiscal year to match
the Grand Master’s term so that the craft can hold each Grand Master accountable

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

17

for expenses incurred on his watch. Stan also led by example. During his term as
Grand Master, Grand Lodge spent no more than the per capita collected for his
term, another important discipline that we have followed ever since.
During Stan’s tenure as Grand Master, other important administrative
changes occurred, but I will mention only one. John Cooper was recommended
by Stan and his leadership team for election to the first of John’s seventeen terms
as our Grand Secretary. Our Grand Lodge office and its staff are the envy of the
Masonic world, and the progression of building the office staff and procedures
now in place began with John’s first election as Grand Secretary in 1991.
Stan’s commitment to excellence continued after he completed his
term as Grand Master. In addition to his return to the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes, the last four years of which he served as President, Stan chaired
the Wardens Retreat Committee from 1992 to 1999. Stan changed the focus of
the retreats from management to leadership, paving the way for a generation of
Masonic leaders trained to pursue excellence. Stan designed a retreat program
offering tools for Wardens, who would later become Masters and then Past
Masters, to bring excellence to all aspects of lodge operations. When men in
increasing numbers began applying to our lodges for the degrees about ten years
ago, our lodges already had a corps of present leaders and Past Masters who had
been trained at our Wardens leadership retreats. New Masons thus found a home
where they felt welcomed, in no small measure due to the leadership training
program which Stan designed and implemented. California has been probably
the most successful American jurisdiction in integrating the new generation of
Masons into the fraternity because Stan re-set our retreat programs to teach our
Wardens how to make our lodges a welcoming place for young men.
Success of course has many parents, and the same may be said of the
success California Masonry has had in the last twenty years. Many important
reforms and innovations with long term benefits to our craft have been added by
Grand Masters who followed Stan, and many other Masons all over California
have made their contributions also. But, in my view, it all started with Stan’s
willingness to question what we do, to strengthen what at the core defines who we
are as Masons and to try new approaches to what is not working well. Masonry
needed a new focus, and Stan in collaboration with his leadership team renewed a
commitment to excellence that remains strong and vibrant today.
As Stan traveled throughout California during his year as Grand Master,
he left the Brethren at each stop with one final thought, a thought which resonated
with Stan because it was a shorthand way to convey his Masonic pathway to
excellence, and I leave you with it today:

18

Proceedings of the
A bell is not a bell until someone rings it.
A song is not a song until someone sings it.
Brotherly Love is not Brotherly Love until you practice it.
And Freemasonry is not Freemasonry until you live it.
And, Stan would then say:
I charge each and every one of you to:
Ring the bell!
Sing the song!
Practice Brotherly Love!
And live Freemasonry!

At 12:00 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 1:15 p.m.

Presentation of the Leadership Training Awards
The Lodge Management Certification Program consists of five courses
that are conducted simultaneously at a particular location or online. The
courses include: Hall Association Management, Lodge Finance, Membership
Development, Program Planning, and Lodge Administration. Each course is a full
day in length. At the end of each course, participants must pass an examination
before they are given a certification in that course.

Curt Conyers
Brother Curt Conyers is a member of Pleasanton Lodge No. 321. He
serves as a member of the Lodge Hall Association; and in addition to his work
with DeMolay, he is the Associate Bethel Guardian for the Pleasanton Bethel of
Job’s Daughters and the 2010 Grand Senior Custodian for the Grand Guardian
Council of California.
He has worked diligently for DeMolay for many years. Curt began as
a youth leader in DeMolay serving in numerous leadership positions concluding
in 1979 as the Northern California DeMolay Association Scribe. As a Senior
DeMolay, he volunteered as a member of the Pleasanton Chapter Advisory Council
eventually holding the positions of Chapter “Dad” and Chairman of the Advisory
Council. Curt continued to assist Northern California DeMolay in several roles
with the Northern California DeMolay Convention Staff and Athletics programs.
Curt stepped-up to assist Pleasanton Chapter again last year filling
a vacancy as Chairman of the Advisory Council. He is a wonderful example
and mentor for the DeMolays he works with in the chapter. His commitment,
dedication, and hard work have been recognized by DeMolay bestowing upon
him the Degree of Chevalier, the Cross of Honor, and the Legion of Honor.
James W. Dole
Brother James W. Dole is a member of Huntington Beach Lodge No. 380
where he has served as Master and Secretary. Jim has been honored for his many
years of service to DeMolay being awarded the Cross of Honor and the Legion
of Honor.
Jim has dedicated his life to the Masonic fraternity, the youth orders,
and especially Rainbow for Girls. He is always there working behind the scenes,
connecting with each youth in an encouraging and constantly fun way. Whether
it is Grand Assembly Sessions, providing a sound system anywhere in the state at
Rainbow Girls Receptions or Grand Worthy Advisor Official Visits, helping his
local assembly, working on the floor crew for Grand Assembly or working on the
State websites, Jim is always there helping, supporting and teasing. He knows
how to talk, relate and reach teens in a nurturing way and always on their level.
In 1993, Jim received the Grand Cross of Color for his dedication and
outstanding work on behalf of California Rainbow for Girls. His service and
outgoing personality made him a natural choice to serve as State Rainbow Dad
in 2007. Jim Dole is among the stalwarts of Masonry committed to youth and
the future.

Rodney B. Haney

Brother Rodney B. Haney is a member of Bay Cities Lodge No. 337. He
has served his lodge as Senior Deacon on four separate occasions.
He has been active with Job’s Daughters for 30 years. Rod has been the
Associate Bethel Guardian for two bethels beginning in the 1980’s and on through
the 90’s. In 1989, he was appointed Grand Inner Guard of the Grand Council
of California Job’s Daughters and was elected Vice Associate Grand Guardian
in 1990 and Associate Grand Guardian in 1991. Rod also served four years on

President of the California Job’s Daughters Foundation.
Rod’s service has far surpassed the boundaries of California. In 2001, he
was the Supreme Bethel Associate Guardian, the Supreme Treasurer in 2005, and
was elected to the Supreme Board of Trustees from 2006 to 2008.
Rodney Haney has been a dedicated volunteer for Job’s Daughters
and continues to be a highly respected advisor and Mason. He is an outstanding
role model for the girls of Job’s Daughters and an inspiration to his fellow
adult advisors.
Robert M. Stevenson
Brother Robert “Mike” Stevenson is a member of Upland-Mt. Baldy
Lodge No. 419. He is serving his fourth straight year as Marshal for his lodge.

Past Master Councilor of San Diego Chapter. He has worked for the past 10 years

men. Mike works beside the young men of the chapter providing encouragement,

Dad Stevenson’s positive attitude and infectious smile welcome all to

by all for “walking the talk.”

Grand Master’s Message
Good afternoon, my brethren. I am pleased to welcome the delegates
and members of the Grand Lodge of California Free and Accepted Masons to this
162nd Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge.
To our guests from other jurisdictions, allow me to extend a warm
welcome on behalf of our fraternity. Our Grand Lodge is honored to have you
here. Enjoy your visit to beautiful San Francisco! If we can assist you at any time,
please don’t hesitate to ask.
Today I stand before you to explain my stewardship of the craft over the
past year, in order to fulfill section 404.130 of the California Masonic Code.
It doesn’t seem possible that a year has passed since I knelt at the altar
of Freemasonry and vowed to serve as your 145th Grand Master. Thank you for
trusting me with this privilege. I am truly humbled, and I am forever grateful for
the warmth and support that you have shown Linda and me this year.
I want to thank Most Worshipfuls William Stovall, William Holsinger,
and Stanley Cazneaux, who I served under in my early years as an appointed
Grand Lodge officer. During those formative years, you each showed me what it
means to be a leader. Thank you for starting me down this path.
To Most Worshipfuls Mel Stein, Dick Hopper, Larry Adamson, and Ken
Nagel: Thank you for your mentorship and your guidance coming up through the
line. For four years, you prepared me for this responsibility. Throughout this year
as Grand Master, I looked to each of you as an inspiration.
OVERVIEW OF THE YEAR
In the days, months, and years to come, I will cherish the memories that
Linda and I made this year. We went up and down this state and shared special
moments with thousands of you and your families. Despite the jet lag, the airport
security lines, the traffic jams, and too many early mornings, I wouldn’t trade
those moments for anything. I am blessed to have met so many of you during
our travels.
And there was a lot of traveling. As a quick recap, Linda and I attended
11 youth events (including a few surprise visits); nine cornerstone ceremonies;
five Diamond Jubilee awards; four 50-year awards; seven lodge anniversaries
(including two for 150 years); four lodge rededications; and made visitations to

and the Royal Order of Scotland;
…to name a few.

All told, from September 2010 through September 2011, we logged
49,541 miles in the air and 53,574 miles on the road. It was all worth it.
You see, our jurisdiction is made up of more than 50,000 individuals,
each one with a story and a place in his heart for Masonry. Thanks to all that
traveling, Linda and I were able to meet a great many of you. And no matter what
the occasion, you really proved something: California Masonry is made up of
extraordinary people who care deeply about their fraternity. That is what I will
remember most from this year.
GENERAL CONDITION OF THE CRAFT
So, after many visits up and down our great state, it gives me great pride
to tell you: Masonry is alive and well in California.
Our 332 degree-conferring lodges conferred more than 4,700 degrees
this year, extending our record growth from the past few years. We raised the
most Master Masons in more than 20 years. Our total gains were the highest since
1999. And we had the least total losses in membership since 1925.
What does all this mean? We’re moving beyond the trend in membership
losses that we’ve faced in recent years, and are closer to seeing a pure increase in
membership. Our current Master Mason membership totals sit at approximately
57,000 with another 9,000 Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts working their
way through the degree process.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

45

I am proud to announce that this year, we constituted Paideia Lodge
No. 852 and General Douglas MacArthur Lodge No. 853, and instituted a brand
new lodge, Oasis Lodge U.D. This growth was balanced against three lodge
consolidations, keeping our overall number of lodges the same.
We’re seeing a new breed of Masons come in. These are men who are
clamoring for more: They want more knowledge about Masonry. They want to be
more involved in Masonry.
This blending of men – from all different generations and walks of life
– is what makes our fraternity unique. It’s one of the reasons we have survived
the centuries, and can still thrive today. With that in mind, I’d like to see more
tolerance between older members of our craft and these younger members coming
in. Change is difficult. But it’s necessary. The older members have important
lessons to teach: they are mentors to our young Masons. But our younger members
can teach us, too. They bring in new ideas and greater ease with technology. Let’s
honor what we each bring to Masonry, and welcome this new generation. Our
ability to adapt to new members, new ideas, and new times will determine how
successful we are in the future.
My theme for the year was: the past is our heritage, the present is our
responsibility, the future is our obligation. In matters such as these, I think it’s
important that we remember it.
We need to honor our past, work our hardest in the present, and have a
vision and commitment to our future. It’s what our forefathers did, and it’s what
we are charged to do, as stewards of this great fraternity.
On the subject of “troubled lodges,” I’ll echo what Most Worshipful
Hopper said in his Grand Master’s Message: Rather than “troubled lodges,” I believe
our attention is best directed at “troubled Masons.” Throughout our jurisdiction,
there are brothers who have turned away from their Masonic obligations, for
whatever the reason – be it a lack of practice, a lack of inspiration, or some failure
on the part of the fraternity. These troubled Masons can put a mighty strain on the
health of their lodges, and we may label the entire lodge “troubled.” But it is never
too late to make things right. It should be the responsibility – and the privilege – of
each of us to restore our brothers’ faith and commitment in our craft. One way,
the simplest way, is for each of us to strive even more diligently to live a Masonic
life. If we do, even the most jaded brother will be able to see that Masonry is alive
and well. He’ll be able to trust us when we reach out to him and help him find his
way back to the fraternity. And his lodge will prosper. So you see, to restore the
well-being of our troubled lodges, we must start with our troubled Masons.
Before concluding my report on the condition of the craft, I want to
address a topic pertaining to our international fraternity. As you may recall, about
five years ago, our brothers at the Grand Lodge of Baja California experienced a
splinter group that left the Grand Lodge. The dissident group has since seen that

46

Proceedings of the

this is not a workable situation, and they want to come back home. These things
can take a long time, but the reconciliation effort is underway. It was endorsed in
writing in February, when our Grand Lodge, the Grand Lodge of Baja California,
and the breakaway group signed an accord to find ways for the group to be
reunified and reabsorbed in the Grand Lodge. We stand prepared to support them
as they work through these issues.
Now, to bring your focus back home to California, I would like to take
the opportunity to acknowledge the incredible efforts of three brothers. Very
Worshipful Paul Hennig retired from the office of Grand Lecturer in April, after
more than four years of outstanding service and dedication to our ritual. In his
stead, I appointed Most Worshipful Ken Nagel, Past Grand Master. In just six
months, I am pleased to say that Most Worshipful Nagel has already proven
himself a passionate and gifted Grand Lecturer.
Very Worshipful Glenn Woody, our Grand Treasurer, has also decided to
retire. For the past five years, Very Worshipful Woody has served our craft with
unwavering dedication and truly commendable work. As we look towards the
future, we owe him many thanks for the secure financial footing beneath us.
PROGRESS TOWARDS STRATEGIC PRIORITIES
Speaking of the future, allow me to update you on our plan for the future
of the craft: California Masonry’s Strategic Plan for 2010 to 2015. In the spring
of 2010 we asked all of you to share your visions for the fraternity. More than
3,500 California Masons and others in our fraternal family spoke up, in Town Hall
Meetings, in an online survey, in letters and e-mails and discussion boards. This
year, we completed a plan that fulfills your visions, and it is moving forward with
great strides. As I already mentioned, Linda and I have traveled a lot this year,
including to other states. I’ll tell you: There are other jurisdictions that wish they
had a strategic plan. We are setting a great example with ours, and we are right on
track to achieve our goals.
on each.

The strategic plan outlines five priority areas. Let me briefly update you
Number one: Improve the membership experience.

Many of our lodges have taken this priority to heart. They’re spending
more time on investigations, and really getting to know applicants. They’re
focusing on the things that get their brethren excited, whether it’s more social
events or community service projects. They’re figuring out ways to help Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts feel welcome right away. To those lodges, keep up
the good work.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

47

But I’d like to add this: Most Worshipful Nagel introduced “Coming
Home” to us last year, which showed all of us the importance of member outreach.
I think that we still need to focus on that outreach programming. A lot of lodges
are doing it. But many are not. Get ahold of lost brethren; check on their wellbeing and invite them back to lodge. We have sworn an obligation to care for
them. Don’t let them down.
Number two: Masonic education.
Our jurisdiction is blessed with resources, and one of the areas that we
see this most is in our Masonic education. Our brethren have access to tremendous
resources, and with the strategic plan, we will continue to expand this. Coming
soon, we will offer informational DVDs for Fellow Crafts and Master Masons;
new and improved resources for prospect education, and a new and improved
candidate coaching program. And of course, we continue to host wonderful
educational events, including a brand-new International conference on Latin
American Freemasonry this coming December. In 2012, we will also hold two
California Masonic Symposia for the first time – one north in San Francisco and
one south in Pasadena.
Number three: Leadership and management.
All of our leadership retreats are going very well. Our members are
getting more out of these leadership programs, and they’re able to return to
their lodges and apply what they’ve learned. We introduced a new treasurers’
component this year. I was able to attend the inspectors spring conference, and the
energy of the brothers assembled there was really something special. Our retreats
have improved with every year, and under the strategic plan, they will continue
to do so.
In my travels this year, a number of jurisdictions asked me for copies
of our wardens’ program. It was a reminder of how fortunate we are to have the
resources for these programs. It was also a reminder of how proud we should be
of the good work we’re doing here in California. We are setting an example for
Masonry throughout the United States.
While we’re on the subject of leadership, I want to issue a personal
challenge to our fraternity’s leaders – present and future. This year, Linda
and I met many fine people throughout our state, both men and women. And
because of it, we got to learn about our California lodges and members from a
firsthand perspective.
It’s a big state, and the obstacles and triumphs in one corner of it can
be vastly different from 10 or 20 miles away, never mind several hundred miles.
Traveling in the field and meeting members the old-fashioned way, face to face,
has given me a greater understanding of how the lodges are doing in their parts
of the state.

48

Proceedings of the

Here’s my challenge to our leaders: Sure, you can sit down and read a
report. But until you get out and talk to the lodges, until you see the communities
firsthand, you don’t get the full picture. Get out in the field. Shake hands with
people. Meet them one-on-one and give them your sincere attention. Really listen
to their stories. Our fraternity is based on an ideal of equality among all men. Let’s
show our membership that we, their leaders, are walking the talk. Show that you
are accessible and respectful to all of our members.
Number four: Beyond the lodge.
This priority encompasses a lot of new programs. Today, I’ll just address
one: the ongoing goal to rebuild our Masonic youth orders.
Overall, I think it’s going very well. We’ve opened up a good dialogue
with the adult leadership; they know that if they ever need assistance, all they
have to do is pick up the phone. And thanks to brethren stepping up to the plate
to be adult leaders, DeMolay chapters are blossoming and reopening throughout
the state.
That said, there are plenty of youth – particularly in the bethels of Job’s
Daughters and the assemblies of Rainbow for Girls – that need our help. They’re
trying hard and they’re maintaining their numbers, but before they can blossom,
they need lodges and members to step up to the plate. Consider this a call to
action: Get out there and visit our youth orders. Go to their meetings, get involved
as adult advisors, and show them that you believe in them. These young people
are our future. Show them that we’re standing by them, ready to offer our support
and encouragement.
On the subject of youth, I’m pleased to note that this was the third year
of Masons4Mitts, and our most successful yet. Northern California lodges and
Masons raised more than $51,000 to provide baseball gloves for boys and girls in
the Junior Giants program. It’s a great program, and a wonderful demonstration
of Masons supporting young people in the community.
And the fifth and final priority area: Philanthropy.
I’m proud to announce that the California Masonic Foundation launched
the Investment in Success scholarship program this year, a new scholarship for
youth that demonstrate extraordinary character and drive. The Foundation is also
forging new partnerships between school districts and communities. Behind all
this good work are dozens of our brethren, who are volunteering their time and
energy to lead community advisory councils throughout the state.
But that’s not all. Earlier this year, the Grand Lodge officers and I dedicated
the new Masonic Center for Youth and Families. The new center, located here in
San Francisco, is an expansion of the fraternity’s commitment to serve children in
a needed, meaningful, and innovative way. The center serves youth ages 4 to 17
struggling with behavioral, academic, emotional, or social difficulties. For those

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

49

of you who are not familiar with the center, it’s an example of true vision and
leadership. The program model is based on research and recommendations from
some of the world’s finest youth psychological centers, including the Anna Freud
Centre in London. We have brought together great minds in every aspect of youth
psychology, and enabled them to collaborate to a degree that is almost unheard
of elsewhere in the United States. As a result, you won’t find this range or caliber
of services under one roof anywhere else in the country. We are the only ones
doing this. And around the world, a lot of people are watching. By opening the
Masonic Center for Youth and Families, our fraternity is setting a new precedent
in the field of youth psychology. At the same time, we are providing help that is
desperately needed by children and families throughout California.
THE BY YOUR SIDE PROJECT
There’s one more part of this year that I want to share with you.
At the beginning of our year, Linda and I had this little idea to help cancer
patients. We decided to raise money to put more oncology nurses into California
medical centers. We named the project By Your Side, and set a goal for $200,000.
I thought, if we can get that, that’ll really be something. Well, we’ve nearly
doubled it. To date, we’ve raised more than $385,000. The participation from
lodges has been overwhelming – as of today, we have 76% lodge participation
– far and away, the highest participation we’ve ever had for a Grand Master’s
Project. That’s outstanding. In May, we presented a check for $50,000 to the City
of Hope, which will certify 50 oncology nurses. And let me tell you: That’s just
the beginning. Going forward, we hope to certify 20 to 25 more nurses every year
through California oncology associations.
I’m so proud and so pleased at the lodges and the brethren that have
stepped up, and gone above and beyond. Linda and I have heard of programs
at lodges all throughout California: Lodges that had dieticians come in during
Cancer Awareness Month; lodges that went to their local hospitals and invited
nurses and doctors to come speak during Nurse Oncology Month. Some of these
programs are still ongoing.
As the saying goes, we all know someone who’s been affected by cancer.
At every lodge I visited, somebody came up to me to share a story. The point is,
you all gave so much more than financial support for this project. You opened
your hearts for it.
As one quick for-instance – I received a DVD a few months ago from
Division VIII, showing highlights from an event that the district planned and
hosted as a group effort. After months of preparation, 16 lodges came together on
June 28. They gathered almost 250 attendees for a candlelight service honoring
those fighting cancer, those who have survived cancer, and those who have lost

50

Proceedings of the

their battle. It was an emotional and a powerful example of a community coming
together to support those whose lives have been touched by cancer. At the same
time, they raised $7,000 for By Your Side – funds that will go towards helping
thousands of others.
This year exceeded my expectations in many ways, but none more so
than seeing brethren and lodges put aside their differences and come together
for this cause. You showed the world what this fraternity is capable of when we
work together. Because of the way you pulled together, you made By Your Side
a success. California will have 50 more oncology nurses this year, and hundreds
more in the years to come. The program is not over. We hope to continue By Your
Side for 10 years, maybe more. Just think how many nurses we can certify. Those
nurses will touch the lives of thousands of cancer patients and their families. And
it’s all because of you.
As Masons, we often talk about making the world a better place. We talk
about making a difference in our communities. That is what this project is doing.
We are reaching people during their darkest hour, and giving them hope, and
encouragement, and someone to lean on. This cause means the world to thousands
of cancer patients and their families in California. And it means the world to Linda
and me. From the bottom of our hearts, thank you.
IN CLOSING
To continue the spirit of thanksgiving, I would like to close by thanking
those who made this year as Grand Master unforgettable.
First and foremost, thank you to our lodge leaders and brethren for your
dedication to our craft.
To our Inspectors, thank you for your continued support of our lodges
and your support of me and my vision.
To all Committee and Board members, thank you for your commitment,
and countless hours on behalf of our lodges.
To this year’s Grand family: It has been an honor. I want everyone here
to know, I am extremely proud of my officers. They were just great. They traveled
and worked hard and mixed and mingled, and were true friends to Linda and me
all the way. I mean it when I say that I couldn’t have asked for a better group of
people. You are family in a very real sense of the word.
Special thanks must go to my Deputy, Frank Loui, and his lady, Jeanie.
Linda and I have enjoyed every minute of our time together. We know you’ll do
great things in your year.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

51

To our Grand Wardens, thank you for your counsel and for always being
there for us.
Once again, to our Grand Treasurer, thank you for all of the great work
that you have contributed to ensure our financial health. Our craft is forever
indebted to you for your fine stewardship.
To our Grand Secretary and his entire staff, thank you for keeping
our jurisdiction running smoothly, and continuing to elevate the quality of our
programs. We are lucky to have you. At the beginning of this year, Linda and I
took a picture with the staff as a token of our appreciation. Sure enough, all year
long, they have gone above and beyond the call of duty. Anything we asked, they
got it done – and the whole time, they have been most, most gracious. They’re the
behind-the-scenes workers that aren’t acknowledged as often as they should be,
and I’ll tell you, they are tremendous.
I’d like to give special recognition to my Grand Marshal, a long-time
friend, Michael Stovall, and his wife, Denise, for their excellent assistance all year
long. And a special thanks to my Grand Orator, Loyal Stark, and his wife, Joan,
for filling in as Grand Marshal when Worshipful Mike and Denise could not make
it up North. Once a Marshal, always a Marshal, I guess.
And to my wife, Linda, thank you for caring and sharing in all of my
endeavors. You have been my best friend, confidant, secretary, and driver. Your
encouragement and support has meant the world to me. I love you dearly.
Brethren, thank you for this year. Thank you for your trust in me. Thank
you for the conversations. Thank you for the questions. Thank you for reminding
me of the best part of this fraternity: all of the extraordinary individuals that
compose it. I have been honored to be your Grand Master, and I am immensely
proud of all the good that we have accomplished together. Thank you.

Respectfully submitted,
William J. Bray III, Grand Master

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2011/2012 Grand Lodge Budget
Frank Loui, Deputy Grand Master

At the 2010 Annual Communication, the brethren approved the per capita
proposal that I submitted. I am very grateful for the support. Since that time,
I have been refining the budget while monitoring current income and expenses
as well as our membership activity. I have discussed the budget further with the
Senior and Junior Wardens at our retreats over the last two years. I have also
worked with the Grand Lodge Finance Committee, our Grand Treasurer, Grand
Secretary and finance staff. All of this collaboration has resulted in the budget I
now place before you for consideration at the upcoming Annual Communication.
The revenue for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,548,440, which
is higher than last year’s budgeted revenue by approximately $14,000. Of this
revenue, $1,842,222 is from per capita. The billable membership is projected to
be 54,183. The final audited membership numbers will not be available for several
weeks, but it appears that the actual will be close to this projection. Application fees
are projected based on 2,400 applications. The distribution policy for withdrawals
from our investments is based on 4.5% of the average Grand Lodge endowment
over the last five years. The dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center will be
$58,037 based on the profits of the corporation for the fiscal year ended October
31, 2010. This dividend is $15,000 more than last year due to improved efficiencies
from the garage automation. Other income includes revenue from a grant from
the California Masonic Foundation, and reimbursements from investments and
the Masonic Service Bureau. These revenue sources are explained further in the
enclosed materials.
Expenses for the upcoming fiscal year are projected to be $2,523,270.
Fraternal expenses, which include expenses for the Annual Communication,
officers, inspectors, awards, dues, and lodge insurance, total $748,299 and are
approximately $15,000 less than last year’s budget. Appropriations expenses for
Grand Lodge Committees and Programs are $492,829, which is approximately
$16,000 less than last year’s budget. General and Administrative expenses are
$1,282,143, which is approximately 4% more than last year mainly due to a 2.5%
increase in wages and 12% increase in health care insurance premiums. Reserving
approximately $8,000 for depreciation, our projected net revenue after expenses
is $17,181.
Though our final membership report has yet to be audited and distributed,
it is clear that interest in Freemasonry continues to grow. Our lodges are busier
conferring degrees than any other time in the last 30 years. Our members are
asking for growth and improvement in the area of masonic education, philanthropy,
the application and investigation process, candidates coaching, and the entire
membership experience. We are looking for ways to expand our positive impact

70

Proceedings of the

beyond the lodge and into our communities throughout the state. Our strategy
with the budget has been to keep cost increases at a minimum without reducing
services or programs. I am proud to say, that with the help and input from a lot of
our members and professional staff, we have achieved that. I thank you, again, for
your previous support and ask for your support now as we consider this budget
for our coming fiscal year.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Fiscal Year 2011/2012
Frank Loui, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue source has been per-capita and
degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates investment income. To better
manage those monies, a four and a half-percent spending policy has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year
valuation to ensure the preservation of the fund principle. The Grand Lodge may have other income like interest on
bank accounts and other financial instruments from time to time. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included
in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for those
purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to
Grand Lodge by all applicants for degrees and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different service
bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for those expenses. The Grand Lodge also manages the
investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of those services. The Grand Lodge is
the sole shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of the corporation.

Installation Address

Frank Loui
Grand Master of Masons in California, 2011-2012
My Brothers and friends, it is impossible to express my feelings of
appreciation for the high honor that has been conferred upon me by you, the
Masons of California, in electing me as your Grand Master. It is with humility
and gratitude that I accept the responsibility you have given me. I vow to do all
within my power to further the principles of Freemasonry and uphold the Laws
of our Grand Lodge.
I wish to acknowledge and thank my installing team this morning.
Kudos to them for a job well done. Each one of these three gentlemen has been an
influence in my Masonic career: MW Allen B. Gresham, whom I had the pleasure
of serving in 1996-1997 as Senior Grand Steward; MW David R. Doan, who also
served MW Gresham’s Grand Family, and who, eight years later, appointed me
Senior Grand Deacon; and MW William F. Stovall, who is currently my Boss, as
I serve as his Personal Representative and General Secretary at the San Francisco
Scottish Rite. Each of these men has shaped my Masonic journey, and they play a
big part in why I stand before you today.
I would like to congratulate the Grand Lodge Officers (elected and
appointed) who have been installed for the ensuing Grand Lodge year.
The progressive line officers have been very busy preparing for the
upcoming year and have worked diligently on your behalf to ensure that we move
this great Fraternity of ours forward while continuing to be effective leaders. We
are ready and excited to support our lodges in all of their endeavors.
I must thank all of our Past Grand Masters for their excellent leadership
and foresight. They have steered the course that brought our jurisdiction to its
present day. Each and every one of them has shown the vision, wisdom, concern
and compassion of a great leader. Their successes have enabled us to set our goals
equally as high. I know that we can count on each of them for guidance. Thank
you from the bottom of my heart for your support and dedication.
I would also like to extend our support to all Concordant and Appendant
Masonic Bodies as well as our youth groups. Your success is our success, and
we stand by, ready to help. Working as a team, there is no doubt that we can all
prosper and succeed.
As we embark upon a new Grand Lodge year, we will continue to work
towards the goals outlined in the Masons of California strategic plan. As you
may recall, in the spring of 2010 we asked all of you to share your visions for
the fraternity. Over the past year, we created a five-year strategic plan that fulfills
your vision. It can be summed up in three words: educate, engage, excel. We

80

Proceedings of the

are already making great strides. Our Boards, committees, and staff have begun
developing and distributing new resources for lodges, and will continue to do so
in the year ahead.
But I want to remind you that this plan began as a fraternity-wide effort,
and it will only succeed as a fraternity-wide effort. We need the commitment of
every lodge. Masters and wardens: If you haven’t already, now is the time to
align your lodge with the plan’s priorities and objectives. Masonry has a long and
distinguished history in California, and we have the privilege and responsibility
of carrying it forward into the 21st century. Let’s work together to honor
that responsibility.
My theme for this Grand Lodge year is Connect Communicate Commit
(the 3 “C”s). Our fraternity was built on the idea of community, and it has thrived
through the power of connection – the bonds of fellowship, the community of
fraternal family. Throughout history, we have maintained strong ties outside our
lodge buildings, too. When California was being settled, Masonic lodges were
among the first establishments. They were pillars of their communities, and they
took their responsibility very seriously. Many lodges still do. Today, men still join
Masonry precisely because of our legacy of community service.
But in some cases, this community connection has been lost. Some lodges
are no longer in the habit of reaching out to their neighbors. Some hardly ever
leave the lodge. With that in mind, I want us to get out of our lodge buildings and
connect with our communities this year. Introduce yourself to your neighbors. Ask
how you can help. Let’s all make a commitment to strengthen our communities.
It’s up to every lodge, and every one of us.
As a whole fraternity, one way we’ll Connect, Communicate, and
Commit is through my Grand Master’s Project, a partnership with Raising A
Reader. With your support, we can turn the page for child literacy in our state.
By the end of third grade, a child’s reading skills determine his ability to
learn and succeed for the rest of his life. Many U.S. states even use these literacy
levels to project how many prisons they’re going to need 20 years down the line.
Well, California currently ranks 49th in child literacy.
To make a difference, our fraternity has partnered with Raising A Reader,
one of the largest and most successful literacy programs in the nation. Raising A
Reader provides each child and family with high-quality books, and then works
with parents to build the language and literacy experiences at home that their child
needs to succeed at school.
Raising A Reader has already helped more than 800,000 children
nationwide. We plan to bring this program to those who need it most: kindergartners
in California’s lowest-performing public schools, who are at the highest risk for
educational failure.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

81

As Masons, we can make a profound difference in child literacy, and
change the lives of thousands of vulnerable children.
In closing, I would like to thank my wife Jeanie. Without her support this
would have been very hard to accomplish. She has been by my side every step of
the way during this fantastic journey. Our family has also been very patient and
understanding, as we have had to miss some celebrations these past three years,
with one more year to go. Thank you for your support and understanding.
And now, I’d like to leave you with one last reminder of my theme:
Connect Communicate Commit. We have a big year ahead of us. Let’s
push ourselves outside the comfort zone of our lodge buildings and into our
communities. Let’s work together to position our fraternity to grow and thrive.
And, by turning the page for child literacy in California, let’s change the lives of
thousands of vulnerable children.
Brethren all: Again, thank you for your confidence.
Now, let’s get to work.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2012-2013
John F. Lowe, Senior Grand Warden

As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2012 to fund the Grand Lodge fiscal year for the period from
November 1, 2012 through October 31, 2013.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked with
the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand Lodge staff to
develop projections of the income and expenses necessary during the 2013 fiscal
year to operate the Grand Lodge, fund our strategic priorities and initiatives, and to
provide programs and services to our lodges and members. We have incorporated
in our planning the important priorities that our members have expressed and
endorsed in the strategic planning process. I have had the opportunity to share
this proposal with the hundreds of Junior and Senior Wardens who attended the
Wardens Retreats this year and their input has been very important in this process.
In order to establish an appropriate per-capita assessment, I have prepared
the budget that was distributed earlier. You will notice that the total expenses are
only 2.0% higher than the proposed 2011/2012 budget prepared by our Deputy
Grand Master. While we have managed to keep expense increases to a minimum,
there are certain factors that will increase the per capita.
•

Membership loss. We project a total loss of 1,625 members, which
represents a loss in revenue of $55,250. This factor taken alone, we would
need to increase per capita $1.05 to make up for the loss in members.

•

Insurance. We estimate that premiums for our lodge insurance will
increase by 3.1% or just over $3,000.

•

Personnel costs. Wages will increase by 3.0%. Together with the health
care expense increase of 10%, personnel expenses will increase by 3.7%.

•

Inflation. Costs for a number of non-labor items are expected to
rise by 2%.

86

Proceedings of the
There are a few factors, however, that will help reduce per capita.
•

Nob Hill Dividend. We project that the dividend from the Nob Hill
Masonic Center will be $100,000, which is $42,000 more than the
previous year.

•

Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that can be held
to last year’s levels without any factor for inflation. You will notice
that the expenses in many categories are nearly the same as the budget
presented by the Deputy Grand Master.

As a result of this increased dividend and our work to contain costs, we
can balance the budget with a per capita of $35.00. While this may seem that the
per capita is increasing, lodges will actually pay less per capita than the previous
year. In the budget presented by the Deputy Grand Master for the 2011/12 Fiscal
Year, the total per capita collected is projected to be $1,842,222. This proposal for
the following year, projects that the total per capita collected will be $1,839,495,
which is nearly $3,000 less than the previous year.
We still live in difficult economic times. Even though we are conferring
more degrees than any other time in the last 30 years, our membership continues to
decline. But we can overcome these challenges with smart planning and creative
thinking. In adopting this per capita proposal, we will insure that the Grand Lodge
can continue to provide the level of programs and services that will be needed
during the period of growth in our organization. I appreciate all of the assistance
I have received in developing this proposal and I look forward to your support.

John F. Lowe, Senior Grand Warden
Revenue Assumptions
PER CAPITA
There are several factors that affect per capita, membership levels and inflation being the
major factors. The membership analysis for the 2012/2013 fiscal year projects a total loss in
membership of 1,626 members. While this is one of the lowest loss of members in decades,
the membership decline will result in lost revenue of $55,284 or $1.05 in additional per capita.
Overall inflation is projected to be approximately 2.0%. This will result in additional per capita
of approximately $0.75. All other things being equal, the per capita would have to be increased
by $1.80 to $35.80 in order to make up for lost members and inflation. Due to improvements in
the Nob Hill Masonic Center operations, the Nob Hill Masonic Center dividend will result in a
revenue increase of $42,000 or $0.80 in per capita reduction. Because of the dividend offset
the proposed per capita will only increase by $1.00 to $35.00.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The general assessment of the financial aspect of your Grand Lodge is
that we continue to deal successfully with a struggling economy, a challenging
employment market and very volatile investment markets.
Each of you is aware of the state of the general economy and the
investment markets over the last year. While those conditions affect the Grand
Lodge’s financial activities, just as they do everyone else, the Grand Lodge has
survived them well, through the hard work and diligent efforts of our efficient
staff, the Grand Lodge Officers, Board members, and Committeemen. Budgets
have been tightened and closely monitored. Efforts to conserve and curtail
expenses have been effectively applied by everyone involved.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee has, yet once again, intensified
their customary diligence over the Grand Lodge’s investment portfolio. They have
given special effort and consideration to the continuation of current economic and
investment conditions. The result is some studied changes in the make-up and
allocation of the portfolio to better reflect the economic and investment conditions
going forward. They continue to recommend the reduction in the percentage of
distribution to be taken from the portfolio for current budgeting purposes from
the traditional 5% per year to a 4.5% level, a move that has been adopted by the
Grand Lodge and each of the other entities participating in that investment pool.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee continues to apply their considerable
expertise to the risk management of the Grand Lodge to keep the various entities
well protected at favorable and competitive premium costs.
The Finance and the Audit Committees perform their respective duties
with business-like efficiency of which any organization would be proud.
The dedicated and efficient financial staff in the Grand Lodge office
continues to provide unexcelled service in the management and reporting on the
financial affairs of the organization. The ability of the Grand Lodge and other
entities to weather the financial storm as they have is a testimony to the disciplined
and conservative manner in which they have conducted their financial affairs for
many years, particularly in the good times. It has allowed the various entities
to continue providing uninterrupted programs and services to their constituents,
without any budget-induced lay-offs of staff and with balanced budgets all
the while.
You can be very proud of the work that has been done by all those
involved in the financial affairs of our Fraternity, as I am, and you should offer
them your thanks. The detailed information I am going to give you today is for
a nine-month period from the start of this current fiscal year, November 1, 2010,

92

Proceedings of the

through July 31, 2011. I will compare that information to like data for the same
period a year earlier. This report is already posted on the Member Center website
under Forms/162nd Annual Communication. It will continue to be available to
you there until the official proceedings of this Communication are published.
Those Proceedings will contain the customary audited financials for the entire
fiscal year. It should be noted that this partial-year information has been prepared
internally by our fine financial staff and has not been audited.
As of July 31, 2011, your Grand Lodge had assets of $7,740,315 and
liabilities of $4,092,630 for Total Net Assets of $3,647,685. Those assets were
some 1.07% higher than at the end of our October 31, 2010 fiscal year. Keep
in mind that most of the assets you might attach to the California Grand Lodge
are not actually owned by the Grand Lodge itself and do not appear in these
numbers. I am referring to major assets such as this facility, which is owned
by the California Masonic Memorial Temple Corp., and our homes in Union
City and Covina, which are owned by the Masonic Homes of California, both
separate corporations.
The last several years have been difficult and volatile ones in the
investment markets. The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge were up 13.8%
for the 12-month period ending July 31, 2011. The annualized return for the
prior three year period was +2.9%, and the return was +3.5% annualized for the
prior five-year period. Your Grand Lodge continues to operate in the black on a
year-to-year basis. For the nine months ending July 31, 2011, the total income
was $1,798,201 while total expenses were $1,707,180. That income is some
1.2% higher than the comparative period last year. Expenses for the nine-month
period ending July 31, 2011 were slightly higher than the same period last year, a
difference largely due to the timing of various expenses. While the Net Excess as
of July 31, 2011, of income over expense is some $91,021, it should be noted that
approximately 20% of the total year’s expenses occur in the last three months of
the fiscal year. The current projection is that the Grand Lodge will end the fiscal
year on October 31, with a slight surplus.
The nine-month expenses were divided in the following manner: 20.2%
for Fraternal matters (such as this Annual Communication, travel expenses of
the Elected and Appointed Grand Lodge Officers and Ritual Committee, and the
insurance for the constituent lodges), 26.2% for Appropriations and Programs
(such as various lodge support Committees, the Freemason magazine, and
Committees such as Policy, Jurisprudence, Investment and Trial Review), and
53.1% for General and Administrative items (such as salaries and benefits,
accounting and auditing, investment management fees, legal fees and general
office operations).
I must again comment on the concern and diligence which your Executive
Committee and the financial staff bring to the monitoring of the actual income and
expenses versus the budget. The numbers are compiled and studied by all parties

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

93

in great detail on a monthly basis, as the year progresses. You should know that
any surplus at the end of the fiscal year is not carried over into the next year, but
rather it is permanently transferred to the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund. The
result is that each Grand Master starts his year with a zero balance, with only the
budget for that year to work with.
I again offer a word of caution about the future. Many of our budgeting
processes use projected investment withdrawal amounts that are the result of
averaging investment values for the prior five years. That policy has served us
very well in that it smooths the ups and downs of the investment markets from
quarter to quarter. However, that five-year averaging process continues to include
the difficult markets of 2007 and 2008 creating a continuing dampening effect on
the calculated withdrawal amounts. In other words, we are not out of the woods
yet in our outlook.
I again pay tribute to the many highly dedicated brothers who serve on
the various Boards and Committees of this Grand Lodge and its related entities for
the extraordinary amount of time, energy, dedication and hard work they devote
to the business and fraternal affairs of our California Masonic community. Each
of you should seek them out and give them a hearty “Thank You” for the work
they do.
The dedication, efficiency and hard work of the Grand Lodge staff
deserve special comment. Under the able leadership of our Grand Secretary,
Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, this group of talented men and women perform
exceptional service for your Grand Lodge, often with little, certainly not enough,
recognition and appreciation. Our Grand Lodge organization and administration is
the model among sister Grand Lodges and it is due largely to our Grand Secretary
and his staff. Please join me in thanking them.
And finally, my brethren, as you know, I have chosen to not stand for
re-election for next year, believing that five years in most any job is long enough.
It is with a great deal of comfort that I turn the job over to Most Worshipful
Holsinger, who I expect you will elect tomorrow. He has served in this position
before, so all I have been doing for the past five years is keeping the seat warm for
him. He comes to the office experienced and well qualified.
I could not begin to thank each of you enough for having allowed me
to work with you and for you during these past five years. I have been extremely
proud and honored to be a part of the California Masonic Grand Lodge team.
Respectfully submitted,
Glenn D. Woody, Grand Treasurer

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present this, my fourth report, to you as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
As of today there are 338 chartered lodges in our jurisdiction, including
two lodges Under Dispensation and five research lodges.
Our membership at the beginning of the fiscal year was 58,886. For the
2011 fiscal year, we had 2,340 gains, another increase over than the previous
year; and 3,628 losses, approximately 500 less than the previous year. The ending
membership on June 30, 2011 was 57,250. While we still recorded a net loss of
1,636 members, this is the smallest loss of members in this jurisdiction since
1966. It is also worth noting that our lodges raised 1,402 Master Masons in this
year, the highest number since 1988 and the most Master Masons conferred per
lodge since 1977. A more detailed report of membership activity, together with a
number of Lodge by-law amendments, life memberships, and veteran’s awards is
included in my written report to be distributed later.
Summary of Accomplishments
Because of the amount of business that will be included in my report,
I cannot elaborate on all of the important accomplishments of this year, but I
want to highlight a few. In 2011, we held the first combined Secretaries and
Treasurers Retreats. Nearly 400 secretaries, assistant secretaries, and treasurers
attended these retreats. It was a huge success and together we made tremendous
progress is improving our understanding of the business in which we are engaged
and learning how to work together as a large team driven by the same mission
and vision.
This year marked a significant turning point in the implementation of
our online membership database, iMember. As of July 1, 2011, 95% of our lodges
were using the iMember system. It might take us a few more months to get the
remaining 16 lodges online, but for now, I want to thank all the lodges for their
efforts to work together to provide this level of team work.
As the Editor of the California Freemason magazine, it was my honor
earlier this year to accept four awards on your behalf. The Association of
Media and Publishing is a trade organization made up of more than a thousand
membership organizations in the United States. These organizations include

98

Proceedings of the

civic organizations like Rotary International, professional organizations like the
American Bar Association, charities like Habitat for Humanity, and university
alumni organizations. Each year, awards are given for excellence in print and
online publishing. There are three top awards that are given in several categories;
a gold for the best publication, a silver for the second, and bronze for the third,
much like the Olympics. This year the California Freemason magazine won
two silver and two bronze awards for general excellence, best magazine design,
best magazine redesign, and best mobile application. Much of the credit for this
recognition is due to our incredible team of editors, writers, photographers, and
graphic artists and I thank them all.
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility as the Grand Secretary to keep the Grand Master
informed on matters pertaining to the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges
and to present to you in the form of a motion the recognition of certain Grand
Lodges which meet our criteria therefore. We are aided in the evaluation of Grand
Lodges seeking recognition by the Commission on Information for Recognition, a
committee of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons of North America. We
are honored in California that our very own Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful
M. William Holsinger, is the president of that important Commission.
Two Grand Lodges have written to our Grand Lodge seeking
mutual recognition.
The Grand Lodge of Cyprus
The Grand Lodge of Cyprus was formed from six Lodges working
under the auspices of the Grand Lodge of Greece on January 15, 2006. Formal
consecration of the Grand Lodge was held on October 8, 2006 by the Grand Lodge
of Greece, the Grand Lodge of Austria, and the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania.
The National Grand Lodge of Azerbaijan
The National Grand Lodge of Azerbaijan was chartered and constituted
on December 8, 2008, by the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia and the
Grand Lodge of Russia in the City of Baku, Azerbaijan. This Grand Lodge was
formed from a Lodge chartered by the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia
in 2002, a Lodge chartered by the Grand Lodge of Turkey in 2003, and a Lodge
chartered by the Grand Lodge of Russia in 2003.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

99

It is the opinion of the Commission on Information for Recognition
that both of these Grand Lodges meet the requirements for recognition.
Therefore, I move that the Grand Lodge of California grant mutual recognition
to the Grand Lodge of Cypress and the National Grand Lodge of Azerbaijan.
Motion ADOPTED.
In 2009, the Grand Lodge of California granted concurrent jurisdiction
to the Grand Lodge of Iran in exile in California. Since that time, lodges under the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Iran in exile have been meeting in this state. On
August 15, 2011, the Grand Lodge received a request from the Supreme Council
of the Thirty-Third and Last Degree of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of
Freemasonry for Iran in exile to allow Masons residing in California to become
members of the Iranian Scottish Rite. Under our law, this permission is granted
by approving the Constitution and Bylaws of the requesting organization. The
Constitution and Bylaws of the Iranian Supreme Council have been submitted
and are in proper order. I note that a Mason must speak Farsi (the language of
Iran) in order to belong to the Iranian Scottish Rite. Because of this requirement,
this action should have little impact on the established Scottish Rites in this state.
Therefore, I move that the Grand Lodge of California approve the Constitution
and Bylaws of the Supreme Council of the Thirty-Third and Last Degree
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry for Iran in exile.
Motion ADOPTED.
Dispensations and Charters
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Golden
Compasses Research Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter.
Grand Master Nagel granted a dispensation to this Lodge on August 31, 2010.
In reviewing the records of the Lodge and from the information provided by
the District Inspector, it has been determined that Golden Compasses Research
Lodge has met the requirements of the petition. Accordingly I move that a Charter
be issued to Golden Compasses Research Lodge U.D. and that it be entered
into the Registry of this Grand Lodge as Golden Compasses Research Lodge.
Motion ADOPTED.
Earlier this month, Grand Master Bray issued a five page report outlining
the background, specification of charges, future plans, and a resolution concerning
the revocation of the charter of Covina Lodge No. 334. Section 813.040 of the
California Masonic Code provides the grounds for revocation of a lodge charter.
One is the neglect or violation of the duties imposed upon the Lodge in its charter
and in the Code. Another is the neglect or violation of the duties imposed upon the
Lodge Secretary. Grand Master Bray’s report outlined 21 specific charges against
Covina Lodge for the neglect or violation of the duties imposed upon the lodge
and 10 charges that the Secretary neglected or violated his duties. This action

100

Proceedings of the

by the Grand Master was preceded by several years of continuous work with
the lodge to correct its serious administrative, financial, and ritual deficiencies.
The lodge charter was suspended by Grand Master Nagel in 2010 and again by
Grand Master Bray later that year. On March 28, 2011, Grand Master Bray met
personally with the officers of the lodge to discuss their situation. The officers
agreed to meet some minimum standards by July 1, 2011. The Grand Master gave
them notice at that time that failure to meet these minimum standards would result
in the recommendation to revoke the lodge charter. Unfortunately the lodge was
not able to correct its problems, even with the help of the Inspector, the Assistant
Grand Lecturer, and the Grand Lodge Support Committee. At the August Stated
Meeting of Covina Lodge, the members present rejected a resolution to form a
committee to explore consolidation. Today the lodge does not have a willing and
capable team of officers, is incapable of conferring the three degrees of Masonry,
lacks a suitable program to coach and advance candidates, and is unable to correct
the administrative and financial problems that have existed in the lodge now
for several years. Therefore, I move that the Charter of Covina Lodge No. 334
be revoked; that the lodge be dissolved; that the Grand Secretary be directed to
preserve the remaining assets of the dissolved lodge for a new lodge in Covina;
and that, when this new lodge is issued a Charter in accordance with the Code, the
remaining assets of Covina Lodge No. 334 then in the possession of the Grand
Lodge be turned over to that newly chartered lodge for benefit of Freemasonry in
Covina. Motion ADOPTED.
Appreciation
As I conclude my report, I wish to extend my appreciation and gratitude
to the 338 lodge Secretaries and 189 Assistant Secretaries in this jurisdiction
whose dedicated work is the backbone of our lodges and our Grand Lodge.
I would also like to thank the District Inspectors and Assistant Grand
Lecturers who work so diligently with the Grand Secretary’s office on numerous
administrative matters throughout the year. Because I work so closely with them,
I see first hand the work of our Assistant Grand Lecturers and I am inspired by
their devotion to our craft.
I also work closely with the many boards and committees of the Grand
Lodge. In total, there were over 190 board and committee meetings during the
year. While I cannot take the time now to share with you the great work of all
of these leaders, allow me to take a moment to express my personal thanks to
Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee
on Jurisprudence. Most Worshipful Doan has provided a great deal of assistance
to the Grand Secretary’s office that, without any doubt, goes above and beyond
what anyone could even expect from a brother; and for his assistance, I am
very grateful.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

101

I have been given the great fortune to work with our Grand Treasurer,
the Very Worshipful Glenn Woody. He is an extraordinary colleague and a great
friend and I thank him for all of the truly excellent work he has done on behalf of
our fraternity. He is also a man of his word. He told me when he took the position
that he was going to serve five years and that is what he did. What I did not know
when he first told me that was how much I would learn from him over that time,
not just about finance and investments, but about being a man and a Mason. I will
always treasure the time we worked together and I look forward to many more
years of our friendship.
I am blessed to work with an incredible staff of men and women at the
Grand Lodge Office, including our offices in Covina and Union City, whose
service to our Grand Lodge is fueled by the good work that each of you do every
day in your communities throughout the state and I thank them very much.
Finally, I wish to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful William J.
Bray III. Most Worshipful Bill has been an incredible leader for our Grand Lodge.
He knows how to inspire people to do their very best. Because of his kind and
generous nature and his devotion to the ideals of Freemasonry, he has helped me
build a stronger team in our office and he has added to my own perspective of
leadership and friendship. It has been an honor to work with you, Most Worshipful.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary
