Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Although I have only been in this position since May 1st, I feel well
entrenched in the duties of the office. I wish to thank Most Worshipful Bill for
having the confidence in my abilities and for appointing me to the position.
But more importantly, I would ask that each of you help me thank Very
Worshipful Paul Hennig for his tireless stewardship and service to our craft. Very
Worshipful Paul has been invaluable to this Jurisdiction for many many years. As
Inspector, AGL and Grand Lecturer, he was the driving force in what our ritual
is today. Always the consummate Ritualist, he imparted his passion for our ritual
demanding only the highest quality. Paul, you will be missed, and we thank you.
This year, with the addition of a tenth division, our Jurisdiction has
been easier to manage and our ten AGLs have also served our Craft in a most
outstanding manner. I wish to thank each of them for their talents and their
service. With the ever-changing landscape of our Ritual Corp, we unfortunately
say good-bye, but, with much thanks to Worshipful Bud Ramsey, AGL for
Division III and Worshipful David Almuth, AGL for Division IV. Dedicated and
loyal members of the ritual team, both have been exemplary in their efforts and
we wish them well in their newest endeavors. With every good-bye, there is also
a hello. And I am pleased to announce that Very Worshipful Frank Loui will be
appointing Worshipful Chuck Jeronimo to assume the duties of AGL for Division
III and Worshipful Ricky Lawler to assume the duties of AGL for Division IV. We
welcome them to the team and know they will be a huge asset to our Jurisdiction.
For budgetary reasons, there was no Ritual Competition held this past
year. I think it was an unfortunate loss for our lodges as well as the jurisdiction,
but I am pleased to announce that we have again found the dollars to fund this
worthwhile project and we will resurrect the competition for this coming year.
It has been decided that the competition will cover the 3rd degree from Opening
to the Junior Warden calling to Refreshment at the completion of the first
section. Part of the reason we are able to fund this endeavor this coming year, is
because we will save travel dollars due to the fact there will only be two levels
of competition. The first being within the district and the second, being within the
division. There will be no statewide level round. Since teams will only be judged
on ritual words and movements, with no subjective scoring, it was decided that
each team will carry their division score into the finals to be matched against the
other nine division winners. The team with the highest score will naturally be
named the state champion. I encourage every lodge to participate. The fact of
putting yourself into a competition mode, can only strengthen your ritual skills
and bring the officers closer as a cohesive unit.

126

Proceedings of the

To date, I have held six Schools of Instruction throughout our state. In
coordinating the calendars of our incoming Grand Master and our AGLs, I have
scheduled a Master Mason School of Instruction in every division this coming
year. I encourage all lodge leaders to determine the date within your division and
ensure that all officers and interested Master Masons attend these schools. It is
a great time to discuss our floor work and answer any questions you may have
regarding our ritual.
Our Inspector Academy continues to be a rousing success. I feel extremely
confident in saying that the IDA Committee is arming our new Inspectors with the
best training possible to assume the daunting task of their position. A huge thank
you goes to the Chairman, Wor. Randy Downey as well as every instructor on
the IDA team. Their talents are strengthening our Inspectoral Corp and I would
urge any interested Past Master to seek admission to the Academy. The training
received is invaluable.
Just a few personal thoughts. Our ritual is not the everything in Masonry,
but it is what sets us apart from every other Fraternal and Service organization.
Each of them do great work for their members and within the community, but it
is truly our Ritual that makes us who we are. If we believe this to be true, then we
owe it to every candidate that comes through our portals, the highest quality and
most professional ritual we can deliver. It can also be said the Lodges in and of
themselves exist for one purpose, to make Masons. Again, if we believe this to be
true, every officer must do his part to ensure our story is told with the dignity that
our ritual deserves. Although we are all volunteers, I hate to hear the term. Too
many of our officers hide behind the fact that we are volunteers, and their focus
on learning the ritual is haphazard at best. Once we volunteer, we have made a
commitment to our lodge and to each other and I would ask that no one dishonor
our ritual by being unprepared to deliver the best that our candidates deserve.
There are numerous lodges and many more of our officers that are performing
our ritual in the most outstanding manner. They are all to be commended for their
efforts. I ask each of you to look within your selves. If you are an officer in name
only, please break the cycle of poor ritual and assist us in ensuring that only the
highest quality will be accepted within our lodges. Help us ensure no one goes
away from a degree feeling just a little ashamed that we did not perform to our
potential. There is no greater Fraternity in the world than our Gentle Craft. Let’s
prove it each and every time we step onto the floor.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Finally, I was thrust upon you at the eleventh hour with the retiring of
Very Worshipful Paul. You had no say in my appointment. But, if I am fortunate
enough to have your trust and confidence and you decide I should continue, I
promise all the passion and commitment I can muster. I truly love our ritual and
I wish to impart to each of you what Masonry means to our ritual and what our
ritual means to Freemasonry.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Kenneth G. Nagel, PGM, Grand Lecturer

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Leonard B. Froomin
Before me are seated hundreds of individuals of a variety of ages, of
both genders, who were born in places far and near, who worship a religious
figure they refer to by a number of names, of different educational experiences,
and a phenomenal collection of interests. What has drawn them to this place at
this time?
The common thread that weaves them into one incredibly beautiful
fabric is their membership or interest in the Family of Freemasonry. With the
diversity I described, what could possibly bind them together? I can express my
opinion based on my life experience. We’ll see if you can agree.
The “thread” referred to previously is goodness. You are good people,
interested in doing good for others, building a good reputation, establishing a
good character, being a good example for others. You accomplish this in countless
ways. Let’s make a list of some of them: you’re good children, loving parents,
grandparents, aunts, and uncles, caring friends, confidants, supporters, benefactors
of charitable causes, attentive to those who are ill (are you ticking these off on
your fingers as each one applies to you?), hard workers, fair employers, followers
of the Golden Rule / the Ten Commandments, your Sunday school lessons – all of
the promises you made when you joined one of the organizations in our Masonic
Family. This list is very lengthy. Is there a way we could summarize? I can offer
this: Do your best! Be a good person!
But, a fabric does not consist of a single thread; each must be bound to
others. I have always been impressed when attending various groups in our Masonic
Family and listening to its ritualistic work. Every organization encourages – no,
requires – its members to give service to others who are in need. It is pointed out
that when we give to others we are lending to the Lord, and we all recognize that
God always pays his “debts.” Keep your eyes open in order that you will observe
every opportunity that presents itself and there will be an amazing number every
day. And just as you were rewarded with gold stars or happy faces early on in
school, your reward in later life will be a clear conscience, a smile and a “thank
you” from the person whose need you met, a peaceful night’s rest, and a variety of
recognition forms from your Masonic organization. I’m satisfied by a “Good job!,
Pops” from our youngest granddaughter. Go forth and satisfy yourself by serving
others and doing good.
What would the aforementioned earn for you? A good memory for all
who knew you or who were influenced by you. The rewards of a residence in
heaven throughout eternity. May God guide you to be good and to serve. Amen.

Session Prayers
Saturday Morning
Dear Lord: Thank you for giving us yet another day in our lives. It is
our responsibility to use it well. Help us to aid a person in need. Give us an
opportunity to be charitable. We promise to show our love for someone else. We
will lend a helping hand to one less strang than we are. We assure you that we will
offer a smile to strangers as well as to friends. Finally, we will observe all of our
vows taken at Your holy altar. We will do all this to give You joy that You created
us and gave us this day. Amen.
Saturday Afternoon
Potentate of our earth: We supplicate ourselves before You and entreat
You to do yet another favor for us all. Please advance the causes of Freemasonry
across the land. Help us to teach those not initiated into our brotherhood what we
stand for. Help them to realize we practice Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. Let
them know that our fundamental goal is to improve our communities in every way
we can. Inform them of the vast array of charitable causes our Masonic Family
supports with our donations of both money and volunteer hours. Please have them
know that our aim is to take good men and women and youths and aid them to
make themselves still better. Finally, Dear Lord, make them aware of the great
numbers of people throughout history and at the present time who they admire for
their character and contributions to humanity who were and are members of our
Masonic Family. Amen.

Grand Oration
My brothers, what an honor it is to address you this morning, as we are
gathered under that letter G and around the square and compass.
This great life of Masonry that gives us the opportunity to be a better
person, to associate with some of the finest brothers and leaders from throughout
the world and still meet on the level as true Masons.
Just look around you here today and observe those brothers that you
would not have known if it were not for that letter G, square and compass. I would
not have known these grand officers and their ladies and we would not have been
able to serve this magnificent Grand Lodge of California in a most successful
year. The success was made possible by you, the brothers of this Grand Lodge,
and the exemplary leadership of our Grand Master, Most Worshipful William J.
Bray III and his lady, Linda. Most Worshipful, you have inspired us with your
dedication, sacrifices and enthusiasm for our craft. On behalf of myself and these
Grand Lodge officers, we thank you so very much for the opportunity to serve
during this year. It has been an amazing experience that we will never forget.
All because of that letter G, square and compass. Symbols that wherever
you see them, whether on a ring, a lapel pin or on a building in a strange town,
there is an immediate bond of trust and comfort. These symbols that have
endured through the years, give us so much solace. Think about the craftsman of
antiquity, with pride, making his mark upon his work, and then to have the artifact
of that structure uncovered today, to bring to light again, that letter G, square
and compass.
There are thousands of eloquent words written about our gentle craft and
its place in the world today. We are very fortunate to have our own website and
the California Freemason magazine to enlighten us, inform us and to promote this
wonderful fraternity. There are many valuable programs provided by our Grand
Lodge for the betterment of Masonry and of ourselves in particular. Consider
our leadership training to assist lodge masters and wardens to successfully
and effectively lead our lodges. The relief provided by our Masonic Homes of
California, are products that have no equal in the care industry of today. The
innovative Masonic Center for Youth and Families. The thoughtful, integrative
care that understands the “whole child.” We are inspired by their motto “young
people don’t need labels, they need to be understood.”
Our Masonic youth groups that we say that we support, or do we? How
inspired we are to listen to the lesson of the robe in Job’s Daughters. The pride
instilled in us, as we witness the flag tribute given by a young Rainbow Girl. The
emotional tug we experience as we witness the ceremony of lights by a DeMolay.

136

Proceedings of the

These are some of the finest young people in the world today!!! We are
so very proud of them!!! I know that I am speaking to the choir, but unless you
sing the song, the melody will soon die.
We can have all of the programs in the world, all of the labors by so
many dedicated workers on behalf of our craft, but unless these efforts reach the
individual member, they are less than effective. Because of that letter G, square
and compass we have the opportunity to reflect upon our heritage of the past, to
accept the responsibility of the present and to commit ourselves to the obligation
of the future. These symbols impress within us a deep and lasting impression. The
true light of Masonry really depends upon what it means to you, what it means
to our brothers and our families. I mean, what does it really mean to you, right
in your heart? Not in titles, badges or honors, but in your innermost thoughts,
in the core of your being. Think about it and maybe we should ask the question
more often.
Through the years, I have asked many individuals this very same
question and here are some of their answers. What does Masonry mean to a nonMason? He stated that it is harmless, it presents no threat to anyone. It is amicable,
rarely is there any contention. This is a most noble characteristic, one that is not
appreciated like it should be by the brothers.
I asked a lady writer what was her view of Masons. She replied that it
demonstrates lessons in morality. It is a safe social association.
An experienced Mason stated that Masonry gives man a choice to choose
his friends. It is a family in a broad sense. The trickle down effect through father
and son, wife, daughter continues this way of life.
Another experienced Mason replied that Freemasonry represents support
in time of need. It is friendships, fraternalism, honesty and integrity; all precepts
missing in today’s society.
A Mason, a little younger gave this response. Masonry has been my
moral compass all of my adult life. Some of my closest friendships have come
from the people I have had the privilege to meet as a Mason.
A Mason of middle age replied that Masonry gives me self-respect,
makes me feel that i am useful to others, and places me closer to god. It is where
I should be, it is where I belong.
Another response was that it is a place for like minded people to come
together and make a difference for the good of communities and mankind.
It began as a fulfillment of family heritage and became membership in a
new family of good men and a way to serve both the community and the greater
good of all. When I asked the wives of Masons they responded:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

137

The day my husband joined the Masons, it opened up a new world
for both of us. We now had friends that have the same views, morals and plans
for the future as we did. Masonry is a bright spirit in a time of unrest in our
world. I would hope that we can make the world better by being part of the
Masonic family.
It is a place to learn, grow and contribute to the community. We can
make lasting friendships while achieving a common goal. Masonry means: family
history, friendships, commitment, striving for betterment. It represents values of a
high minded, caring fraternity of men; for the friendship and knowledge gained,
especially for men in retirement. It is a community of people to know, places to
go, support and friendship.
When I asked younger Masons, they responded: I am a member of a
brotherhood of good men. I am encouraged to live and support the values that I
believe in. Masonry encourages me to do the right thing, even though no one is
watching. I am asked to live by values and principles that I support and live by.
Masonry is the ethics in my life.
A young Mason: my lodge is a place where I can confidentially trust
every person and trust my family to be safe in their presence.
A young Mason’s wife stated: I have confidence that he is associating
with men of good will, someone we both can trust. It encourages him to be a better
role model for our son.
Most impressive response: Middle aged Mason, with a mobility challenge
stated that Masons are my 3:00 am friends. I know that whatever the hour, even at
3:00 am, that if I call for help, they will respond.
These are some very inspiring words, expressions of feelings and
thoughts by very sincere individuals. This is an exercise that I hope that you take
back to your lodge and see what they say to you and to each other. It is a ready
made inspirational message of what your brothers experience and what your lodge
can do. These words would mean nothing, were it not for that letter G, square
and compass.
As for me, I thank DeMolay for the virtues and lessons that molded
an impressionable teenager. DeMolay allowed me to associate with some of the
finest young men in the world. They are now responsible adults and many have
been led to that letter G, square and compass. A place where moral virtues are
taught and illustrated by honorable men. Those great men that we know, or have
known, that have been our mentors and our friends and protectors.
The story of my mother-in-law illustrates our Masonic value of trust.
When she was nine, her mother died. Her father worked for the railroad in
Winnemucca, Nevada, and had limited means to care for his children. The next
summer when she was ten and her brother was three, their father placed them on

138

Proceedings of the

a train and sent them to Ontario, Canada for the summer. As they were departing,
her father placed his Masonic pin on her lapel and assured her that she would
be cared for. Needless to say, they reached their destination, even with a change
of trains in Chicago, because the Masonic brothers of the railroad were their
protectors. This great Masonic fraternal family that pulls us out of an ordinary
existence and enables us to live a better life. It is a maker of friends, of brothers
and sisters among whom there is trust and friendship for the rest of our lives. It
is a producer of confidence, virtue and loyalty. It is a successful support group
for responsibility, ethics and justice in a world that does not always recognize
these virtues.
Again, just look around you and see all those wonderful, really good
brothers that you would not have known if not for that letter G, square and
compass. You are the men in the world who give life a special meaning because
you represent the best and highest ideals. You make a positive difference in the
life of someone every day!!!
Now, my brothers, my dear friends, may the spark of your spirit and
character, reach out and kindle the flame of others so that the light of this great
fraternity, this wondrous fraternal family, may burn brightly for many years in the
future.
God bless you, god bless this noble Grand Lodge of California and thank
you for being a Mason and my brother.
Respectfully submitted,
Loyal L. Stark, Grand Orator

Grand Master’s Recommendations
Grand Master Bray’s Recommendation No. 1
Provides Criminal Background Checks on Applicants
Today, more and more men are seeking out the privileges of Freemasonry.
The number of Entered Apprentice degrees conferred by our Lodges has
increased 81% since the year 2000. On average, our Lodges are conferring more
degrees than at any time since the 1970s. The pathway a man takes to apply for
the degrees of Masonry has changed considerably since that time. There was a
time when most applicants were known by members of the Lodge. They were
the relatives, colleagues and neighbors of existing members. Today, most men
make contact with a Lodge through the internet and are virtually unknown to
the members. Lodges take seriously the investigation process and some have
gone to great lengths to get to know a prospect well before ever handing him an
application. However, despite these best efforts, men with unacceptable criminal
records have been initiated, passed, and raised in our Lodges. The criminal
background of some of these men emerged over time, and a number have been
automatically expelled because they were convicted or pled guilty or no contest
to a crime of moral turpitude. Others have been adjudicated in Masonic trials.
With the advancing information age, we can avoid initiating a man who does not
qualify for membership because he has committed a crime involving a violation
of the moral law. We can also verify the information concerning his prior criminal
history that he provides on his application.
The California Masonic Code §804.210 states that no person shall be
“eligible for membership in any Constituent Lodge who has pleaded guilty or
nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a crime involving a violation of the
moral law” unless it is later determined that he did not commit the offense. At
present, there is no system in place to make an inquiry into the criminal history of
an applicant. I am recommending a plan to obtain this information and provide it
back to the Lodge in a timely, efficient and cost effective manner.
To begin the process, the Lodge Secretary (or other person designated
by him) will enter the applicant’s information into iMember including the date
the application was read in the Lodge. This should be done immediately. When
the Secretary submits the information, it will be processed for a comprehensive
criminal background check. If information is returned that the applicant has pled
guilty or no contest to, or has been convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude, an
immediate review will be done to verify the information. Upon verification of
the information, his iMember record will be updated with a status indicating
that he is not eligible for membership in a Constituent Lodge. Such change will
have the same effect as the application being rejected, except that the individual
will not have the opportunity to apply for membership again at any future time

142

Proceedings of the

unless, for the reason that he did not commit the offense, he either has been
pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. A letter will be
sent to the applicant by the Grand Lodge informing him of the information that
was obtained, his current status as an applicant, and the procedure to appeal the
information if he believes it is incorrect. The Lodge Secretary will be advised
of the action taken. If no criminal history is discovered, the applicant’s status
will be updated to indicate that he is eligible for membership, and the Lodge
Secretary will be so informed. If a criminal history is discovered, but the crime or
crimes do not involve moral turpitude, the information will be sent to the Lodge
to determine whether the crime involves a violation of the moral law. If the lodge
makes that determination, then the applicant is ineligible for membership. Unless
the applicant has clearly violated the moral law by committing a crime involving
moral turpitude, the Lodge will determine in the exercise of its sound discretion
whether the applicant’s criminal record disqualifies him to receive the degrees. So
long as the applicant data is entered into iMember in a timely manner, this entire
process can be completed well before the Stated Meeting following receipt of the
application, unless there is an unusual or unforeseen circumstance or the applicant
appeals the decision.
We have negotiated a reasonable fee with a third-party reporting agency
for this service. Initially, the cost for the background check will be $15. Annually
Grand Lodge will set the fee when it adopts the Grand Lodge Budget. The fee will
be paid by the applicant to the Lodge with his application and later paid by the
Lodge to the Grand Lodge along with the other annual fees and assessments. The
background check will not be required for applicants for affiliation from another
California Lodge. If approved at this Annual Communication, the process,
including a new application, will be implemented by January 1, 2012.
It should be noted that this proposal is for a background check of criminal
record only. It will not cover credit history which a Lodge may choose to do on its
own as part of its investigation of applicants.
With all of the information we have at our disposal, there is no reason for
a Constituent Lodge to ballot upon the application of a man who does not qualify
for membership because of his criminal background. I ask you to support this
Recommendation so that this new process can be implemented in the next Grand
Lodge year.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

143

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
From time immemorial, it has been the custom and practice of our
Fraternity to investigate the background of a candidate for degrees to ensure
that he is of good moral character. When a man is made an Entered Apprentice
Mason, he is admonished never to recommend anyone to membership unless he
has strong reason to believe that the candidate’s admission would “reflect honor
on our ancient Institution.”
Grand Master Bray’s Recommendation 2011-01, which requires that a
criminal background check be made on all degree applicants, is designed to take
advantage of the information age in which we now live. Currently, even the most
rigorous investigation of a candidate’s background may fail to ascertain whether
he has a criminal history. However, this type of information is readily available
electronically and may be obtained for a nominal fee. As Grand Master Bray has
stated, “With all of the information we have at our disposal, there is no reason for
a Constituent Lodge to ballot upon the application of a man who does not qualify
for membership because of his criminal background.”
This Recommendation is consistent with the policy and general purposes
of this Grand Lodge.
Recommendation APPROVED.

Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 1
Increases the Representation on the
Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee
Our California Masonic Code defines the membership of the Junior
Grand Warden Recommending Committee as the Grand Master, Deputy Grand
Master, Grand Wardens, Past Grand Masters, and three members of Grand Lodge
appointed annually by the Grand Master.
Since being elected Junior Grand Warden in 2006, I have been a member
of the recommending committee on four consecutive occasions, including this
year when I chaired the committee as Grand Master. This experience has bolstered
my confidence in our procedure for recommending a candidate for the office of
Junior Grand Warden. However, I believe there is room for improvement.
As Grand Master, it was my responsibility to appoint three members of
Grand Lodge as members of the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee.
As Grand Masters have done before me, I considered the many Masters, Wardens,
and Past Masters of this jurisdiction and tried to appoint three brothers who were
representative of the Craft as a whole. This is a very difficult task in a state as
large and diverse as California. The recommendation of a brother for election as
Junior Grand Warden is one of the most important decisions to be considered each
year, and in my view, there should be greater representation of the membership on
the committee.
Our jurisdiction is already divided into Divisions and Districts as a way
to insure proper representation of the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge around
the state. It seems to me that this existing structure can aid in an effort to increase
the representation on the recommending committee.
I recommend that the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee
be expanded from three members of Grand Lodge to one member of Grand
Lodge from each Division appointed by the Grand Master annually. To assist the
Grand Master in surveying the entire state for possible appointments, I further
recommend that the Assistant Grand Lecturer recommend three members of
Grand Lodge from his Division to be considered by the Grand Master.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 404.420 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

§404.420. RECOMMENDEE FOR JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN.
The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Wardens, the Past Grand
Masters, and a three members of Grand Lodge appointed annually by the Grand

for a single term only concurrently with his term and who are not past or present
elected Grand Officers, shall constitute a committee to recommend to Grand

The members of Grand Lodge appointed annually by the Grand Master from each

To such other members of Grand Lodge as the Grand Master determines.

of reproduction.

Resolution No. 10-04
Establishes Mandatory Closing Time for Lodge Meetings
The proponents of this Resolution seek to include in the California Masonic Code
the prohibition on Lodge meetings lasting beyond Midnight.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 807.020 requires only
that a Constituent Lodge must be closed when the business for which it was
opened is completed; and
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 807.020 also prohibits
the adjournment of a Constituent Lodge; and
WHEREAS, these two sections might be considered in conflict and
confusing; and
WHEREAS, a meeting spreading over two days must result in conflicting
dates in the minutes; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

147

WHEREAS, those attending at the beginning of the meeting might
not be the same as those in attendance after the adjournment thus causing an
inaccurate Tiler’s Register; and
WHEREAS, we have long been governed by the traditional rule that a
Lodge must be closed by midnight.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO
MEETINGS.
No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be held on Sunday except for the
annual Installation of Officers or funeral services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar
Lodge falls on a Sunday, the Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.
All business, except the examination of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of
the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy
Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Masons.
A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done or business
transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under the continual direction
of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand Master or the Grand Master’s
designated representative.
No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless the Charter of the Lodge is
present. A photocopy of the Charter may be made under the direction of the Grand
Secretary at the request and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary shall
attach thereto a certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy is a
true copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead of
the original Charter at any time.
The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all meetings of a Lodge. At the
annual election of officers, and at such other meetings as may be deemed desirable
by the Master, the Flag shall be formally presented at the Altar and received in
the manner prescribed in the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated
with any flag.
No Lodge shall transact any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge
present except the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his post
in the Tiler’s room.
Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when the Lodge is in session.
There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each meeting of a Lodge must be closed
when the business proposed for transaction has been concluded, but in no event
later than the close of the day on which it was opened.

148

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Currently California Masonic Code Section 807.020 requires that
a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for transaction has been
concluded. It also does not permit a Lodge to adjourn. This resolution would add
the requirement that a Lodge must be closed in no event later than midnight of
the date it was opened. Adjournment is defined as “a suspension of proceedings
to another time or place.” Legislative bodies are usually opened at the start of a
session, adjourned from time to time, and then closed months or years later by
adjourning sine die until the next session is opened. Unlike a legislative body,
a Lodge meeting must be closed when it has concluded the specific business for
which it was opened. It may be temporarily called from labor to refreshment, but
ultimately must be closed in the same place that it was opened. A Lodge may
not remain perpetually open. At present, nothing in the California Masonic Code
prohibits a Lodge from opening on one day, calling from labor to refreshment, and
then resuming business on a later date. Such an action is effectively an adjournment
under a different name. This resolution would codify the long-standing practice
that any suspension of business is temporary and for a duration measured at most
in a few hours, not days or weeks.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The proponents of this resolution seek to include in the California
Masonic Code the prohibition of Lodge meetings lasting beyond midnight.
Many in the fraternity believe that this provision already exists in the
California Masonic Code. In fact it does not. Section 807.020 of the California
Masonic Code only requires that a lodge must be closed when the business
proposed for transaction has been concluded. The same section of the Code
prohibits a meeting from being adjourned. At present it is possible that a lodge
meeting could be called to refreshment and labor resumed the next day or some
other time in the future. Keeping a lodge open past midnight or resuming work on
another day could preclude some lodge members from participating. It could also
lead to small groups making important decisions. It is reasonable for a Brother
attending a meeting to expect that he will be able to participate in all business
or degree activity. It is also reasonable for a Brother to know that there is a time,
beyond which, no further business may be conducted. This resolution provides
that certainty.
This resolution is administrative and does not affect Ritual. The
Committee on Ritual recommends its adoption.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

§810.050. LODGE ROSTERS.
A Lodge may publish a roster for Masonic purposes and for the benefit of

Current Masonic law allows a Lodge to print a member’s name, mailing

of this Resolution seek to allow a Lodge to include a Mason’s email address in the
Lodge Roster with the Mason’s permission.

long before email addresses were as commonplace as telephone numbers. Today,
email communication is widely used; our own Grand Lodge publishes and uses
email to communicate with its members. Passage of this Resolution would
enhance the ability of the Lodge to communicate with its members, and the ability
of its members to communicate with each other.

Resolution No. 11-02
Increases Lodge Refreshment Revolvoing Fund
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the maximum amount allowed
in the refreshment revolving fund from $500 to $2,000.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Lodge may establish a revolving fund, consisting of not
more than $500, for the use of its Stewards or Junior Warden, as the Master may
determine, in providing refreshments for all regular lodge functions; and
WHEREAS, when several events that require refreshment coincide in
the same month, such as stated meetings, degrees, installation and special events,
the $500 amount is inadequate to cover these expenses; and
WHEREAS, to comply with the California Masonic Code, the Junior
Warden would need to acquire funds directly from the Master or Treasurer, or pay
these expenses out of pocket and be reimbursed; and
WHEREAS, increasing the amount permitted in the refreshment
revolving fund from $500 to $2,000 would allow for additional funds when
needed for the month; and
WHEREAS, during normal months, a smaller amount could be
deposited in the refreshment revolving fund.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.120 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.120. LODGE REVOLVING FUNDS.
A Lodge may establish two revolving funds. One such fund, consisting of not
more than $500 $2,000, may be established for the use of its Stewards or Junior
Warden, as the Master may determine, in providing refreshments for all regular
Lodge functions. One such fund, consisting of not more than $500, may be
established for the use of its Secretary for his incidental expenses. Each such
revolving fund may be replenished monthly on presentation of receipted vouchers
and shall remain subject to provisions of this Code.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

155

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the maximum
amount allowed in a Lodge refreshment revolving fund from $500 to $2,000.
The proponents argue that when several events coincide in the same month, such
as stated meetings, degrees, installation and special events, the $500 amount is
inadequate to cover all expenses.
In 1974, the maximum amount permitted in the revolving fund was
$250. In 1990, the maximum amount was increased to the current $500. Although
the increase sought by this resolution is proportionately much higher than the
previous raise, it does take into account not only the fact that many lodges today
have more social events than in the past, but that inflation is taking its toll on
all of us.
The purpose of having this revolving, or petty cash, fund is so a Lodge
can provide refreshments for its members without knowing in advance the amount
that will be needed. A dollar limit is placed to cap the amount of discretionary
spending without a vote of the members. This would not change how much a Lodge
is allowed to spend per month; it simply defines how much the Junior Warden and
or Stewards are allowed to spend without a vote of the Lodge. Currently, Junior
Wardens and Stewards must spend their personal money for expenses that exceed
$500 and request reimbursement at a subsequent Stated Meeting.
This resolution, if passed, would not require that any Lodge use the full
$2000 nor would it change the total amount a Lodge could spend on “Social and
Fraternal” expenditures. While those expenditures remain capped at 30 percent of
total income, the Lodge would have more flexibility in carrying out social events.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

§804.740. ADMISSION TO MEMBERSHIP OF MASTER MASONS BY

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.370 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
If a member has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the Secretary
shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment of dues unless at
the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have been paid or sickness or
inability to pay is shown as the cause for the failure to pay. The notice shall be
given either by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, addressed
to his last known address, or by actual service of notice, duly certified by the
Tiler. If all dues due and payable have not been paid by the time of the Lodge’s
next Stated Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless for
special reasons shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him further time for
payment. No worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended for
non-payment of dues.
No member who has attained the age of 80 years or who has attained an aggregate
number of years in age and years as a Master Mason in good standing equaling
120 or more shall be suspended for non-payment of dues without a written report
to the Lodge from the Member Retention Committee evidencing when and where
the committee interviewed the delinquent member, why the delinquent member
has not paid his dues and whether the delinquent member has the ability to pay his
dues. A copy of this report shall be provided to the Grand Secretary at least thirty
days before the vote may be taken on the suspension.
A member shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.

Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

163

§812.010. GENERALLY.
It is the duty of every Lodge to aid and assist every needy Master Mason of that
Lodge, wherever he may reside, and every needy Master Mason of another Lodge
in this or any other Jurisdiction who resides within the vicinity of that Lodge.
This duty extends to the needy widow and dependant orphans of a Master Mason
of that Lodge and the needy widow and dependant orphans of a Master Mason
of another Lodge in this or any other Jurisdiction who reside within the vicinity
of that Lodge. A Lodge’s duty of relief is limited only by its own circumstances
and ability.
For purposes of this Code, a “widow” is one who was married to a Master Mason
at the time of his death. A widow who remarries forfeits all rights to Masonic relief
from her previous husband pursuant to this section, even though such remarriage
is later terminated by divorce, dissolution, or otherwise.
For purposes of this Code, an “orphan” is the son or daughter under the age
of majority of a deceased Master Mason. No man or woman over the age of
majority shall be entitled to relief as a matter of right. However, a Lodge may,
in its discretion, provide relief in exceptional circumstances to the adult child
of a deceased Master Mason where a need arises by reason of a physical or
mental impairment.
Every Lodge may, at its discretion, aid and assist every needy Entered Apprentice
or Fellow Craft of that Lodge, wherever he may reside, and every needy Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft of another Lodge in this or any other Jurisdiction who
resides within the vicinity of that Lodge.
Money given a Mason or his family as relief by a Lodge cannot be charged to him.

405.050 of this Code.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

165

§1404.910. GRAND LODGE REVIEW.
All trial records under Chapters 3 and 4 of this Part 14 shall be reviewed by Grand
Lodge, as follows:
A.

All trial records received by the Grand Secretary under this chapter or
under Chapter 3 of this part shall be forwarded by him to the Committee
on Trial Review for review.

B.

If either an Accused or Accuser desires to have any evidence considered
that could not have been produced before the verdict was rendered, a
written statement setting forth the substance of such evidence and
explaining why it was not produced before the verdict was rendered
may be filed with the Grand Secretary not later than 15 days prior to
the commencement of the next Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Any arguments or representations which the Accused, the Accuser, or
any other Mason desires to present must be in writing and filed with the
Grand Secretary not later than 15 days prior to the commencement of the
next Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.

C.

The Committee on Trial Review shall examine each trial record
together with such statements or arguments in writing, if any, as may be
presented and shall report its recommendations at the next succeeding
Annual Communication.

D.

1.

The Committee shall review the record to determine whether
the verdict is supported by substantial evidence. All evidentiary
conflicts and all legitimate and reasonable inferences that may
be drawn from the trial record shall be in favor of sustaining
the verdict. Where the evidence supports more than one
inference, the Committee may not substitute its determination
in place of the determinations made by the trier of fact. The
Committee may recommend that the verdict be overturned
only if the verdict is not supported by substantial evidence. If
the Committee recommends that the verdict be overturned, it
shall include in its report the specific facts contained in the trial
record upon which it makes such recommendation.

2.

Based on its review of the record, the Committee may
recommend that the penalty be modified for good cause and
in the interest of justice. If the Committee recommends that
the penalty imposed should be modified in any respect, it shall
include in its report the specific facts contained in the trial
record upon which it makes such recommendation.

After receipt of the report of the Committee on Trial Review, Grand
Lodge may affirm, modify, or reverse the verdict and/or penalty, remand

166

Proceedings of the
the matter to the Trial Master with instructions or make such other order
as it deems proper. The Grand Secretary shall send a copy of the Grand
Lodge action to the Trial Master as soon as possible.

E.

Pending Grand Lodge action on the trial record, no Lodge may not take
action toward the modification of the penalty or upon the restoration of a
Mason under penalty of suspension.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In 2006, the Fourth Revision of the California Masonic Code was
approved by this Grand Lodge. In 2010, section 14 of that code, dealing with
Masonic trials, was rewritten and adopted. Over the course of the time since these
revisions became law, a number of inconsistencies or unclear passages have been
identified. It is the intent of the proponents of Resolution 11-03 to reword these
sections of the CMC in order to correct these problems and have a code that is
written as clearly as possible.
Almost all of the proposed changes are such housekeeping items.
However, this committee would call your attention to the proposed change to
section 812.010. The prior version of our code, dated 1991 with revisions through
2005, defined a member in section 23010 as being a man who was a Master
Mason. The insertion of the word “Master” in the first paragraph of the proposed
revision makes the new code consistent with the old one. However, in the second
paragraph of section 23090 of that old code, it is stated that Entered Apprentices
and Fellowcrafts are not entitled to relief from a lodge. Of course, since, in
principle, Masonic relief can be provided to anyone, the fact that a class of Masons
did not have a legal entitlement did not mean that relief could not be provided to
them. The current proposal now specifically provides for the possibility of relief
to Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts at the discretion of the Lodge.
Since a law that is as clearly written as possible is an objective of this
Grand Lodge, and since relief is a principle tenet of Masonry, this Resolution is
consistent with the policy and general purposes of this Grand Lodge.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

167

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
This resolution seeks to amend various sections of the California
Masonic Code to clarify certain sections affected by the passage of the Fourth
Edition of the Code in 2006. Specifically, as to the amendments affecting the filing
of Masonic Charges and Masonic Trials it seeks to accomplish the following:
1.

It modifies Section 404.130 to provide that if the Grand Master
issues an order directing a member to act in accordance with
the requirements of the Code and the member fails or refuses
to conform his conduct to the Grand Master’s order, the Grand
Master may, instead of referring the violation to a Junior
Warden of a Lodge for the filing of Masonic charges, refer the
matter to any Master Mason in good standing for the preferment
of charges. It also allows the Grand Master to suspend the
offending brother pending the conclusion of the trial process;

2.

It modifies Section 803.040 by expanding the disciplinary
jurisdiction of the constituent lodges to include any Mason
residing in this jurisdiction and living closer to the constituent
lodge than to any other lodge;

3.

It modifies Sections 807.010 and 807.020 by excepting from the
business to be done in a Lodge of Master Masons the delivery
of a reprimand to an Entered Apprentice or a Fellowcraft Mason
and provides that any reprimand of an Entered Apprentice or
Fellowcraft Mason may be done in a Special Meeting;

4.

It modifies Section 1404.910 by providing that following a
Masonic Trial proceeding and before Grand Lodge takes action
on a trial record a Lodge may not take any action concerning
the restoration of a suspended Mason.

The reviewed revisions to the Code are necessary to resolve ambiguities;
accordingly, the Committee on Trial Review recommends that Resolution Number
11-03 be adopted.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 11-04
Allows Lodge Treasurers to Receive Compensation

The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the Lodge Treasurer to receive
compensation for his services.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Lodge Treasurer is the Chief Financial Officer of the
Lodge and currently receives no compensation; and
WHEREAS, the traditional duties of the Lodge Treasurer are “to
receive all money from the Secretary, keep a just and accurate account thereof,
and pay out the same by order of the Worshipful Master, with the consent of the
lodge;” and
WHEREAS, the duties of the lodge Treasurer are more fully described
in CMC Section 805.220; and
WHEREAS, in addition, the Lodge Treasurer has a significant role in
the creation of the Lodge Annual Budget and its subsequent management; and
WHEREAS, in order to successfully perform these duties, the Lodge
Treasurer should have skills, education and training related to accounting,
budgeting and tax preparation; and
WHEREAS, a well-skilled Lodge Treasurer provides a safeguard and
deterrent against any misappropriation or expropriation of Lodge funds or any
other financial wrongdoing; and
WHEREAS, the Lodge Secretary, Assistant Secretary, Tiler and Organist
may be compensated for their services from Lodge funds.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.030 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.030. COMPENSATION.
No Lodge officer may receive compensation for his services as such, except as
provided in Sections 805.220, 805.230, 805.320 and 805.330 of this Code.

§805.220. DUTIES OF TREASURER.

Receive all monies from the Secretary and shall keep an accurate and

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the Lodge Treasurer to
receive compensation for his services. Currently the California Masonic Code
provides that no Lodge officer may receive compensation for his services except
the Lodge Secretary, Assistant Secretary, Organist and Tiler, if so directed by
the Lodge.
The reward of serving as an officer of a Masonic Lodge is the personal
satisfaction of working together with other officers in support of the objectives
of Masonry in general and of a given Lodge in particular without anticipation of

170

Proceedings of the

personal financial remuneration. However, some offices require particular talents
and dedication of time. These requirements may vary from Lodge to Lodge
and therefore only the individual Lodge can adequately determine the need for
compensation for a particular officer.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 11-05
Makes the Jewel March Optional
The proponents of this Resolution seek to make the jewel march optional.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Ritual requires an officer jewel march at the opening of
a Lodge of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, the current instruction at the opening of Lodge can be
interpreted to mean that each brother filing an officer at the opening should be
wearing his officer apron and jewel without further ceremony
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Ritual be amended
to make optional the jewel march at the opening of a Constituent Lodge.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that such amendment result in making
available the following option in lieu of the third and fourth full paragraphs
in the Ritual for opening a Lodge of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and
Master Masons:
WM* The brn wl com to O @ clo thsl. Ofs tk yr stas and pls. (When Mstr sits dn
sgnl to oths to b setd.)
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the current ritual for
opening a Lodge by making the Jewel March optional. Resolutions to modify or
eliminate the Jewel March have been proposed in 1985, 1995, 1996, and 2002. On
each occasion the resolution was not adopted, except in 1996, when the resolution
was carried over to 1997 and not adopted.
In its report to the Grand Lodge in 1995, the Ritual Committee stated:
“We are, in general, not in favor of changing a practice that has not proven a
burden to the Lodge over the years. The practice of obtaining the jewel of office

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

171

from the Master of the Lodge has some symbolic significance, for it reminds
the office holder that it is the Master of the Lodge that continues to give him the
right to wear the jewel of office. It emphasizes the right of the Master to govern
the Lodge over which he is called to preside, and confirms that the holding of a
Masonic office is a privilege.”
This resolution could result in different Lodges having a different
opening ritual. Maintaining uniformity of ritual throughout this Grand Lodge is
one of its policies.
One of the beauties of Freemasonry is the continuity of its traditions and
ritual, stretching back in an unbroken chain to its earliest years. Changes in that
ritual should be made only for the most important reasons and then only after
thorough review. It is up to the members of this Grand Lodge to decide if this
resolution meets these criteria.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Since October 1995, three separate Resolutions, 95-06, 96-04, and 02-15
have been proposed to make optional, modify or eliminate the ritual regarding the
distribution of officers’ jewels at the opening of a lodge. Resolution 11-05 again
proposes to make the Jewel March optional. The Ritual Committee published a
recommendation in opposition to Resolution 95-06, which was also relevant to
subsequent resolutions of a similar nature. The Ritual Committee recommendation
is stated as follows:
“The Ritual Committee is opposed to the adoption of Resolution 9506. As with other such proposals, we are, in general, not in favor of changing a
practice that has not proven a burden to the lodge over the years. The practice of
obtaining the jewel of office from the Master of the Lodge has some symbolic
significance, for it reminds the office holder that it is the Master of the Lodge that
continues to give him the right to wear the jewel of office. It emphasizes the right
of the Master to govern the ldoge over which he is called to preside, and confirms
that the holding of Masonic office is a privilege.
The Ritual Committee urges a “No” vote on Resolution No. 95-06.”
The 1995 Ritual Committee recommendation opposing the Jewel
March ritual change is as valid and comprehensive today as when first published.
The above stated quotation withstands the test of time and needs no further
embellishment.
The Ritual Committee urges a “No” vote on Resolution No. 11-05.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 11-06
Restores the Historic Role of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Craft Masons
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have most Lodge business conducted
in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons and to allow Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft Masons to speak but not vote on any matter before the Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, before 1842, lodge business was conducted in the Entered
Apprentice Degree; and
WHEREAS, this practice gradually changed after that time as a result of
the Morgan Affair and the subsequent Anti-Masonic movement; and
WHEREAS, Section 807.020 of the CMC now provides that all business
except the examination of candidates in the lecture of Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy Mason shall be done in a lodge
of Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, California is the only one of the ten western United States
that still conducts business in the Master Mason degree only; and
WHEREAS, Section 804.860 of the CMC states that an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft is not entitled to vote or speak on any matter before
the Lodge; and
WHEREAS, all Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons are
Masons under the jurisdiction of a Lodge and are subject to all the rules and
regulations of Freemasonry.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.860 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.860.
ADDITIONAL RIGHTS OF AND PROHIBITIONS ON
ENTERED APPRENTICES AND FELLOW CRAFTS.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may sit in the Lodge in which he has
received the degree or degrees when open in a degree taken by him, while he
conducts himself with due order and propriety. He may speak but may not vote on
any matter coming before the Lodge. He may advance after satisfactorily passing
a strict examination in a tiled Lodge. He may visit another Lodge working in a
degree taken by him, with the consent of the Master of his Lodge and the consent
of the Master of the Lodge visited, if accompanied by a Master Mason who has
sat with him in a tiled Lodge and vouches for him.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

173

He shall not pay dues. and is not entitled to vote or speak on any matter before
the Lodge.
He may be buried with Masonic honors upon the request of his family, unless he
was a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or expelled Mason at the time of his death.
Neither he nor his widows or orphans are entitled to relief from the Lodge.
He shall not exercise any control over Lodge funds for charity or for
other purposes.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
A.

Sunday Meetings. No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be
held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers or funeral
services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar Lodge falls on a Sunday, the
Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.

B.

Work to be Done in Lodge of Master Entered Apprentice Masons. All
business, except the examinations of candidates in the Candidate’s
Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft and Master Mason
degrees, the conferring of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
and Master Mason degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy
Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Entered Apprentice Masons.
A Lodge of Master Masons may be called down for the examinations
of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees.

C.

Quorum. A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done
or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under the
continual direction of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand Master
or the Grand Master’s designated representative. No Lodge shall transact
any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge present except
the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his post in
the Tiler’s room.

D.

Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless
the Charter of the Lodge is present. A photocopy of the Charter may
be made under the direction of the Grand Secretary at the request
and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary shall attach thereto a
certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy is a true
copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.

174

Proceedings of the

E.

Presence of Flag. The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all
meetings of a Lodge. At the annual election of officers, and at such other
meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag shall be
formally presented at the Altar and received in the manner prescribed in
the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.

F.

No Smoking. Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when
the Lodge is in session.

G.

No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each
meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for
transaction has been concluded.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 11-06 seek to have most Lodge
business conducted in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons and to allow
Entered Apprentice Masons and Fellow Craft Masons to speak but not vote on
any matter before the Lodge. Similar proposals have been presented in the past
to determine whether our Grand Lodge would change its long standing custom
and rule of conducting business only in the Master Mason Degree. All have been
rejected by this Grand Lodge.
The proponents are correct in indicating that in the formative years of
Freemasonry, Lodge business was conducted in the Entered Apprentice Degree
due to the fact that Entered Apprentices made up the bulk of the membership
in the Fraternity. Fellow Craft Masons and Master Masons were rare. During
the 1840’s, many of the Grand Lodges in the United States revised their rules to
require Lodges to hold Stated Meetings only in Lodges of Master Masons. The
change was instituted to encourage all Masons to become Master Masons. Lodges
in other countries may meet in the First Degree where several years are required
to proceed to advance through the Degrees. However, in recent years our Grand
Lodge has adopted changes in our proficiencies whereby we have shortened the
time and difficulty for advancement.
As Masons, we are taught that Masonry is a progressive moral science
taught by degrees only. Upon completion of the three degrees, the candidate
becomes a Master Mason and is informed that he is now entitled to all the rights
and privileges therein. Until he becomes a Master Mason, he does not pay dues
nor is he entitled to vote or speak in the Lodge. This proposal does not provide for
the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to pay dues and/or vote while participating
in the business of the Lodge. It would also prohibit the Lodge from conducting
Fellow Craft or Master Mason proficiencies at the Stated Meeting.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

175

While it is desirable for a candidate to participate and learn as much as
possible about the Fraternity, he can do so by spending time with his coach or
Mentor while the Stated Meeting or other meetings are in progress. Presently,
nothing prohibits
Entered Apprentice Masons or Fellow Craft Masons from attending
and participating in non-tiled functions of a Lodge or in the Degree that he has
been through.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.
Resolution No. 11-07
Requires Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to Pay Lodge Dues
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Masons to pay Lodge dues.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts are Masons under
the jurisdiction of a lodge; and
WHEREAS, Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons are required
to comply with all the rules and regulations of Freemasonry and are subject to the
disciplinary processes of the fraternity; and
WHEREAS, an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason remains
active on the roster of the Lodge even if he does not advance and even if his
degree fees have been forfeited; and
WHEREAS, Section 804.860 of the CMC states that an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft shall not pay dues; and
WHEREAS, Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons enjoy
many of the benefits of the Lodge including receiving a bulletin or Trestleboard,
attending social events, education classes and other programs and services that
utilize lodge funds;
WHEREAS, the payment of annual dues would allow an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason to contribute to the costs of these programs
and services; and

176

Proceedings of the

WHEREAS, the adoption of this resolution will lower the Grand
Lodge per capita because the Grand Lodge budget will be spread over Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts as well as Master Masons.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 407.020 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§407.025. PER CAPITA LODGE CONTRIBUTIONS.
Each Lodge, whether chartered or under dispensation:
A.

B.

Shall pay with its Annual Returns the following contributions:
1.

For each Master Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th, such
per capita sum, not less than $.50, as Grand Lodge requires, and

2.

Each Master Mason carried on its rolls as of June 30th, such per
capita sum as Grand Lodge levies for the support of Masonic
Homes of California;

Shall not pay per capita sums for:
1.

Master Masons whose dues have been remitted by Lodge action
for the preceding calendar year, and

2.

Master Masons whose dues have been remitted because of
residence in the Masonic Homes of California.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.135 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

179

§804.135.
WITHDRAWAL OF ENTERED APPRENTICES AND
FELLOW CRAFTS.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft, in good standing, against whom there is
no pending Masonic charge or charge under the criminal laws of the United States
or of any other governmental entity involving moral turpitude, may withdraw
from the Lodge at any time if the Lodge approves his request by a majority vote
at a Stated Meeting and issues a Demit. The request shall be made in writing, over
his signature. Upon report of the request at the next Stated Meeting, the vote shall
be taken. If approved, the Master of the Lodge shall order the Secretary to issue a
Demit immediately, in the form provided, as evidence of the withdrawal.
When an Entered Apprentices or Fellow Craft of the Lodge has been elected to
advance in another Lodge pursuant to a Waiver of Jurisdiction without first having
been issued a Demit, the Secretary shall immediately issue a Demit on receipt of
the notification of election in the other Lodge, using the form provided by the
Grand Secretary. The Secretary shall report its issuance to the Lodge at the next
Stated Meeting.
The withdrawal shall be effective as of the date of the Demit.
A duplicate Demit may be issued if the original is lost.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may not resign from Masonry.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.820 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.820. RIGHT TO BURIAL.
It is the right of every Mason, other than a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or
expelled Mason, to a Masonic memorial service or burial with Masonic honors.
The foregoing notwithstanding, a demitted Master Mason has the right to a
Masonic memorial service or burial with Masonic honors if he dies within a year
after receiving a Demit.
It is the duty of the Lodge to bury an eligible Mason of that Lodge, wherever
he may have died, and an eligible Mason of another Lodge in this or any other
Jurisdiction who dies within the vicinity of the Lodge. If such deceased Mason’s
financial circumstances require it, the Lodge shall pay the necessary expenses of
the burial, even if the deceased Mason’s Lodge refuses to reimburse the Lodge
for such expenses. The Lodge shall reimburse any other Lodge for the reasonable
expenses incurred by it in suitably burying one of its deceased Masons. No Lodge
shall fix in advance the amount to be paid for such burial.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

181

When financial circumstances require it, it is also the duty of the Lodge to pay all
the necessary expenses of the burial for one of its deceased member’s widow and
orphans dependent upon her and to reimburse any other Lodge for the reasonable
expenses incurred by it in suitably burying them. No Lodge shall fix in advance
the amount to be paid for such burial.
A Lodge may, in its discretion, conduct Masonic funeral or memorial services for
a member Mason of the Lodge suspended for non-payment of dues, if there is no
other Masonic offense established against him, but it shall not pay the expenses
of the burial.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.860 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.860.
ADDITIONAL RIGHTS OF AND PROHIBITIONS ON
ENTERED APPRENTICES AND FELLOW CRAFTS.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may sit in the Lodge in which he has
received the degree or degrees when open in a degree taken by him, while he
conducts himself with due order and propriety. He may advance after satisfactorily
passing a strict examination in a tiled Lodge. He may visit another Lodge working
in a degree taken by him, with the consent of the Master of his Lodge and the
consent of the Master of the Lodge visited, if accompanied by a Master Mason
who has sat with him in a tiled Lodge and vouches for him.
He shall not pay dues and is shall not be entitled to vote or speak on any matter
before the Lodge.
He may be buried with Masonic honors upon the request of his family, unless he
was a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or expelled Mason at the time of his death.
Neither he nor his widows or orphans are entitled to relief from the Lodge.
He shall not exercise any control over Lodge funds for charity or for
other purposes.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.310 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.310. DUES.
A Lodge’s dues shall be established in its Bylaws. The minimum annual dues shall
be $12. The Lodge Secretary shall issue to each Mason member paying his dues
a receipt using, without change, the uniform receipt for dues available from the
Grand Secretary.
Dues shall commence with the first day of the month next following the
conferring of the Master Mason Entered Apprentice Degree or as provided in
Sections 804.740 or 804.750 of this Code for members Masons joining the Lodge
by affiliation.
If a Lodge increases its dues, the increase shall become effective upon the start of
fiscal year of the Lodge following the Grand Master’s approval of the increase.
Members Masons of the Lodge who have paid their dues in advance for such
fiscal year must pay the increase.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.350 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.350. RETURN OF DUES.
If a Mason of the Lodge member dies, is issued a Demit or discontinues his multiple
membership, the Lodge shall refund to his authorized successor in interest or to
him dues paid in advance of the month when he died or his membership affiliation
with the Lodge terminated; provided, however, that a Mason member issued a
Demit or discontinuing multiple membership may only obtain a refund of his dues
paid in advance if he has returned his dues receipt in such Lodge with his request
for a Demit or Certificate of Discontinuance of Multiple Membership. There shall
be no refund of a life membership to a member who dies, is issued a Demit or
discontinues his multiple memberships.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.360 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

186

Proceedings of the

§809.360. REMISSION OF DUES.
If recommended by the Charity Committee, a Lodge, without giving the name of
the delinquent Masons members except to the Secretary, may remit to December
31st of the current calendar year the accrued dues of those of its Masons members
who are unable to pay.
The Charity Committee should review the situation of a Mason member whose
dues were remitted by a Lodge the preceding calendar year before the February
Stated Meeting. If, in the opinion of the Charity Committee, the necessity for the
remission of his dues still exists, it shall recommend to the Lodge that the dues be
remitted to December 31st of the current calendar year. A Lodge shall not remit
the dues of any of its Masons members, for any stated period, or in advance,
except as herein provided.
A Mason member who is mentally incompetent to such an extent as to be incapable
of taking care of himself, or a member who is a resident of the Masonic Homes of
California, may be considered as unable to pay dues.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.370 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
If a Mason member has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the
Secretary shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment of dues
unless at the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have been paid or
sickness or inability to pay is shown as the cause for the failure to pay. The notice
shall be given either by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid,
addressed to his last known address, or by actual service of notice, duly certified
by the Tiler. If all dues due and payable have not been paid by the time of the
Lodge’s next Stated Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless
for special reasons shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him further time
for payment. No worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended
for non-payment of dues.
No Mason member who has attained the age of 80 years or who has attained an
aggregate number of years in age and years as a Master Mason in good standing
equaling 120 or more shall be suspended for non-payment of dues without a
written report to the Lodge from the Member Retention Committee evidencing
when and where the committee interviewed the delinquent Mason member, why
the delinquent Mason member has not paid his dues and whether the delinquent
Mason member has the ability to pay his dues. A copy of this report shall be
provided to the Grand Secretary at least thirty days before the vote may be taken
on the suspension.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

187

A Mason member shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.380 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.380. RESTORATION OF A MASON MEMBER SUSPENDED FOR
NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
A Mason member suspended for non-payment of dues:
A.

Shall be automatically restored if, within two years, he pays any arrearage
due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues as
would have accrued against him had he not been suspended, to the date
of his payment, unless such arrearage and dues have been remitted by his
Lodge; and

B.

May make a request to his Lodge for restoration if he has not paid
them or had them remitted by his Lodge for the period of two years.
The Mason member shall not be restored except by a two‑thirds vote
by ballot of all the members present at the next Stated Meeting after the
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration, he
shall pay any arrearage due at the time of his suspension, together with
such further dues as would have accrued against him had he not been
suspended, to the date of his payment, unless the arrearage and dues have
been remitted by his Lodge. A petition denied may be renewed at any
future Stated Meeting.

The Secretary shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary of the restoration.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.560 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.560. SOCIAL AND FRATERNAL EXPENDITURES.
A Lodge may expend Lodge funds for the following purposes, subject to the
following limitations:
A.

A Lodge may expend Lodge funds for purposes of its social and fraternal
activities, promoting fraternal intercourse, community improvement, its
charitable activities and its programs that will benefit residents of the
community in which the Lodge is located. Except for expenditures from
funds collected for specific social purposes as otherwise provided in this
section, the aggregate annual expenditures by the Lodge for the purposes

188

Proceedings of the
described in this section shall not exceed thirty percent of the Lodge’s
total revenue derived that year from member dues, application fees and
net income from investments;

B.

Contributions, gifts, bequests and other financial assistance received,
receipts on trust funds, financial support received for the Lodge’s
fraternal operations or charitable activities and profits realized from the
sale of capital assets shall not be included in total revenue for purposes
of calculating the thirty percent limitation;

C.

Expenditures of financial support received for the Lodge’s fraternal
operations or charitable activities shall not be subject to this thirty
percent annual limitation when spent as follows:
1.

To pay the expenses of the activity through which such
support was raised, such as the expenses of staging the event
at which the support was received or the expenses of printing
and distributing the publication in which the permitted paid
advertising appeared; or

2.

To pay the expenses of the Lodge’s other social and fraternal
activities, promoting fraternal intercourse, community
improvement, its charitable activities and its programs that
will benefit residents of the community in which the Lodge
is located;

D.

Lodge contributions to the Masonic Homes shall not be subject to this
thirty percent annual limitation; and

E.

In the discretion of the Lodge, any portion of the annual thirty percent

§1404.940. REVERSAL BY GRAND LODGE.

rights and privileges at the time of his death. If he were a Master Mason,
Hhe shall be considered as having been in good standing at the time of
