Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution would require Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
Masons to pay Lodge dues, which includes the assessed Grand Lodge per capita.
The proponents of this legislation point out these Masons enjoy many Lodge
benefits, but do not help offset the costs that the Lodge and Grand Lodge incur
on their behalf.
Currently, there are 9,623 Entered Apprentice’s and Fellow-Craft
Masons, none of whom pay dues or per capita. Adoption of this resolution would
lower the Grand Lodge per capita because the Grand Lodge budget would be
spread over nearly 10,000 Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts as well as
Master Masons.
Requiring Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to pay dues would not
entitle them to all of the privileges of being members of the Lodge. However, as
they currently enjoy the most costly benefits, such as receiving a monthly bulletin
or Trestleboard, attending social events, education classes and other programs
and services that utilize Lodge funds, it would put them on an equal footing with
Master Masons in terms of their financial support of the Lodge.
While requiring Entered Apprentices and Fellow Craft Masons to pay
dues is a change in current law, it is consistent both with economic reality and
with our Masonic principle that Masons, unless destitute, should not be a financial
burden to their Brothers.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 11-08
Removes Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from
Lodge Rolls After Five Years

The proponents of this Resolution seek to remove an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft Mason from the Lodge rolls five years after his fees and contributions have
been forfeited.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, many California Lodges carry on their books a significant
number of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons who have exhibited no
intention to advance to higher degrees; and
WHEREAS, after three years of no response to requests of these Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to encourage them to continue, their fees
and contributions are considered forfeited; and
WHEREAS, in most cases, contact can no longer be made with these
brothers because of change of residence without notification to the Lodge and
being unable to trace said brothers by any of the standard methods available to
the Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.690 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.690. FORFEITURE OF FEES AND CONTRIBUTIONS.
When a candidate does not present himself qualified for the Fellow Craft and
Master Mason Degrees within a period of three years from the date of his initiation
as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall appoint a committee of two or more
members of the Lodge to investigate and report back to the Master the reasons why
the candidate has not presented himself for advancement. If the candidate does
not supply any explanation satisfactory to the Lodge, the Master shall direct the
Secretary to forward to such candidate by certified mail, return receipt requested,
postage prepaid, deposited in the U.S. Post Office, addressed to him at his last
known address, a notice advising him that unless he shall present himself qualified
for advancement, on or before a specified date (at least 60 days in advance), his
fees for the unconferred degrees and all of his previous contributions shall be
declared forfeited.
On the date specified, the Master shall declare the fees and contributions forfeited
unless further time shall have been granted by a vote of the Lodge.
A candidate thus denied advancement shall be considered only as an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft of the Lodge with the right to apply for the remaining
degree or degrees, and again paying the fees and contributions therefor, subject to
investigation and election, the same as any other candidate.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

191

If, after five years from the date his fees and contributions were declared forfeited,
he has not applied for the remaining degree or degrees, the Lodge may issue him
a Demit.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend section 804.690 of the
California Masonic Code regarding forfeiture of fees and contributions when a
candidate for degrees fails to advance.
The proponents seek to add a provision that after five years from the
forfeiture, the Lodge may issue the candidate a Demit. This would remove the
individual from the Lodge rolls.
This Resolution appears to add a natural succession in the forfeiture
process and simplifies the record keeping of the Lodge.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 11-09
Preserves Santa Barbara Masonic Temple as a

The proponents of this resolution seek to preserve Santa Barbara Masonic Temple
as a meeting place for Masonic Organizations and Masonic Youth Orders in the
event of the dissolution of Santa Barbara Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, in 1925 the members of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 and
Magnolia Lodge No. 242, together with other concordant bodies, financed and
erected a Masonic temple at 16 E. Carrillo Street in Santa Barbara; and
WHEREAS, the temple has been preserved for Masonic purposes ever
since, first as the Santa Barbara Masonic Temple Association in 1924 and then
under the auspices of Masonic Properties of Santa Barbara, Inc. since 1941; and
WHEREAS, a third lodge, La Cumbre Lodge No. 692, joined the
Masonic Temple Association in 1926 and later Masonic Properties of Santa
Barbara, Inc., and subsequently consolidated with Magnolia Lodge in 1990 as
Magnolia-La Cumbre Lodge No. 242, which consolidated with Santa Barbara
Lodge No. 192 in 2006 as Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192; and

192

Proceedings of the

WHEREAS, Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 is now the majority member
of Masonic Properties of Santa Barbara Inc., and
WHEREAS, the majority membership would be held by the Grand
Lodge of F&AM of California should the charter of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192
be ever surrendered or revoked; and
WHEREAS, the mission of Masonic Properties of Santa Barbara Inc. is
to preserve the temple for Masonic purposes; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge has maintained other historic Masonic
properties in California even when no Lodge is chartered in the same city.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 813.060 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§813.060. EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION.
The dissolution of the Lodge upon the surrender or revocation of its Charter shall
be conclusive upon the Lodge and its members. Upon the dissolution of a Lodge,
the Grand Secretary, or his duly authorized representative, shall, in such manner
as shall seem to him most judicious:
A.

Proceed at once to receive its funds on hand, except the Life
Membership Fund;

B.

Collect outstanding dues;

C.

Dispose of its jewels, furniture, and other property; and

D.

Place the proceeds thereof, after the payment of all just debts and
necessary expenses, among the unrestricted funds of Grand Lodge.

The assets in the dissolved Lodge’s Life Membership Fund, after the payment
of all just debts and necessary expenses of the dissolved Lodge, shall be held,
managed and distributed as provided in Section 815.000.K of this Code.
Upon dissolution of the Lodge, all memberships in the dissolved Lodge shall
terminate. No Demits shall be issued to any of the candidates or members of the
dissolved Lodge. Those of the dissolved Lodge’s Master Masons who are plural
or dual members in other Lodges shall remain members of such other Lodges.
Those of the dissolved Lodge’s remaining Master Masons and all of the dissolved
Lodge’s Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts shall become members of the
Grand Master’s Lodge, as provided in Section 815.000 of this Code.

If on the dissolution of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 or on the dissolution of

The Santa Barbara Masonic Temple is owned by Masonic Properties of
Santa Barbara, Inc. The majority ownership of said corporation is held by Santa

Rite Bodies and Santa Barbara York Rite Bodies.
The proponents of this resolution seek to preserve Santa Barbara Masonic

proposed amendment would add a specific exception that would provide that in
the event of the dissolution of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 or the dissolution of
any successor Lodge, the Grand Lodge shall retain such majority interest for so
long as the property is financially self sufficient. The property is to be maintained
as a meeting place for Masonic Lodges, Masonic organizations and / or Masonic
Youth orders even if no constituent Lodge meets there.
The current minority interest holders of Masonic Properties of Santa
Barbara, Inc., namely the Santa Barbara Scottish Rite Bodies and the Santa
Barbara York Rite Bodies support this Resolution. It has long been the policy
of this Grand Lodge to ensure that not only Lodges, but Concordant and
Appendant bodies as well, have facilities that are adequate for their meetings and
social events.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 11-10
Creates a Newe Classification of Historic Lodges

The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide a classification of special

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State
of California has, or has had, a Masonic presence in many historic communities
in this State; and
WHEREAS, the loss of a Masonic Lodge in these communities often

WHEREAS, the chartering of special-purpose Lodges in these historic

our heritage in California.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to create a new classification
of Special Purpose Lodges for the preservation of our Masonic heritage. Such
Lodges, to be known as Historic Lodges, would have the authority to preserve
buildings with historic Masonic significance owned or leased by them. Historic
Lodges would consist of Master Masons in good standing who are members of
California Lodges or of Lodges under the jurisdiction of Grand Lodges recognized
by this Grand Lodge.
Historic Lodges would not confer degrees but rather would obtain
members by affiliation only. They would be required to meet a minimum of
once annually to transact business. Historic Lodges would be exempt from per
capita and the officers would be exempt from the usual qualification requirements
except they would be required to demonstrate their proficiency in opening and
closing ceremonies.
However, there is no statement in the resolution that indicates how
such lodges would be supported financially. For this reason, the resolution is not
consistent with the policy and General Purposes of this Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 11-11
Clarifies Current Masonic Law Regarding the Circumstances
Under Which a Lodge Master May be Reprimanded
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the circumstances under which
a Lodge Master may be reprimanded.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, current Masonic law provides that a Lodge Master found
guilty of one or more specifications filed against him shall be removed from office
whether or not the specifications constitute unmasonic conduct; and
WHEREAS, current Masonic law provides that the trial of a Lodge Master
shall continue even after the Master has completed his full term in office; and
WHEREAS, current Masonic law is not clear as to the penalty that may
be imposed against a Lodge Master who has completed his term of office and is
found guilty of specifications that do not constitute unmasonic conduct.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Section 1403.040 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as follows:

198

Proceedings of the

§1403.040. PENALTY AND ITS IMPOSITION.
The Accused shall be removed from office without further action upon the
Commissioners’ determination that he is guilty of one or more of the specifications.
In addition, if the Accused is found guilty of one or more specifications which
constitute unmasonic conduct, the Commissioners shall proceed to vote upon a
penalty under Section 1404.620 of this Code. A majority of the Commissioners
shall be required to determine the penalty.
The Commissioners shall provide the Grand Secretary with a signed written
report of the results of the proceedings. The Grand Secretary shall then notify
the Accused of these results, by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage
prepaid, addressed to the Accused’s last known address as shown in the Grand
Lodge’s records. The Grand Secretary shall also notify the Accusers and the
Accused’s Lodge of these results. If the Accused is a member of more than one
Lodge, the Grand Secretary shall provide notification of these results to every
Lodge of which the Accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records.
If the penalty includes suspension or expulsion, it shall be effective immediately
upon the Grand Secretary’s receipt of the Commissioners’ written report fixing the
penalty. The notice to the Accused shall include an explanation of his status as a
suspended or an expelled Mason.
If the penalty is reprimand, the Commissioners shall summon the Accused to
appear at a Stated Meeting of the Constituent Lodge of which the Accused has
been removed from office as Master. The Commissioners, or such other person as
the Grand Master may designate, shall deliver the reprimand.
If the Accused has completed his term of office prior to the determination of
his guilt and if he has not been found guilty of a specification which constitutes
unmasonic conduct, the Accused shall be reprimanded in the manner set forth in
Section 1404.630 of this Code, and the presiding Commissioner, or his designee,
shall deliver the reprimand.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Current Masonic Law provides that if a Lodge Master has been found
guilty of abuse of his authority as Master he must be removed from office even
if he has not committed unmasonic conduct. Current law also provides that the
prosecution of charges against a sitting Lodge Master may continue to verdict even
if the Master has completed his term of office. However, the law does not provide
any penalty that may be imposed against a Lodge Master who has completed
his term of office and is found guilty of having abused his authority by conduct
that does not amount to unmasonic conduct. This resolution would amend section
1403.040 to provide the penalty of reprimand in that situation.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

199

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
This proposed revision to the provision of the Masonic Code which
provides for the trial of a former Master on charges arising during his tenure as
Master on which he is found guilty of a specification which is determined not to
be unmasonic conduct answers an ambiguity in the Code as to what penalty is
allowed by requiring him to be reprimanded in open lodge in the same manner as
any other Mason who is ordered to suffer a reprimand.
This revision to the Code is necessary to resolve the ambiguity currently
in the Code as to the proper penalty to be assessed; accordingly, the Committee on
Trial Review recommends that Resolution Number 11-11 be adopted.

Resolution ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 11-12
Adds Explanation of Other Recognized Jurisdictions’ Grand Hailing Signs
to the Lecture of the Master Mason Degree
The proponents of this Resolution seek to include an explanation of the Grand
Hailing Signs of other jurisdictions, recognized by the Grand Lodge of California,
in the Ritual.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, all Masons have an indispensable duty to come to the aid
of a distressed worthy Brother Mason; and
WHEREAS, Masons of other jurisdictions may have been taught Grand
Hailing Signs that differ from those taught within California Lodges; and
WHEREAS, international travel brings many Masons from diverse
jurisdictions to our area and many of our Brothers travel abroad on occasion; and
WHEREAS, some jurisdictions already demonstrate Grand Hailing
Signs of other recognized jurisdictions, including Lodges of the United Grand
Lodge of England; and
WHEREAS, the failure to come to the aid of a distressed Brother for
lack of recognition of a sign of distress would weigh heavily on the heart and
conscience of a Brother.
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Committee on
Ritual determine which Grand Hailing Signs of recognized Grand Lodges should
be made known to Master Masons under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.

200

Proceedings of the

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Lecture of the Master Mason
Degree be modified by the Committee on Ritual to add a demonstration of these
Grand Hailing Signs.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Grand Hailing Signs selected
by the Committee on Ritual be demonstrated at Officers Schools of Instruction
and at least once a year at Stated Meetings of Constituent Lodges until the Lecture
of the Master Mason Degree has been modified as provided in this resolution.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Proponents of this Resolution seek to add to our ritual the
requirement that Grand Hailing Signs of other Grand Lodges be made known to
Master Masons in California.
The Proponents speak to the ease of international travel and the possible
exposure of California Masons to situations where a Grand Hailing sign may be
given, without the proper response by our Brother.
While this is may be a noble request, the possible implementation in
California presents some logistical obstacles. For example, there is no guidance as
to which Grand Hailing Signs should be taught and how they would be presented
in our Ritual.
Our Grand Lodge has a long and enduring record of maintaining our
Ritual intact and there does not appear to be any specific need to add to it.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The Proponents of this Resolution seek to include an explanation of
the Grand Hailing Signs of other jurisdictions, recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California, in the Ritual. There are well over a hundred recognized foreign
jurisdictions, the jurisdictions of each state, and an additional number of Prince
Hall Grand Lodges. It would be a significant amont of work to pull together the
Grand Hailing Signs of these jurisdictions, although many would be the same or
similar. It would also be a fairly large task to document, learn and modify ritual
to include them. As jurisdictions are at times removed or added to our recognition
list, this could promulgate multiple ritual changes over time. Acknowledging that
the signs could be demonstrated again later, we believe it is also unlikely that any
candidate would remember any but our own jurisdiction’s.
The proponents have also suggested that the Ritual Committee should
determine which Grand Hailing Signs of recognized Grand Lodges should be made
known to Master Masons under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge. Determining

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

201

which to teach and which to leave out is subjective and could imply a judgment
that one jurisdiction is more important than another. This would further place the
burden on all AGL’s, Inspectors and Officer Coaches to learn, to retain and to be
able to teach these signs during ritual instruction.
The Ritual Committee does not support Resolution No. 11-12.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
A.

Sunday Meetings. No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be
held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers or funeral
services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar Lodge falls on a Sunday, the
Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.

B.

Work to be Done in Lodge of Master Masons. All business, except the
examination of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, and the consideration of relief of a
worthy Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Masons. A Lodge of
Master Masons may be called down for the examination of candidates
in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft degrees.

C.

Quorum. A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done
or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under the
continual direction of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand Master
or the Grand Master’s designated representative. No Lodge shall transact
any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge present except
the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his post in
the Tiler’s room.

D.

Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless
the Charter of the Lodge is present. A photocopy of the Charter may
be made under the direction of the Grand Secretary at the request
and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary shall attach thereto a
certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy is a true
copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.

E.

Presence of Flag. The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all
meetings of a Lodge. At the annual election of officers, and at such other
meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag shall be
formally presented at the Altar and received in the manner prescribed in
the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.

206

Proceedings of the

F.

No Smoking. Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when
the Lodge is in session.

G.

No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each
meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for
transaction has been concluded.

H.

Good Standing Requirement. No member may make a motion, second
a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion, recommend anyone for
membership or ballot on membership at a Lodge meeting unless he is
then a member in good standing of that Lodge. He must present a current
dues receipt to the Tiler to demonstrate that he is a member of the Lodge
in good standing or be verified by the Master, Senior Warden, Junior
Warden, Secretary or Assistant Secretary as a member of the Lodge in
good standing.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the California Masonic
Code in several areas regarding Masons not in good standing. These changes can
be summarized as follows:
1. Require the Secretary to notify each member annually of the
consequences of not being a member in good standing.
2. Require that a Mason be in good standing to serve on a Lodge
committee, make a motion, second a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion,
recommend anyone for membership or ballot on membership at a Lodge meeting.
3. Require any Mason desiring to speak, vote, or otherwise participate
in a Lodge meeting to present a current dues receipt to the Tiler or be vouched for
by the Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden, Secretary, or Assistant Secretary as
being in good standing.
The first change (annual notification of the consequences of not being a
member in good standing) is consistent with Grand Lodge policy of encouraging
member retention and does not impose an undue burden on a Lodge.
The second change (limitation of the rights and privileges of a member
not in good standing) must be viewed as directed primarily at a member who
is not in good standing but has not yet been suspended, because, according to
Section 804.155 of the California Masonic Code, a suspended member is already
deprived of all rights, privileges, and benefits as a Mason and prohibited from any
Masonic communication until legally restored.
Currently, a Brother who is not in good standing but has not yet been
suspended may not serve on a Grand Lodge committee, receive an award from
Grand Lodge, apply for dispensation to open a new Lodge, affiliate with another

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

207

Lodge, transfer his membership to another jurisdiction, apply for a Demit, serve
as a Lodge officer, vote in Lodge elections, prefer Masonic charges, be recognized
as a Past Master, or be eligible for admission to the Masonic Homes. He is not
otherwise restricted from participating in Lodge.
This resolution would place further restrictions on such a Brother’s
activities in Masonry, such as not serving on a Lodge committee or balloting
on membership. This proposed change is consistent with the other restrictions
already placed on a Brother who is not in good standing. It is the policy of Grand
Lodge that a Brother who wishes to be active in his Lodge should pay his dues.
The third change (requiring a member to present a current dues receipt
or be vouched for) is intended to enforce the restrictions of this resolution. In
practice, the Master and Secretary should know which Brothers are not in good
standing and can enforce this requirement as needed. Requiring a Brother to
present a current dues card on request is not unreasonable.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to require that the Installing Officer and
Master of Ceremonies for Lodge installations be certified as proficient by the

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Lodge installations are most often open to family and

WHEREAS, the Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges can and

WHEREAS, when the ceremony is done poorly, it can be embarrassing
to Lodge officers and their guests, and reflect negatively upon the fraternity; and
WHEREAS, we currently require certification to conduct the Funeral
Service, as a way to ensure that the service is conducted only by those who have
the ability to perform it well; and

§405.030. DUTIES.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.510 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.510. INSTALLATION.
Lodge officers, including incumbents succeeding themselves in office, shall be
installed as soon as is practical after their election or appointment. There can be
no installation by proxy. The installation may be private or public. Two Lodges
may participate in a joint installation.
Lodge officers shall be installed using the Installation Ceremony for Constituent
Lodges, with the Master serving as the Installing Officer. Alternatively, by
invitation of the Master, the Installing Officer may be any qualified Past Master of
any Jurisdiction. It is not the privilege of the Master-elect to select the Installing
Officer or in any way interfere with the duty and privilege of the Master to install
his successor in office, if he so chooses. If the Installing Officer is a Past Master,
the Master or a Warden of the Lodge must be present. The Master of Ceremonies
may be any qualified Past Master of any Jurisdiction. The Installing Officer and
Master of Ceremonies at the Installation Ceremony must be certified pursuant to
Section 405.055 of this Code.
Lodge officers shall hold their respective offices until their successors have been
duly elected or appointed and installed.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

211

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution would require that the Installing Officer and Master of
Ceremonies be certified before being permitted to preside at a Lodge Installation.
The proponents point out that a majority of our installations are held with
our families and the public present and should be an impressive ceremony, by
which our fraternity is cast in only the most positive light. When the ceremony is
done poorly, it can be embarrassing to Lodge officers and their guests, and reflect
negatively upon the fraternity.
It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge to require that all Masonic
ceremonies, particularly those open to the public, such as funerals, be presented
in the best manner possible. This proposal would not guarantee perfect work at
an Installation; but it does insure that those who preside at this most important
ceremony have proven their ability to perform the work in a proper fashion.
We make every effort to maintain a high standard of ritual work while in
lodge; we should do the same in public. It is important to remember; we have very
few opportunities to highlight our Fraternity in the public eye.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.
Resolution No. 11-15
Allows Grand Lodge to Use the Same Auditor for
More Than Five Consecutive Years
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow Grand Lodge to use the same
auditor for more than five consecutive years.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Grand Lodge Committee on Audit was added to the
California Masonic Code with the requirement that the firm acting as auditor be
changed every five years; and
WHEREAS, neither the California Non Profit Integrity Act of 2004
applicable to California non-profit organizations nor the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of
2002 applicable to U.S. public companies requires that the audit firm be changed
every five years; and
WHEREAS, it may not be in the best interests of the Grand Lodge or its
related entities to change the audit firm every five years.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 406.015 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

212

Proceedings of the

§406.015. AUDIT.
The Committee on Audit shall consist of not less than three or more than seven
members. Any other provision of this Code to the contrary withstanding, the
Committee on Audit shall consist solely of members of the Grand Lodge. At
least one member of the Committee on Audit should have sufficient education
and experience as a public accountant, auditor or principal accounting officer to
be a financial expert. The Committee on Audit may not include a member of
the Grand Lodge staff. The Committee on Audit may not include any member
of the Grand Lodge who receives any compensation (other than reimbursement
of necessary, out-of-pocket expenses incurred for serving on the Committee on
Audit) from Grand Lodge or who has any material financial interest in any entity
doing business with Grand Lodge. Members of the Committee on Finance may
serve on the Committee on Audit; however, the chairman of the Committee on
Audit may not be a member of the Committee on Finance, and members of the
Committee on Finance may only constitute a minority of the membership of the
Committee on Audit. The Committee on Audit shall:
A.

Cause the annual Grand Lodge financial statements to be certified by
the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer (and the
chief accounting officer of the Grand Lodge if not the Grand Treasurer)
as presenting fairly the financial condition and operations of the
Grand Lodge;

B.

Cause the annual Grand Lodge financial statements to be audited by a
firm of independent certified public accountants pursuant to standards
for auditor independence;

C.

Obtain from the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and the Grand
Treasurer an evaluation of the effectiveness of the Grand Lodge’s
internal controls;

D.

Require the auditor to disclose to the Committee on Audit all critical
accounting policies and procedures used by Grand Lodge as well as to
share with the Committee on Audit any discussions with senior Grand
Lodge staff and officers about such policies and practices;

E.

Confer with the auditor to satisfy its members that the financial affairs of
the Grand Lodge are in good order, to review and determine whether to
accept the audit, and to recommend to Grand Lodge whether to accept or
reject the audit;

F.

Cause the Grand Lodge’s audited financial statements to be made
available for inspection by all members of the Grand Lodge in the same
manner that is currently prescribed for IRS Form 990 upon request and
no later than nine months after the close of the fiscal year;

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

213

G.

Subject to the supervision of the Grand Lodge, to retain, supervise,
terminate and settle the compensation of the firm acting as auditor. The
firm acting as auditor shall be changed every five years The Committee
on Audit shall review the firm acting as auditor every year. If the same
firm is selected to act as auditor for more than five consecutive years, the
Committee on Audit shall report such fact to the Grand Lodge together
with the reasons therefor; and

H.

Assure that no nonaudit services are performed by the auditing firm,
other than tax services and tax preparation when specifically authorized
in advance by the Committee on Audit.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Current Masonic Law requires that the Grand Lodge outside auditing
firm must be changed every five years. This Resolution seeks to amend the Code
by deleting the five-year limitation. In its place, the Resolution would require the
Grand Lodge Committee on Audit to review annually the outside auditing firm
and, if it deems it appropriate to retain the same firm for more than five years, to
report that fact to Grand Lodge together with the reasons therefore.
It is common for an entity to change auditors every so often so as to lessen
the possibility that a less than arms-length relationship might develop between
the auditor and the entity it audits. The auditors might become too trusting of
management and not remain truly independent.
Offsetting these concerns is the efficiency and resulting lower costs
that come from the people involved, both on the audit side and the management
side, learning to work well together over a period of years. Grand Lodge has
great confidence in its current financial staff, in its ability and in its integrity. It
also has great respect for its outside audit firm and the principals who have been
working on its accounts. More importantly, the Grand Lodge Audit Committee is
comprised of experienced, career accountants and auditors who are very diligent
in overseeing the audit process and the people involved.
The proponents of this Resolution point out that neither state nor
federal law require an auditing firm to be changed every five years. As the policy
considerations for the current five-year limitation are not of concern at this time,
there is no logical basis for requiring a change in auditors every five years simply
for the sake of change.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

Resolution No. 11-16
Adds Chaplain to the List of Lodge Officers

The proponents of this Resolution seek to add Chaplain to the list of
Lodge Officers.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a member of the lodge is installed as Chaplain at the
Lodge’s annual installation of officers; and
WHEREAS, the Monitor & Officers Manual as well as the California
cipher spell out the Chaplain’s duties.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.010 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.010. OFFICERS.
The officers of a Lodge are Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden, Treasurer,
Secretary, Chaplain, Senior Deacon, Junior Deacon, Marshal, Senior Steward,
Junior Steward, Tiler and other officers as the Lodge may deem proper to appoint.
The Master, Senior Warden and Junior Warden, Treasurer and Secretary shall be
elected in conformity with this Code. The other officers shall be appointed by
the Master. Any Master Mason in good standing, whether or not a member of the
Lodge, may be appointed Tiler or Organist. All other officers shall be members in
good standing of the Lodge.
A member may not be Master, Warden or Secretary, or any combination thereof,
of more than one Lodge at the same time. A member may not hold more than one
office in a Lodge at the same time.
The title of Master applies not only to him who has been elected and installed as
Master, but to either of the Wardens while acting as Master.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
California Masonic Code section 805.010 specifies the officers of the
Lodge, such as Master, Wardens, Deacons, and the like. For reasons that are
not clear, the Chaplain, which every Lodge has, is not listed as an officer of the
Lodge. This Resolution would amend section 805.010 to include the Chaplain as
an enumerated Lodge officer.
The position of Chaplain is one of the most important of all officer
positions. It is the Chaplain who invokes the aid and blessing of Deity at the
beginning and end of every Lodge meeting. The Chaplain receives his jewel

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

215

during the officers’ jewel march. The position of Chaplain is one of the enumerated
Grand Lodge officer positions. Passage of this Resolution would give the same
dignity to the office of Lodge Chaplain as to all other Lodge officer positions.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 11-17
Modifies Funeral Service Certification Procedure
The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify the Funeral Service Certification
procedure to conform it to current practice.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 405.030.F of the California Masonic Code lists
as one duty of an Inspector the duty to issue certificates to perform the Funeral
Service; and
WHEREAS, Section 405.050 indicates that the Inspector is to apply to
the Grand Master for the certificate; and
WHEREAS, the language of sections 405.030 (Duties of Inspector),
and 405.050 (Funeral Service Certifications) are currently in conflict; and
WHEREAS, there has been, over the last several years, a lack of
consistency as to how information relative to Funeral Service Certification is
reported to Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the language of Section 405.050 should be consistent with
current procedures and practices.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 405.050 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§405.050. FUNERAL SERVICE CERTIFICATIONS.
Master Masons may be certified to officiate at Masonic funerals and memorial
services in this Jurisdiction as follows:
A.

The Inspector of the district shall certify to the proficiency of all who
perform the Funeral Service for the Lodges within his district, or those of
adjacent districts. Upon being completely satisfied as to the proficiency

216

Proceedings of the
and qualification of such Master Masons, the Inspector shall, forward
to the Grand Master a request that issue to each such Master Mason a
certificate of qualification and authorization be issued which shall grant
to him each such Master Mason the authority to perform the Funeral
Service of this Jurisdiction when properly requested to do so;

B.

Prior to officiating, the Master must be certified in the Funeral Service.
If the Master is not certified, it shall be the responsibility of the Master
and the Inspector to have a certified Master Mason available at all times;

C.

In order to be certified, a Master Mason must demonstrate the following
to the complete satisfaction of the Inspector:
1.

Delivery of the Funeral Service in its entirety in a creditable
manner, either by total memorization or the ability to read and
deliver it in a creditable manner;

2.

Proper pronunciation and enunciation;

3.

Complete knowledge of duties and responsibilities of the
Funeral Service officiant;

4.

Personal habits, dignity, and appearance appropriate to the
solemnity of the Service; and

5.

Emotional stability;

D.

All requests for certificates shall be submitted on the Grand Lodge form
to be furnished to the Inspector and shall be effective for a period of three
years from date of issuance;

E.

The Inspector shall maintain a current record of all qualified Master
Masons in his district, with date of certification and expiration date
and shall forward a copy to the Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand
Lecturer each year on July 1st, when filing his annual report the names
and qualification dates of those Master Masons issued certificates by him
to the Grand Secretary as soon after issuance as is practical;

F.

The Inspector shall furnish annually to the Master of each Lodge in his
district, and the Executive Secretary of all adjacent Masonic Service
Bureaus, a written list of all Master Masons who are currently qualified
in his district. He shall also notify the above named individuals of any
additions or deletions during the year, at the time such changes occur;

G.

Prior to renewal of any certificate, the Inspector must satisfy himself as
to the Master Mason’s continued proficiency; and

H.

Any Inspector desiring a certificate must be examined and certified by
another Inspector who has already been certified, by his Assistant Grand
Lecturer or by the Grand Lecturer.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

217

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to conform the law to the current
practices followed in the issuance of certificates to perform funeral services. As
it is now written, California Masonic Code section 405.050 requires an Inspector,
after he certifies a Master Mason’s funeral proficiency, to request that the Grand
Master issue a certificate to the qualified individual so that the qualified person
can conduct a funeral service.
Currently, each Inspector is given Funeral Certificate cards at the
beginning of each year and is required to keep a list of those men he certifies.
The Inspectors are not expected to contact Grand Lodge staff or the Grand Master
when they make such certifications.
Passage of this Resolution would change current law to conform to
current practice. In addition, as this Resolution also provides that the Inspector
must notify the Grand Secretary that a certificate has been issued, it would ensure
that Grand Lodge can maintain an appropriate record.
District Inspectors are, in essence, Grand Master deputies and as such
are given some autonomous authorities. The authority to qualify Master Masons
in various aspects of the ritual is one such example.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 11-18 seeks to waive all application fees and the first
year’s dues for a DeMolay or Senior DeMolay who applies for the degrees
within four years after his eighteenth birthday. This waiver provides that the
applicant will not make contributions to the Masonic Homes of California, the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial, or the California Masonic
Memorial Temple.
This Resolution proposes to establish preferential treatment within the
membership of the Order of DeMolay and create two classes of applicants which
are contrary to Masonic principles and the policy of this Grand Lodge.
While it is in the best interest of Masonry to provide an avenue for anyone
who meets the age criteria to join the ranks of Masonry, it might be condescending
to waive all application fees only for members of the Order of DeMolay. One
of the many lessons that we are taught in Freemasonry is that of charity, and by
waiving those fees that provide the initial funding for our Masonic Charities, we
are not providing the charitable lesson that is an extremely important principle
of our Order. By waiving these fees we are not providing our Masonic Youth
with the lessons that we must live our daily lives in accordance with certain
responsibilities, financial and otherwise.
Many of our Brethren would gladly aid and assist a qualified DeMolay
with the necessary fees for his degrees if it was known that he was financially
unable at the time to submit a petition for Masonic degrees.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Prior to the adoption of the Fourth Revision of the California Masonic
Code in 2006, a Mason who had been convicted of, or entered a plea of nolo
contendere to, a crime of moral turpitude was subjected to a Masonic Trial. At that
time, any extenuating circumstances could be introduced with regard to the setting
of the penalty. Section 1404.820 of that Fourth Revision requires an automatic
expulsion of such an individual without the benefit of any such due process.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

223

The manner whereby such a man may be restored is described in
section 1404.1050 of the California Masonic Code. This process begins with
that man accepting responsibility for his actions, expressing credible remorse
for his behavior, making amends and financial restitution for his crime, and
demonstrating, through his subsequent actions, a change in his life as seen by his
current acquaintances, significant involvement in community, charitable, church,
or other programs that favorably enhance the society in which he lives, a stable
family life, a stable and consistent economic life, and a change in attitude. He
must have completed his period of probation or parole and a period of at least
five years should have elapsed since that completion. In other words, he must be
fully rehabilitated. The members of his prior lodge have to be convinced of these
facts and conduct a formal ballot in which at least two-thirds of the votes have
to be in favor of restoration. The lodge then presents a formal application for
restoration which must be passed by Grand Lodge with the same requirements as
those needed for a change in our laws.
Since 2006, three men have sought restoration. In all of these cases, the
resolution failed to achieve even a majority vote that would have allowed it to
be carried over to the following year. One of those men is again the subject of
Resolution 11-19, and the arguments either in favor or against his restoration are
not the province of this committee. However, this committee would note that,
in each of the floor discussions in the past, an argument has been put forth that
the mere fact that a person was convicted of a felony is a suitable reason to deny
future restoration.
Such an argument is contrary to our current law; clearly any man seeking
restoration has committed a crime in the past. Since our law does allow for the
possibility of restoration, each case must be judged on its own merits.
This Resolution is consistent with our policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
In 2009, Grand Master Adamson’s Decision Number Three set forth a
detailed set of criteria to be considered when determining whether an expelled or
suspended Mason has demonstrated rehabilitation from his past conduct so that
his reinstatement would not be contrary to our Masonic principles. These criteria
include the likelihood that he will repeat the conduct which gave rise to the
suspension or expulsion; his acceptance of responsibility, remorse and atonement
for his conduct; and, a change in attitude.
Dr. Valenton was convicted of insurance fraud and income tax evasion
arising from a scheme involving personal injury cases. The conduct giving rise to
the convictions occurred almost 20 years ago. The proponents of this Resolution,
and of the Resolution presented to this Grand Lodge last year, have provided letters
of support, court and other documents, and interviews that show the following:

224

Proceedings of the

Dr. Valenton accepted full responsibility for his misconduct and expressed
shame and remorse directly to the Grand Master. He changed his manner of
practice after his convictions and refused to accept any personal injury cases. For
the past 8 years he has been a “house doctor” at a psychiatric hospital. He has been
married for 34 years and has three children: one is the ob/gyn Chief Resident at
Cedars-Sinai Hospital, one is an occupational therapist with a Masters degree, and
one is at the University of Arizona. He and his wife, an anesthesiologist, have paid
and are still paying for their educations.
For the past 10 years, Dr. Valenton has participated in medical missions
lasting up to 2 weeks, rendering medical aid to indigents in the Philippines. He
is currently in the process of setting up, with the Master of his former Lodge, a
group to organize medical and dental missions to serve the Aetas, an indigenous
Philippine tribe that has no medical services.
Based on the above, this Committee last year recommended that Dr.
Valenton had met Grand Master Adamson’s criteria for rehabilitation and therefor
was a suitable candidate for reinstatement.
However, following our report last year a Past Master of Dr. Valenton’s
Lodge reported to Grand Lodge that he did not report the conviction on his
application for membership. At the request of the Committee an investigation
was performed and it was discovered that he relevant questions on the application
were left blank but that the application in the archives of the Lodge had an
attachment which listed the conviction. The Committee cannot determine based
on the evidence whether the attachment to the application was submitted with the
original application or was attached later.
In either case, however, this presents the Committee with two possible
scenarios: either Dr. Valenton did not report the convictions on his application
or he did and the Lodge improperly balloted on it despite the fact that he was
clearly disqualified from petitioning the Lodge because of the conviction. In
either case, the end result is that if our rules had been complied with he could
never have joined the fraternity in the first place but now, having been improperly
admitted and then expelled,. he is technically qualified to apply for re-admission.
Whether by design or not, this presents an “end run” around our rules which
this Committee cannot endorse. This resolution is in effect special legislation
allowing Dr. Valenton special status within our fraternity by allowing him alone
membership despite the provision of our law which prohibits a man convicted of
a crime of moral turpitude from becoming a member.
Based on these facts, the Committee recommends that Dr. Valenton not
be reinstated.

Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Report of the President of the
Board of Trustees
It has been another eventful and productive year for Masonic Homes
of California.
Finances. In past years I reported on the financial challenges we faced
as a result of the downturn in economy and decline in our investment portfolio.
I also advised you that we were meeting those challenges by anticipating trends
and carefully managing our resources. I am pleased to report that we continue
to be successful in dealing with the challenge. Let me recount what we faced.
As you know, we have sound investment and distribution policies that have
served the organization well for many years. This includes a distribution formula
that protects the corpus of our endowment. It also includes a 20-quarter trailing
average on which our distribution formula is based to smooth out the natural
fluctuations in the portfolio’s value. Our special challenge was caused by the
biggest drop in the stock market in decades beginning in the Fall of 2008. As the
negative quarters replaced the positive quarters in the 20-quarter average, there
would be a natural reduction in our revenues, and so we created an eight-year plan
to deal with the lean years. At the same time, we were advised by the Investment
Committee that the coming decade was likely to see a reduction in the total return
we had enjoyed in the preceding decades—not because of poor investment advice
but because of the natural fluctuations of a market economy. Two years ago the
Investment Committee recommended a reduction in the distribution formula from
5.0% to 4.5%. The Board of MHC went a step further and reduced our distribution
to 4.25%.
Through the good work of the Finance Committee and management, we
ended fiscal year 2010 with a surplus of $4.3 million and we are projecting a
surplus of $2.3 million for this fiscal year, which we had expected to be a very
difficult year. Even discounting some unusual revenues, we are still doing well,
and we have met this financial challenge without compromising the quality of our
services and while implementing our new Philosophy of Care, which emphasizes
wellness, quality of life and empowering our residents and clients to achieve their
full potential. We have also continued to fund our projected pension fund liability
by an additional $1 million per year.
While we are encouraged by our success thus far, we understand the
challenge remains. If we needed a reminder of that, the market gyrations in
August, 2010 provided it.
Partly in recognition of the good work we have been doing, our “AA”
rating was reaffirmed in the past year by both Fitch and Standard & Poors. I
thank Chairman Glenn Woody and his committee for their exemplary service the
past year.

230

Proceedings of the

MCYAF. Last year, I reported at length about the process by which
Masonic Center for Youth and Family was planned and developed. As a reminder,
MCYAF is a unique place for the treatment of youth with emotional or behavioral
issues. First, we conduct comprehensive assessments at the very beginning of
treatment so that we have a full picture of the child or teen. Second, a treatment
manager coordinates the various aspects of services so that we manage treatment
in as seamless a way possible for the patient and his/her family. Third, our
clinicians (all of them senior clinicians with years of experience in the field)
develop detailed treatment plans at conferences with the entire team so that he
or she has the best thinking of many minds. Fourth, we provide individualized
treatment that can include integrated family or couples counseling if the needs of
the child or teen require it. Fifth, we are committed to outcome studies so that we
are constantly improving as a team and—in the future—contributing to the body
of knowledge in the field.
I am happy to report that in February of this year, we opened MCYAF’s
doors. It was a few months later than we had projected because of the difficulty
getting our license in the face of budget cutbacks to the Department of Public
Health, the State agency that has jurisdiction. At this writing, our assessment &
testing service is fully booked several months in advance, and our clinical hours
are being filled such that we are planning to add staff soon. As of the end of July,
we had served 32 patients, of whom 6 had Masonic affiliation. In addition to the
6 receiving clinical services, we also have provided an additional 26 Masonic
families with case management, information & referral, and other services to
help them with their particular issues. Masonic calls of inquiry and visits have
been coming from throughout the state. Thus far, 25 different cities have been
represented. For a more detailed breakdown of these numbers, please see the
Steffani Kizziar’s staff report on MCYAF.
As important as these numbers are, the difference we are making in the
lives of kids and their families is best told in human terms. To illustrate, let me
tell you a story.
Worried parents recently called Masonic Center for Youth and Families
about their ten-year old “Sam”. He was struggling academically and had difficulties
making friends. As his frustration and isolation grew, so did his acting-out and he
was suspended from school for throwing a book at another student.
During their initial interview, the parents expressed their confusion,
concern, frustration and guilt. Their son, an only child, was inventive, curious
bright – he would take apart old electronic equipment to see how it worked and
fixed their vacuum cleaner when he was eight. He spent hours drawing intricate
designs for new machines that would do such things as fill the car up with gas
or mop the floor. Yet, he was falling further and further behind in his studies.
He was often obstinate and moody and refused to follow directions. They both
expressed regret and guilt over frequently becoming short-tempered with him

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

231

and they acknowledged the difficulties in their marriage. When he met with the
social worker at Masonic Center for Youth and Families he described himself as
“stupid” and said with a shrug, “Yeah, I’m irritating.”
The staff of the Center talked with his teacher who described Sam as
having a difficult time concentrating and acting like a bully with other children.
She thought he “had ADD and should be on medication.”
His coach described Sam as ‘likeable and shy’ and struggling to
follow directions.
The picture that emerged was complicated and clearly indicated a child
in pain. We needed to understand what was happening so we could understand
how to help.
Sam spent three days with one of our Assessment Psychologists who
conducted personality, academic and emotional testing. The doctor was committed
to understanding how Sam learned and processed information, how he coped with
stress, how he made sense of his world and how he felt inside.
The test findings validated all that his parents, teacher and coach
had indicated.
He was very bright, curious and inventive – in fact; his IQ scores placed
him in the exceptional range.
He did have a difficult time concentrating and following directions – in
fact, Sam had a particular type of disorder that slowed down the speed at which
he processed information. So peers thought that he was ignoring them – instead
he was desperately trying to make sense of what they were saying. Despite being
exceptionally bright, he was in fact having a hard time understanding what was
happening. And so he was growing frustrated and without understanding what
was happening, would end up in a rage and throwing things.
Our emotional testing confirmed how much Sam was suffering. He
was depressed and growing increasingly hopeless and thought of himself as
“unlikeable” and “stupid”. Where the teacher saw a “bully”, we found a frightened,
lonely boy desperately fighting to establish himself as a real person in the minds
of his peers.
We met with the parents and with Sam and we described how very
bright he was and we described his processing disorder. We also acknowledge
how lonely and hurt Sam had been by the difficulties caused by this disorder
and the pain the parents were experiencing in their marriage and in parenting
Sam. We recommended individual therapy for Sam to help him come to a better
understanding and acceptance of himself as a basis for better understanding and
acceptance of others. We also recommended family therapy for the parents to help
address the difficulties in their marriage and to learn new ways of parenting Sam.
With the parents’ consent, we shared our findings with the school and his new
teacher is working with Sam to ensure his academic success.

232

Proceedings of the

Two months later, the therapy continues and Sam is in his second week
of school and just got 100% on his first spelling test. This is significant because
Sam had to carefully listen to the words to spell them correctly. He is learning
new ways of listening and this is translating to academic success. And academic
success is translating to improved self-esteem. Just yesterday he announced to
his therapist with shy excitement that he received an invitation to a classmate’s
birthday party.
At the Masonic Center for Youth and Families we are committed to
caring for children with behavioral, learning and emotional problems in way no
one else in the country is doing. Our team of experts learns about the child in all
their strengths and vulnerabilities. We don’t label children – we understand them.
And such understanding is the key to unlocking their potential.
Strategic Planning. Under the chairmanship of Fred Avery, the
Strategic Planning Committee has embarked upon an exciting new direction for
the organization, targeting the changes MHC will need to make to its services and
structures in the year 2020, when the demographics of the organization will be
much different than it is today. By 2020, the average age of members will drop
from the current 64 years old to 54, a remarkable drop of one year of age for every
year that passes. Almost 40% of our members will have minor children (up from
21% today). Almost 55% will have aging parents (up from 43% today). One of
the fastest growing age groups in recent years has been Masons in their twenties
and thirties. What will put stress and strain on the “typical” Mason of 2020 will be
different than it is today, and so MHC must also expand and evolve to meet those
needs. Now is the time to begin planning for those changes.
The demographics of older Masons are also changing. The number of
members over 60 is expected to decline from 38,000 today to 23,000 by 2020,
a drop of 40% in less than ten years. The number of members aged 75-85 (the
typical age range of an MHC resident) will decline from 14,000 today to 8,000, a
drop of 44%. Overall, the average age of members will drop from the current 64
years old to 54 by 2020.
At the same time, the lifestyle preferences of Masons are also
changing as it relates to aging. A survey of member needs and attitudes was
conducted in the Spring of 2011. In total, 880 fraternal family members
participated in the survey in live or online forums. Some of the key findings:
•

85% said they preferred to have services offered in their own homes as
they aged

•

Their number one future concern was the cost of health care

•

77% agreed with offering fee-based services to the public in order to
support programs that benefitted the fraternity

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

233

A significant related statistic: currently, MHC serves only about 1%
of age-eligible Masons. This very low percentage suggests we should be doing
more for our aging members, their wives and widows. But their declining overall
numbers over the next ten years and the stated preference of Masons to have needed
services brought to them in their own home strongly suggest that our enhanced
services should not be via large-scale construction or expansion of independent
living units, but rather through the creation and refinement of alternative services.
Strategic Planning and management are working together to help the
Board develop a new Vision for MHC that will help it meet these new challenges.
At the annual Board retreat in May, four strategic initiatives were identified that
will be explored, refined and developed into potential business models for the
Board’s consideration at various points in the next year. As I write this, Strategic
Planning is developing the action plan and early timetable for deliverables. The
four initiatives:
•

Lodge Outreach

•

Youth & Family Services

•

Cutting Edge Memory Support/Dementia Care

•

Care at Home

I expect to report more specifically about our direction in my report to
you in 2012. I thank Brother Fred for his exemplary leadership in guiding the
Strategic Planning Committee and management staff in this bold new direction.
Board Development. Three years ago, the Board embarked on a special
emphasis to improve its internal processes and functions. Under the able leadership
of Jack Rose, the Board Development Committee has continued the fine work
of previous year. Our confidential survey of trustees’ self-evaluation showed an
across the board improvement in results and satisfaction of 10-20% on top of
very similar improvements the prior year. The committee has helped to guide the
Board in this endeavor in a number of ways: special emphasis on goal-setting and
goal-tracking by all of the major committees; refinement of the outreach program
to identify potential future trustees for consideration by the Grand Master; a
more systematic approach to outside educational opportunities for trustees; and
planning for more comprehensive and relevant internal education, including the
use of WebEx and other web-based tools.
Children’s Homes Alumni. We continue to provide support to the kids
who were residents of the children’s homes at the time we transitioned from the
residential program. Two of the 13 children were reunified with their families and
no longer needed assistance. Three children graduated from high school this year.

Proceedings of the

Two of them were approved for scholarships and the third plans to enlist in the
Army when he turns 18 at the end of summer. At the start of July, we were serving
8 former residents, all of whom were receiving financial case management to
some degree.
Scholarships. In April we approved scholarships beginning with
the fall semester to 21 alumni of the children’s homes, a record number. They
are attending four-year colleges, two-year community colleges, and a variety
of vocational programs. The 12 alumni who were scholarship recipients for

be proud of their achievements. During the year, we instituted some policy &
procedural changes to the scholarship program designed to improve the longevity
of the program, encourage more accountability by the recipients and improve its
flexibility. For instance, we now allow scholarships outside of California when
there are good reasons, and we provide case management when needed for kids
who may need a small amount of assistance adjusting to life in college.
Old Children’s Homes. The old children’s homes are being used for
planning and training retreats by various Masonic or affiliated groups. They have
been used for Inspector trainings, and DeMolay and Job’s Daughters have used
them for planning and training several times. We continue to search for a more
permanent use. Our efforts this past year have been hampered by regulatory
restrictions (for example, the need to fingerprint permanent users) and the
specialized nature of the architectural design. We expect to shortly retain a real
estate specialty firm to conduct a “highest and best use” analysis at the same time
we retain a local realtor to explore rental of the houses.
Family Outreach. We launched the program in October 2009 in
response to brothers affected by the severe economic downturn and have been
refining the program ever since. In the past year, we have seen the amount of
direct financial assistance provided per person go down, but our non-financial
case management go up slightly. We are finding that providing good guidance,
support, encouragement , and referrals is sufficient for many Masons, who need
just that level of help to navigate the sometimes confusing system. On average
Masonic Family Outreach has been serving about 17 financial clients and 35 nonfinancial case management clients each month.
Senior Outreach. In contrast to Family Outreach, the need for assistance
from Senior Outreach has never been higher. We are seeing a steady increase in
applications for the program. Seniors are especially vulnerable in these tough
economic times because one’s assets and income are usually fixed, and the
opportunity to go back into the workforce is limited. We are also finding a higher
number of “young retirees” who left the workforce earlier than they had planned
because of the economy. In the past year, we provided direct financial assistance
to 188 clients. We also gave information & referral to about 260 and provided case
management to another 50 clients. The benefit of Masonic Senior Outreach can
best be told in a story. Here is just one.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

235

An elderly couple was referred to MSOS by their lodge. Despite careful
planning and frugal living, they had outlived their financial resources and were
scraping by on his social security income each month. They lived in an unsafe and
rough neighborhood in which their car had been broken into four times over the
past year and they were afraid to leave their apartment after dark.
Upon approval by the Board for Masonic Assistance, their case manager
helped identify a better, safer neighborhood with supportive services. The client
called his lodge brothers for help with the move. The response was overwhelming.
Almost twenty lodge brothers pitched in and helped sort, pack, haul and move the
couple into their new apartment. MSOS helped pay for the apartment and the
deposit yet the move cost nothing thanks to the effort of these brothers. Together
we ensured that our fraternal family members were safe and secure within our
circle of care.
The quote from the Care Manager best sums it up “Our client was able to
turn to his lodge like family and ask for help and they were happy to do it. I gave
a presentation at the lodge recently and it was heartwarming to see how everyone
was so eager to help them move. They are lodge brothers and true family.”

Admissions Committee
By Timothy A. Wood, Chairman
The Admissions Review Program of the Board is a carefully developed
analysis and evaluation process that continues to be improved and refined to meet
the evolving needs to our applicants, as well as the Homes Staff and the Board.
The interview process and on site evaluation is done at the same time
the applicant visits one of the two facilities. A Staff report on this overnight visit,
together with the Medical Director’s comments on his/her review of the medical
information, is then added to the application. The staff then develops an executive
summary on the applicants and presents that to the Admissions Committee for
review and approval. Anytime the Staff recommends against admission the
full application is given to the Admissions Committee for detailed review and
discussion during the Admissions Committee meeting. Any recommendation
against admission requires the full Board confirmation.
Prior to the regular Admissions Committee meeting on the second
Tuesday of each month, the three Trustees, who form the Admissions Committee,
each receive and carefully study the complete applications not recommended
for Masonic assistance and the executive summaries for applications
recommended for Masonic assistance. Each Trustee reviews and evaluates
the applications and accompanying data and then discusses his viewpoint
during the Admissions Committee meeting. Home’s Staff and Administrators
attend the Admissions Committee meeting to answer committee member’s
questions and to provide additional information to the committee members. The
committee’s recommendations and comments are then presented to the full Board
for confirmation.
The number of applications handled by the Admissions Committee
varies from month to month. During July 1, 2010 to June 30, 2011, there were 31
applicants admitted to the Union City campus, which currently has a total of 256
residents, including 16 residents in the Traditions Special Care Unit. In addition,
our Covina campus admitted 6 applicants which brought a total of 74 residents
which include 4 residents of whom are outplaced.
The Masonic Outreach Service program continues to grow, serving our
eligible Brethren and their families or widows within their local communities or
residence. Masonic Outreach provides case management to those in need of such
service and financial-case management to those who qualify. The Masonic Senior
Outreach program serves clients age 60 and older, and is currently serving 192
clients; 3 of whom are on outplacement by the Masonic Homes. In conjunction
with Masonic Outreach services, the Masonic Family Outreach program provides
service to the growing fraternal needs of our younger members, under the age of
60. The Masonic Family Outreach program is currently serving 58 clients.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

237

This year the committee has reviewed and approved a total of 67
applications for both of these programs. The care managers work closely with
the clients to ensure that their needs are being met, while fulfilling the programs’
guidelines. Through Masonic Senior and Family Outreach, we are able to serve
our “whole” fraternal family.
I would like to thank the other Trustees of the Admissions Committee,
Richard W. Hopper, PGM and John R. Heisner, who labor long and hard over
the applications. I would also like to express my appreciation to the Executive
Directors of Covina and Union City Homes, their supporting staff, and the
continued dedication of the Masonic Outreach staff and the Board of Trustees.

Finance Committee
By Glenn D. Woody, Chairman
It has been an honor for the members of the Finance Committee to serve
your Masonic Homes of California this past year. This committee monitors and
manages the finances for the Masonic Homes of California and is charged with
the important responsibility of ensuring that we serve our residents today, while
protecting our legacy for future generations.
The Masonic Homes of California uses a fiscal year ending on October
31st. For the eight months ended June 30, 2011 the Masonic Homes recorded
a surplus of income over expenses of $2.496 million. This result represents a
favorable variance from budget of $2.874 million, and was achieved by overall
revenues which exceeded the budget and expenses which were less than budget.
Operating expenditures of MHC have been guided by the Investment
Distribution Policy. This policy is set as a percentage of a five-year rolling
average of the General and Endowment Funds’ market value. This approach
insures our operating budget will be somewhat buffered from significant year toyear market swings while protecting the integrity of the fund balances for future
generations of residents. The financial market turmoil in 2008 and 2009 caused the
Investment Committee to recommend that the Masonic Homes consider lowering
its Distribution Policy Payout from 5.0% to 4.5%. The Finance Committee took
this recommendation seriously and reduced the payout further, to 4.25% in 2010
and 2011. This Committee is committed to constantly re-evaluating the operations
of the Homes to ensure we are operating efficiently, all the while maintaining the
highest level of care and resident satisfaction. In addition, we continue to explore
opportunities to diversify the revenue sources of the Homes to better protect our
assets for future generations.
The Finance Committee reviewed regular reports from the Grand
Treasurer and Chief Financial Officer. These reports include quarterly investment
performance reports, monthly operating statements, quarterly capital project
reviews and various others. Moss Adams, LLP, the auditors for Grand Lodge and
the Masonic Homes, have completed the annual external audit for the fiscal year
ended October 31, 2010, which was reviewed by the Finance Committee. The
audit was unqualified. The Audit for the fiscal year ending October 31, 2011 will
be completed in early 2012. The Committee also reviewed the IRS Form 990 and
the California Franchise Tax Board Form 199 regarding the Masonic Homes.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

239

The Finance Committee worked with management to develop the
fiscal year 2012 budget using a zero-based approach. In the face of ever rising
costs, management proposed, the Finance Committee continued to recommend
and the Board approved a budget which again used a 4.25% Investment
Distribution payout.
The Finance Committee also worked with management to develop a
capital project budget to assure the Homes remain well-maintained and safe to
protect the comfort and safety of our residents. The Homes continues to fund
the Capital Reserve Fund from a percentage of the annual depreciation through
the operating budget. This fund is used to pay for capital projects and to build a
reserve for future needs. The budget developed for FY2012 will allow the balance
in this fund to grow for future capital needs.
During the course of this year, the Committee also oversaw the
development and implementation of several new and important initiatives and
accomplishments, which include:

In preparing for the Acacia Creek Senior Living Communities, in 2007
Masonic Homes obtained, for the first time ever, a credit rating for the
Masonic Homes of California. The Fitch Ratings Agency and Standard
& Poors gave us a rating of AA, making us the highest rated senior living
community in the United States. The Masonic Homes has maintained
this rating through 2011.

Consistent with the senior living industry and the business community
at large, we froze the California Masonic Retirement Pension plan
