Strategic Planning Committee
By Fred L. Avery, Chairman
The Strategic Planning Committee is charged with the development and
update of the Masonic Homes of California Strategic Plan and oversight of new
initiatives to insure they are aligned with the mission and vision of the Homes and
with good governance best practices. The committee also supports the Homes in
implementing best industry standards for quality of care and service. In addition
to my own role as chair, the committee members include John L. Cooper, Gary G.
Charland, Michael Cornell and John W. Herring.
This has been a very active and exciting year for our committee as we
support the board in developing a new strategic plan for the Homes aligned to the
strategic plan for the Masons of California which challenges Masonic Homes to
continue to provide exceptional health care to our members.
This planning process began in May when our board held a threeday planning retreat in Covina out of which emerged four critical elements of
a renewed strategic vision for the Homes: developing continuing care at home;
developing state-of-the-art dementia care; providing outreach to youth and
families and outreach to lodges.
These four elements emerged not only from discussions with trustees and
management but from listening sessions held with members within a fifty-mile
radius of our Union City and Covina Campuses, reporting from online surveys
of our membership and feedback at presentations given at the Secretaries’ and
Treasurers’ retreats this spring as well as discussions with the Grand Master and
the leadership of our craft. The strategic planning will define the Masonic Homes
as a leader in the field of aging services that is well prepared to meet the needs of
our community and serve our members’ needs effectively and efficiently through
the next five years and beyond to the year 2020.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

241

In addition to the feedback provided by our members, the Strategic
Planning Committee and the board reviewed updated demographic information
about the fraternity that demonstrates the shift taking place in our membership.
Today, the Homes serves just one percent of the total eligible members. As
we look ahead, dramatic shifts in our membership will challenge us to reimagine
our service offerings if we want to reach out to a larger portion of our fraternity.
Looking ahead to 2020, average member age will fall from 64 years old
today to 54, a remarkable drop of one year of age for every year that passes. About
40% of our members will have minor children (up from 21% today) and 55% will
have aging parents (up from 43% today).
Feedback from our members shows that the vast majority prefers to
access services in their own homes and communities and that affording such
care is one of their biggest concerns. To effectively meet the needs of our
changing membership, the Masonic Homes must expand its commitment to youth
and families and develop services that can be provided across the state while
maintaining exceptional care standards at our two campuses.
The Strategic Planning Committee, our board and management are
working together develop a new Vision for Masonic Homes that will help it meet
these new challenges. This process will continue throughout 2012 and I, along
with my fellow committee members, the board and management are enthusiastic
to see the vision of the Homes realized.
Scholarship Program Committee
By Jack M. Rose, Chairman
The Masonic Homes of California Scholarship Program oversees the
scholarship available to the children who were former residents of the Masonic
Children’s program at the Masonic Homes at Covina.
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program has undergone significant
improvements over the past 3 years, which has been towards strengthening the
student’s accountability for their own performance and changing the mindset
of the scholarship as an entitlement to an earned privilege. The result of these
changes have led to students’ increased accountability and commitment to
their own education; improved academic performance; expanded educational
opportunities; enhanced case management support as well as academic workshops
and information sessions offered to the scholars and their parents.
In 2009, the Masonic Homes Scholarship Program provided partial
financial assistance to applicants pursuing a college leading up to a bachelors
degree. Initial applications needed to be made within 2 years following high school
graduation. The MH scholarship awards typically ranged from $10,000-$18,000
per academic school year. Moreover, there was no cap on the total amount that a

242

Proceedings of the

student could receive. Scholarships were renewable for three consecutive years,
for a total of four years, provided the student maintained a 2.0 or higher GPA and
submitted a renewal application each year with all the necessary documentation.
For the 2009-2010 academic year, 19 scholars were approved to receive a total of
$194,453 in scholarship support.
In June 2010, the Masonic Homes Scholarship Program was expanded
to include scholarship renewal for up to 5 years toward undergraduate studies, 2
years toward graduate studies and 5 years toward doctorial studies. Additionally,
the initial application age was extended to 25. An exception was granted to this
age-limit for those serving in the military, but required applicants to apply within
2 years of discharge from military. The program was also extended to include outof–state colleges/universities. Scholars were required to maintain a 2.0 G.P.A.,
minimally, in order to remain eligible for the program and would be placed on
academic probation if they fell below this mark.
To better manage the funds available for the scholarship program financial
awards were changed to a set dollar amount with an annual cap. Scholarship
awards were based on a student’s type of school (vocational, community college
or university), full-time or part-time status, and housing accommodations
(off-campus or on-campus). Additionally, the cap was established so that the
maximum amount of scholarship offered would not exceed 50% of the total cost
of a Cal-State full-time/off-campus education for the given year. This resulted
in scholars taking increased responsibility for determining how they would fill
their “financial gap” through other forms of financial aid such as grants, workstudy, parent loans/student loans and/or other outside scholarships. This decision
would be made by each scholar in conjunction with their eligibility, determined
by the federal/state government, for other funding sources. For the 2010-2011
academic year, 16 scholars were approved to receive a total of $193,815 in
scholarship support.
The scholarship program bolstered its case management support by
providing a Scholarship Coordinator who would assist the students with meeting
a variety of their needs such as academic, financial, mental health, health and
independent living. Visiting schedules were established and increased based on
the scholars’ needs. Academic workshops and information sessions were created
to better prepare students for college and to educate parents regarding the college
application process and the Masonic Homes Scholarship program.
In 2011, the Masonic Homes Scholarship Program received the most
number of applications since its inception and the Board of Trustees approved the
largest group of scholars for an academic year. For the 2011-2012 academic year,
21 scholars were approved to receive a total of $217,744 in scholarship support.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

243

Students were informed that they could only be placed on academic
probation one time. If the students’ G.P.A. fell below a 2.0 a second time, then
they would need to successfully attend school on their own accord for one full
academic year before being eligible to reapply. The Scholarship Committee took
into consideration the student’s overall GPA as well as their last semester/quarter
grades, and the Scholarship Committee made recommendations for full-time or
part-time award amounts, based on the students past performance. The purpose
was to increase the student’s likelihood to succeed academically. Finally, scholars
were apprised that future scholarship awards may be reduced, given the program
demand and limited amount of funding.
Post-graduate workshops were be added to the scholarship program
to support college seniors as they prepare for employment, independent living
and applying for graduate studies, if applicable. This transition period will be
challenging for some students and therefore additional support services will
be needed.
Much of the above work could not have been accomplished without the
support of Brad Colby, Judy Player, Steffani Kizziar, and Sabrina Montes and I
sincerely appreciate their assistance and support.

Report of the Executive Vice President
I am honored to introduce the staff reports on each of our service lines
by its executive or director and to report on some of the unifying themes that
guide our work each and every day. Masonic Homes of California is blessed
with a committed and capable executive team. I work with each member of that
team, which I count it as one of the privileges of my job, and so I can say with
special emphasis that the residents and clients of Masonic Homes of California
are blessed to have them guiding our operations.
New Philosophy of Care
I reported last year on the new philosophy of care that was beginning
to change the way in which we provided service and care in our communities.
I am pleased to report that the new philosophy of care is becoming more and
more imbedded in the life and activity of all of our service lines. With the new
philosophy of care, we are moving from a primary focus on care toward an
emphasis on the empowerment of residents and clients to fulfill their highest
potential. When a Mason, his wife or widow becomes frail or disabled, excellence
in care is absolutely critical. But as a guiding principle, the new philosophy of
care’s emphasis on wellness, quality of life and fulfillment of potential subtly
shifts our emphasis in a powerful way. Aging does not have to be a slow, gradual
descent into frailty; it is our goal to continue to encourage growth and wellness
for our residents and clients. Please note the new philosophy of care in action
throughout the staff reports.
Excellence in Service
President David Doan and Finance Committee chairman Glenn Woody
report in these proceedings on our continuing success in meeting the financial
challenge posed by the severe downturn in the economy. They also note that we
have done so without compromising the quality of care, service and activity.
Our annual satisfaction surveys continue to outpace the national norms overall.
How is this possible? Don’t cuts inevitably mean loss of quality? And how is it
possible to maintain appropriate merit increases for hard-working staff on top
of this? This is one of the hidden benefits of having a capable executive team.
Across-the-board cuts without thoughtful targeting would indeed diminish
quality. A practical benefit of the new philosophy of care is that it forces the team
to re-think day-to-day operations almost from ground-up. Business types call this
zero-based budgeting. In re-thinking operations in this way, one usually finds
savings without loss of quality. In addition, good solid day-to-day management
has hidden financial benefits. An example of this is management’s emphasis on
employee safety. First and foremost we want employees to be safe because of
its effect on their (and their family’s) quality of life. But a side benefit is lower
workers compensation cost, which can be very significant.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

245

Innovation
The centerpiece for innovation for Masonic Homes of California in the
past year is the newly opened Masonic Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF),
a one-of-a-kind treatment center for integrated psychological services. It is
described in President David Doan’s report and in the staff report of Steffani
Kizziar, Executive Director of Children’s Services and Masonic Outreach. We are
justifiably proud of MCYAF and expect the fraternity will be as well, as the full
impact of what we are doing becomes more widely known. But innovation does
not stop with MCYAF. Spurred by the new philosophy of care, staff is developing
new programming that emphasizes wellness, empowerment, and fulfillment of
potential for residents and clients. You will see that each of the executive reports
are filled with wonderful new ideas and programs, from the campus-wide joint
resident-employee Walk to Wellness at Union City to the self-help training
program regarding one’s health at Covina under Partners in Care.
Strategic Initiatives

in service, and innovation finds a point of confluence in the emerging strategic
initiatives of MHC. I urge you to read the report of Fred Avery, Chairman of
MHC’s Strategic Planning Committee, elsewhere in these proceedings. Under
Fred’s and President David Doan’s leadership, we are poised to address our future
as we continue to evolve to meet the needs of the fraternity. I believe you will be
pleased by the direction we are headed.

This past year we have adopted a Philosophy of Care that is moving
beyond the provision of comfort or meeting basic needs. The Philosophy
addresses health in a person - centered perspective using the four components
that will focus on aging successfully. These components are physical, intellectual,

challenge. Residents and staff were eager to take on the challenge of
climbing the twenty foot rock wall. Ninety-two year old Rose Monroe
provided a significant challenge to others when she successfully
completed the climb. Other games included Wii bowling, shuffle
board, and bean bag baseball. The event was extremely well received
and attended.

•

Events planned for each of the remaining months include celebrating
long term marriages, posting wedding pictures, playing the ‘not-sonewlywed’ game, and a tomato festival.

248

Proceedings of the

The introduction of the wellness initiative has required the development
of new metrics (indicators) to evaluate individual and group progress. An early
indicator is tracking resident use of the Grider Gym and Fitness Classes, including
the pool. The initial programs that have been introduced include Vertical, a
six week course teaching strategies to Fall Prevention and Neurobics, a brain
fitness program.
“Know Your Numbers” is a wellness program that provides support for
Assisted and Independent Living residents to keep track of their weight, blood
pressure and glucometer readings.
In support of the Philosophy of Care and the wellness perspective,
the Admissions Coordinator title has become Transition Coordinator and the
Recreation Department is now the Department of Active Living.
The wellness focus in the Skilled Nursing Department (Lorber) continues
with the team actively participating in California Coalition for Culture Change.
Primary areas of focus have been creating bathing areas that are relaxing
and allow for greater privacy, personalizing resident rooms, and consistent
assignments for Certified Nursing Assistants. A serenity room has been created
for residents and their families to have a private area in the final days of a
resident’s life.
Another addition to Lorber is the video conferencing option, Vital Link.
This option is comprised of a new touch screen computer with a video camera.
Residents and family members are now able to see each other while they are
talking. This new technology has been very well received. Visiting that could
not have been done due to distance is being accomplished. One resident, unable
to travel due to her infirmity, has been able to see her great-grandchild using
this process.
“Sketches of a Memory” is a program that allows residents to share
the stories of their lives. This program has been brought to MHC by Moreau
Catholic High School students. Following interviews with selected residents,
the students created an Art Exhibition to share the residents’ stories. Exhibits are
in the form of singing, dancing, art, photography, and videography. Residents
and staff have enjoyed the opportunity to gain a deeper connection of those that
were interviewed.
The Director of Health Services & Director of Resident Services
have worked together to revamp the current MHCUC Medical Office resident
appointments transportation service. The progress is monitored to maintain the
highest customer service available.
A video equipment upgrade for the Siminoff Chapel has improved the
reception for those present and those watching on the in-house channel. The
improvements include a drop down screen and mounted projector, enhanced
wiring to ceiling speakers, as well as lighting adaptations.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

249

An additional project has begun to upgrade the wiring for television
throughout the community. This is in response to the advances in technology that
require the ability to provide a digital signal through fiber-optics. The project is
anticipated to be completed by the end of August 2010.
The Pharmacy has expanded its service to include the Acacia Creek
residents, thus increasing the work load. Pharmacy is closely monitoring the
effects of Medicare D. Further changes are anticipated as the new Health Care
Reform Law is fully implemented.
To take further steps toward Disaster Planning, Certified Emergency
Response Training (CERT) was completed by three MHC residents, who are
members of the Emergency Team (ET) and three MHC employees. Staff and
some ET members were also trained on the use of evacuation chairs, which are
located in each stairwell. Acacia Creek and Masonic Homes teams are working
closely on this project. Search & Rescue practice in apartment setting has been
provided to all staff and interested residents. Floor-to-floor evacuation drills have
been performed for all buildings.
Resident Activities:
•

Jam and Jelly was held on August 21st with attendance of 325 with the
theme of ‘I am proud to be American’

•

‘Let’s go to the Tropics’, the annual family BBQ, was well attended by
312 residents and families.

•

On October 17th the Fifth Masonic Youth Senior Ball was held with a
theme of “USO’. Over 100 Rainbow, Jobs Daughters and DeMolay were
in attendance along with adult advisors and 110 residents.

•

December 4th was Holiday Tree Decorating Day, 195 volunteers
decorated 24 trees on campus.

•

East Bay Past Matrons & Past Patrons held a Christmas Party for the
residents on December 6th. They brought home-baked ‘goodies’ including
specially baked cookies.

•

10th Annual Tree Lighting was held on December 9th.Approximately
900 people enjoyed the fellowship and entertainment. Mrs. Betty Byars,
a resident of 25 years, was chosen to light the tree this year.

•

Annual Super Bowl Party was a huge success. Residents enjoy this
annual event hosted by Pleasanton Lodge, Martinez Lodge and OES.

•

Annual Volunteer Brunch was celebrated on April 2nd with theme of
“Our Volunteers Are Our Good Fortune”. Eden Aoba Taiko Japanese
drummers provided outstanding entertainment and were enjoyed by all.

Report of the Director

of Masonic Outreach Services

CHILDREN’S SERVICES- Family Resource Center
Upon closure of the Masonic Homes Children’s Residential program
in 2009, we began serving our residents, who were discharged at that time,
through case management and financial support. During this second year of the
Transition Program, we provided financial and non-financial case management
to the 13 children and their families, who still needed our on-going support
to ensure their successful transition. At the end of this school year, 3 more
children graduated from high school. One of the graduates will be enlisting in
the military and the other 2 graduates have been approved to receive a Masonic
Homes Scholarship. Additionally, 2 children no longer need our support and have
successfully reunified.
In this upcoming and third year of the Transition Program, we will
be serving 8 children and their families. Of these 8 children, 2 will need outplacement support, 1 child will need financial case management and 5 will need
case management, with nominal financial support to help meet their educational,
extracurricular and clothing needs. These remaining 8 children are those in most
need of our continued support, due to their vulnerable family environments.
Overall these children have done well in school and have made good strides
adjusting to their new family environment. All of the children will be in high
school this fall and 2 of the children have Masonic affiliations.
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program has undergone significant
changes since 2010 to ensure the longevity of its financial endowments and to
further broaden the opportunities for the scholarship recipients. These changes
extended the time period for which alumni can make their initial application;
increased the number of years toward undergraduate studies; included graduate
studies; and allowed for scholars to attend colleges/universities outside of
California. Finally, due to the increasing number of scholars and the extended
reach of the scholarship program, annual caps were put in place on the awards for
a given year. The scholars were also provided with case management support to
ensure their academic success and to assist them with accessing needed resources,
as well as academic workshops. These changes have led to strengthening the
student’s accountability for their own performance and financial commitment
toward their own education. Moreover, the changes have helped reshape the
mindset of the scholarship as an entitlement to an earned privilege. This upcoming
school year, the Scholarship Program will serve 21 students. This is the largest
group of scholars approved for one school year, since the program’s inception.
We are pleased to see so many of our former alumni pursuing a higher education
to better themselves and their futures.

260

Proceedings of the

MASONIC FAMILY OUTREACH SERVICES – Family Resource Center
As part of our strategic shift, we expanded the services of the Masonic
Family Resource Center, to better meet the needs of our fraternal family. In
October 2009, we formally began providing financial and non-financial case
management support to members and their families under the age of 60, currently
known as the Masonic Family Outreach Services Program. The parameters of this
program are defined by eligibility requirements for financial support as well as the
time limits for such support. Financial support is short-term and intended to act
as a bridge from economic hardship toward self-sufficiency. All financial clients
agree to partner with their Care Manager toward this goal and must also apply and
access any public benefits for which they qualify.
Case management support has been extended to our entire Masonic
family, with no eligibility requirements or time limits. Our case management
services are broad, flexible and we are able to serve families in their own
communities. Our support includes identifying resources for families struggling
with today’s complex issues, such as the impact of divorce, unemployment, heath
problems and other significant life challenges, as well as assistance with applying
for public benefits and other programs. The Care Managers are able to provide
support that meets the member’s individual needs. Our Masonic Assistance line
provides information-referrals to all callers in need of community resources.
We are able to serve callers with a wide range of needs and across different age
groups. On average, the MFOS program is now serving approximately 30-35
clients per month with case management and 17 clients per month with financial
case management.
MASONIC SENIOR OUTREACH SERVICES
Many of our elderly brethren and their wives and widows have been hard
hit by recent economic events and some members have had to seek earl retirement
due to loss of employment and health related issues. As a result, we are serving
more members through our MSOS program than ever before in our history. This
year, approximately 188 members received direct financial assistance through our
MSOS program; another 260 received information and referrals; and another 50
received ongoing case management services. Through the generous support of
Masons who give to our annual fund help ensure that we are always in a position
to the meet the needs of our members.
We believe we have been successful with the identification of one
Centralized Intake line as the single and direct point of inquiry for all Masonic
Assistance Programs, making it easier for our callers to obtain information about
any of our programs. The intake line telephone number is printed on the new
dues cards of our members, so that it is readily available. We continue to expand
our outreach efforts by conducting lodge presentations through out the state on a

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

261

routine basis to ensure that all of our members know about our services and how
to access them. Our future plans include strengthening our partnerships with our
lodges and Masonic leadership by formalizing our communication process and
working together to better serve our members.
It has been a productive year for the Masonic Outreach Services
Department and Family Resource Center. We have expanded our programs,
improved the delivery of our services and are now prepared to embark upon on
our strategic initiatives that will improve our services to our fraternal family
and meet the needs of our members, across the generational spectrum. We look
forward to the work ahead.
Respectfully submitted,
Sabrina Montez

Proceedings of the

Report of the Administrator

of the Masonic Home at Covina

On behalf of the residents and staff of the Masonic Homes at Covina,
we are pleased to present the following Annual Report highlighting the successes
and challenges of the past year. As you read our report we hope you will sense our
continued commitment to excellence as we serve our residents. We would like to
also express our appreciation to the Board of Trustees and our Masonic Lodges
for their dedication and support of our community.
During the past year we served a senior population which averaged 75
residents. The population represented a resident mix of 60% Independent Living;
33% Assisted Living and 7 % Skilled Nursing. We had six admissions; eight
deaths and two transfers to our Union City Campus.
Our Waiting List includes thirty-four prospective residents representing
twenty-seven households. The average waiting period for admission was
approximately ten months. Our staff is committed to call each prospective
applicant monthly to inquire on their well being: physically, emotionally and
financially. Referrals to our Masonic Outreach Program are made if services and
support are needed.
Our Senior Community offers a “Continuum of Care” model that
provides a full spectrum of care and services. Residents are treated with respect
and dignity while partnering with staff to define what quality of life means to
each individual.
As a resident-centered, mission-driven community, we are dedicated and
committed to carry out our mission to provide quality of care to California Master
Masons, their wives, widows and mothers with dignity and compassion within an
atmosphere based on Masonic tenets, which fulfill the physical, social, spiritual
and nurturing needs of our extended community.
During this past year our focus has been on “Healthy Living”. At the
conclusion of our “2010 Wellness Challenge”, our residents had an overall weight
loss of 210 lbs. This was due to the residents’ enthusiasm with our monthly
education sessions, exercise programs and nutritional consultations.
We are now working on our 2011 Healthy Living by challenging both
residents and staff in a “Pound for Pound Challenge”. Residents and staff are
teaming together in education programs and physical activities. For each pound
we lose, a pound of food will be donated to a local food bank.
During this past year our residents have started a vegetable garden. The
garden has been such a success we have expanded the size. The residents are
growing zucchini, tomatoes, onions and rosemary to name a few.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

263

A new program on Healthy Living was implemented this year called
“Partners in Care”. Two residents and one staff member are taking classes to
become a Healthier Living Leader. This class provides tools to better manage
health problems, decisions-making and better communication skills. It‘s all about
empowerment. When this class is finished the residents will have the training to
train other residents in our community.
In working with the surrounding communities, we have many
organizations visiting our campus and using our facilities for meetings throughout
the year. We are the polling destination for three precincts in the community, Census
Bureau, Charter Oak Unified School District and the Chamber of Commerce to
name a few. This year the Masonic Home at Covina is celebrating thirty-five years
as a member of the Covina Chamber of Commerce.
Our residents are also involved in community volunteering. We have
residents who volunteer at Badillo Elementary School tutoring students,
volunteering at the Police Department as Senior Police Cadets. We also have many
residents volunteering on campus. Our resident committees consist of: Resident
Council; Health Service, Dietary, Activities; Disaster Preparation; Buildings and
Grounds; Housekeeping and Spiritual. Residents also volunteer in other areas
such as; Gift Shop, Grocery Store and the New 2 U clothing store. During the past
year we had a total of 14,666 volunteer hours from our residents.
On June 5, 2011 our campus enjoyed our sixth successful Summer
Festival. The Summer Festival joins together our local Masonic Lodges and
Eastern Star. The Grand Master‘s Summer Festival theme for this event was golf.
There were over 300 guests that attended this event.
During this past year, our campus Retreat Program included the Demolay,
Sweetheart Leadership Camp and the Inspectors Development Academy. Our
residents enjoy the fellowship with these groups when visiting the campus. We
look forward to continuing the relationship with these groups in the future.
Our campus is proud to be the training site for two programs. The
East San Gabriel Occupational and Technical Program which provides in home
patient care training for Certified Nurses Assistants. USC students working on
their Masters Degree in Social Work provides training in the geriatric field on our
campus. Our dietary and housekeeping departments are also training sites.
Each year our residents participate in a Resident Survey. The survey is
an indication as to how well staff is accomplishing healthy living and quality
of life for the residents. On our last survey we had 100% participation from
our residents.

Proceedings of the

Report of the Executive Director

of Masonic Center for Youth and Families

The Masons in California have a long tradition of caring for vulnerable
youths in our State and have provided shelter and services to the orphaned,
abandoned and abused since opening the Masonic Homes of California in 1898.
In keeping with this important tradition, on February 16, 2011 the Masonic Center
for Youth and Families opened its doors in San Francisco’s historical Presidio
neighborhood to serve children and families in distress.
On March 20, 2011, Most Worshipful William Bray presided over
the dedication ceremony of this new Center, which demonstrates the fraternal
commitment to the principle that every youth deserves to be understood, loved and
allowed to realize his or her potential. During more than a century of service, the
name and offering of the Masonic Homes of California has changed in response
to the changing needs of our fraternity and society while remaining firm in this
core commitment.
The opening of the Masonic Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF)
was the culmination of more than two years of planning and research that involved
Masonic Homes Trustees, masons across the State, parents, teachers, social
workers and top clinical professionals from around the world. In our planning
phases, we asked participants to describe the needs of children in distress and the
optimal conditions under which they can be treated. Together, we developed our
“best possible” model of care.
We serve youth between the ages of 4 and 17 who struggle with
behavioral, academic, emotional or social difficulties. Our services include:
Ø

Comprehensive assessment including personality, cognitive and
neuropsychological testing and interviews with friends and family. Such
a comprehensive approach allows our youth the profound relief of being
understood and our clinicians the information necessary to focus their
treatment, while laying the foundation for far-reaching and nuanced
outcome studies.

Ø

Individual psychotherapy for youth and parents and family and couples
treatment. The frequency, duration and range of services will be based on
the youth’s needs and the recommendations from our multi-disciplinary
Treatment Conference. Once accepted into our Center, each open case is
discussed by the entire staff at ongoing case conferences.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

269

The aspects of our program that are qualitatively unique - comprehensive
assessment, treatment management, case conferences, internal consultations,
coordination of providers - are those for which there is no ready reimbursement.
We use our charitable resources to support these qualitatively necessary yet
traditionally unfunded services and to serve those who are otherwise underserved.
Since opening our doors six months ago, we have provided comprehensive
assessments to 34 youth and families; consultative services to another 20 families
and begun ongoing therapeutic services with 30 families. When fully staffed, we
anticipate serving between 150-180 families per year.
We are focused on serving our fraternal family and have provided
comprehensive assessment to 6 masonic children from around the state and
provided ongoing case management and consultative services to another 12
families. We recently hired a new Masonic case manager who will focus on
outreach to our vulnerable families and providing services to masonic families
across the state.
By any measure, it is a difficult time economically in our state and in our
country. In response to these pressures, an increasing number of families are in
need of supportive services at the same time community agencies are closing due
to funding cut-backs. By some estimates, as many as 15% of community service
agencies serving distressed youth have closed due to loss of funding. For the
Masons to invest in the services that are so needed at a time when everyone else
is closing their doors; for the Masons to insist on the highest quality of service
available when everyone else is ratcheting back on the quality and quantity of
services just to survive - is for the Masons to make a loud and very public statement
about the strength of our organization and our deep and active commitment to the
health of our youth and our communities. Our ambitions are great in keeping with
our founding ideals.
Respectfully submitted,
Steffani Kizziar

Proceedings of the

Report of the Directors of the
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
On behalf of the Board of Directors of Acacia Creek, I am pleased to
report on the progress over the past year of the Acacia Creek Community in
Union City.
Perhaps one of the most significant developments came in November
2010 when Acacia Creek received its Provisional Certificate of Authority (PCOA)
from the Department of Social Services. This certification allowed Acacia Creek
(officially opened in March 2010) to operate as a CCRC (Continuing Care
Retirement Community) which meant that residents living in our Community
could convert their month-to-month rental agreements into resident contracts
and Acacia Creek could begin collecting over $10 million in entrance fees
– an important factor in maintaining smooth cash flow for our operations. We
are currently completing the application to renew the PCOA, well ahead of the
November 2011 deadline.
Continued economic volatility and a soft housing market presented
significant challenges to Acacia Creek and occupancy levels, while rising, did not
keep pace with the original pro forma for the project. The board worked closely
with management to reorganize, renew and re-energize our marketing strategies
to address these economic factors and incentivize prospective residents to make
deposits and to move into our Community.
A comprehensive external marketing audit was conducted by the
nationally recognized firm Retirement Dynamics and, based on this analysis and
our own internal review, the board authorized the termination of our marketing
consulting agreement with PRS in May 2011and approved a reorganization of
our sales and marketing team, a new market demographic study and enhanced
communication to our own fraternity.
The board also approved a series of additional marketing incentives
including new pricing for garden units; a skilled nursing benefit; a bridge loan
program; additional refund options; move-in home assistance; health care assisted
living benefits and 4% interest on all deposits. Taken together, these incentives
made it easier for prospects to put deposits down and move into the Community.
Improvements were also made to the campus itself such as new signage and
landscaping that more clearly identified Acacia Creek and made the entryway
more welcoming.
At the end of December 2011, Administrator Lydia Hertzler left Acacia
Creek after serving in that position since July 2009. The board conducted a
comprehensive national search and, after careful review, selected Jeffrey Dillon

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

271

to serve as Interim Administrator starting on February 1, 2011. Jeffrey, a certified
RCFE administrator, had an extensive background in marketing and sales and a
proven ability to develop daily operations, resident satisfaction and delivery of
quality services.
Throughout this period, Acacia Creek continued to work closely with the
Masonic Homes, receiving additional support from their Executive Vice President
Mel Matsumoto and Executive Director and Administrator Dixie Reeve and their
staff. The close relationship with the Masonic Homes is an invaluable asset to our
community, not only at the level of its operations, but also at the level of daily
resident life.
Since the New Year, Acacia Creek has collaborated with the Homes to
offer more opportunities for residents of both communities to get together socially
and discuss issues of common interest. This spirit is evident in the number of
Acacia Creek Residents who have petitioned to join the lodge on campus, our
Resident Council’s effort to develop a guide to Masonry for new members of
Acacia Creek, collaboration on campus-wide wellness programs and even the
recent marriage between a resident of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek.
Working closely with the Grand Master and the Executive Committee, as
well as the Board and leadership of the Masonic Homes, Acacia Creek identified
the need for a full-time executive vice president to give undivided attention to
the operations and marketing of the organization as it grows against the backdrop
of prolonged economic volatility. The board took time to identify the important
characteristics required of such a position and appointed a search committee that
identified several prominent figures in the field of aging services as finalists. After
very careful deliberation, Charles (Chuck) Major was selected and began his role
as the new Executive Vice President on July 11, 2011.
Chuck Major brought a wealth of experience spanning 22 years in the
senior living and hospitality fields, having been for the previous ten years the
Vice President of Management Services at Seniority, Inc., a division of American
Baptist Homes of the West and Vice President of Operations for Regent Assisted
Living, Portland, OR. Prior to holding these positions Mr. major served as an
Executive Director for several communities and Administrator at a number of
senior living communities including Woodside Terrace in Redwood City and The
Altenheim in Oakland. Jeffrey Dillon, who ended his role as interim administrator
on July 15, has been retained on a short-term consulting contract to assist
with marketing.
In his first month at Acacia Creek Chuck has won the confidence of our
residents and staff alike and partnered with the board on key initiatives. At the
board’s August 16, 2011 strategic planning retreat Chuck secured support for a
comprehensive new marketing plan that includes initiatives to drive occupancy;
strategic outreach to non-Masons and Masons; and a comprehensive re-branding

272

Proceedings of the

developed in collaboration with the Masons of California Communications
Department that includes a re-invigorated Web presence, new collateral and a
compelling new tag line: “Acacia Creek: Living the Dream.” As of the writing of
this report, he is also finalizing a comprehensive business plan for the organization.
As a result of these efforts, Acacia Creek has seen a steady rise in the
number of $1,000 and 10% deposits and move-ins to our Community. As of the
writing of this report, 53 apartments are occupied by 72 residents. The FY12
budget assumes that 110 units will be occupied by October 31 of next year with
154 residents in the Community. We anticipate that $9 million in entrance fees
will be collected; in addition to the over $15 million collected to date and every
effort is being made to achieve these goals. Staffing levels will continue to be tied
to occupancy and rise accordingly and our management has made every effort to
insure that cost efficiencies are captured while maintaining the highest quality of
resident life.
Recently reported resident satisfaction survey results indicate a very high
degree of satisfaction with these efforts as well as progress made to resolve the
last outstanding building issues with regard to our hot water system and acoustics
in units adjacent to our kitchen and dining areas. The expanding social life of
Acacia Creek residents attest to the fact that they are putting down roots and
deepening their connections. This August, after receiving a liquor license from
ABC, Acacia Creek residents christened their new bar as the “Turkey Roost” in
honor of the wild turkeys that continue to roam the beautiful hillsides and fields of
our Union City campus. A new game room is being set up on the 5th floor, a new
farmer’s market brings the best of local produce to our doorstep and recreational
offerings continue to expand to the delight of all.
As Acacia Creek looks to the year ahead with confidence, it is important
to take time to pause and to express our gratitude to those who have worked
so tirelessly to help our Community navigate through these first years. I most
especially want to recognize the countless contributions of founding Directors
Loyal Stark and Mark Gibson (also Vice President), and Treasurer Glenn Woody
who are all leaving the board at the end of this term. Each of them, along with every
member of our Board of Directors, has given their very best to the development
of Acacia Creek and shown tremendous dedication to ensuring its stability and
growth even during difficult economic times.
I also want to express my gratitude to Masonic Homes Executive Vice
President Mel Matsumoto and Executive Director and Administrator Dixie Reeve
who have now entrusted daily operations to our new Executive Vice President
Chuck Major but who no doubt will remain very important as Acacia Creek
continues to grow in the coming years.

of the Masons of California, in particular, Chief Financial Officer Tom Boyer,

Board Governance Brad Colby who have, through Grand Lodge Shared Services,
under the very able leadership of Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, provided
expert professional support in managing our finances, licensing and legal needs,
marketing and communications, personnel and the ongoing development of our
governance policies and practices.

Proceedings of the

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Your California Masonic Foundation has made aggressive progress this
past year in aligning our activities with the new Strategic Plan of the Masons
of California and implementing the two initiatives specifically assigned by the
Executive Committee. In addition, on-going programs continued to be reviewed
for relevance and continuing impact, and changes made to improve output and
increase focus on making a profound impact on students’ lives in this jurisdiction.
Strategic Initiatives
The Executive Committee assigned two initiatives to the Foundation in
2010; (1) establishing a comprehensive public education support program, and (2)
developing approaches for local Lodge involvement in the community. Substantial
progress was made in 2011 on both of these fronts. The public education program
was focused on three strategic goals – addressing literacy in the Kindergarten
through third grade age group, addressing middle school math, and revamping our
heritage scholarship programs for post high school success. The effort to increase
local Lodge involvement in the community was focused on the implementation of
Public School Advisory Councils in three key urban school districts.
In addressing both of these initiatives, the Foundation, through the
Executive Vice President and Grand Lodge leadership, has further cemented
relationships with the California Board of Education and the Superintendent of
Schools. This summer the Foundation successfully hosted the new Superintendent
at a reception for the education leadership of San Francisco. The Superintendent
has since requested the Foundation and the Masons of California to assist in
similar receptions throughout the state. Our fraternity has gained a seat at the
table and has begun to be recognized as a convener, an integrator, who can bring
focus and resources to problem at hand. This has been a major accomplishment.
Literacy
Statistically, the state of California forecasts the amount of prison
square footage needed by the number of students failing to read at grade level
in third grade. This statistic alone emphasizes the critical need for focused
literacy improvement. As 2011 began, the cornerstone of our literacy thrust was
implementation of the Take Home Book program which had been initiated in
2010. As the year progressed, the Foundation found that Take Home Book was
limited in its ability to meet our ultimate objectives of a sustainable program
with measurable impact on the child as well as their parents. Early in 2011,

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

275

the Foundation assessed other on-going programs throughout the country and
determined that alignment with Raising a Reader offered a more comprehensive
and closed loop learning experience for the child and the parents. The Board has
since moved to form a strategic partnership with Raising a Reader and will begin
to implement the program in successive years throughout the state. We believe
that the national stature and ability to integrate other literacy thrusts into their
model enables Raising a Reader to offer the measurable, sustainable, profound
impact that the Foundation desires. We believe that this program will potentially
become the MSAP of literacy, a program with a far reaching and long term impact
in our communities.
Middle School Math
One of the most difficult transitions for a child is the move from
fundamental arithmetic to the understanding of abstract mathematical concepts
such as algebra and geometry. Without a successful transition, the student is
ill prepared for higher level careers in science and engineering. Impacting this
transition most profoundly has proven to be a difficult undertaking. Currently,
there is not a well identified national approach to addressing the teaching
of middle school math. This year, the Board has been assessing how best to
formulate a program for California. We have been begun dialogues with several
math educators as well as the Board of Education and plan to synthesize a
recommended approach next year.
Pathways to Success
During the last eighteen months, the Foundation has reassessed its
approach to providing scholarship support to graduating seniors as they move
to higher education. Over 3,500 scholarship applications were received this year
and processed by your Scholarship Committee, and our general scholarship funds
supported granting 41 scholarships worth about $546,000 in 2011. In addition, we
continued to grant scholarships to nurse leaders through the Claire Cunningham
Fund for Leadership in Nursing. Our Grand Master’s project this year, By Your
Side, has been hugely successful and led to funding the first scholarships for
Oncology nurses.
Yet, with our rigorous criteria aimed at aiding the best and the brightest,
our scholarships have many times become secondary source of funding and do not
create the impact on the student’s life that we desire. This year the Board began
a review of our program and the funds that support it, including the Raymond
Levy Fund for Public Education. Many of our scholarship funds are earmarked
for certain careers, have specific criteria for recipients or are otherwise limited.
These will also be assessed for possible changes in criteria to help assure those
funds are making the biggest impact.

276

Proceedings of the

This year the Board took a major step by implementing the Investment
in Success program. This program recognizes that the most impact comes from
funding the student who has the drive and willingness to succeed and make a
difference in their lives and in their communities. They have acute financial need,
may be the first in their family to go to college, may have only a B average, and
may choose not to pursue college unless they can find help, yet have the persistence
to move forward in spite of these obstacles. Investment in Success identifies
these students through recommendations from their counselors and principals in
partnership with the Foundation and our new Public Schools Advisory Councils.
The Board was pleased this year to award on your behalf the first 21 scholarships
worth $147,000. We expect to further expand the program next year.
Public Schools Advisory Councils
To achieve the goal of increased local Lodge involvement impact in the
community, the Board set up Public Schools Advisory Councils in three major
urban school areas – San Diego, San Francisco and Glendale/Pasadena/Burbank.
Local Lodges were asked to provide interested and motivated brethren to populate
a Council that would be the direct interface to the school districts in the area. Three
Councils were formed and were instrumental in organizing three Public Schools
Month Kickoff ceremonies in April, with members of the Executive Committee
present. The Council members then conducted the candidate interviews for
the Investment in Success scholarship program and made the final recipient
recommendations. These successful efforts demonstrate that the local Lodges and
brethren can make a significant, visible impact in their communities. Next year
the number of Councils will be expanded to seven and Public Schools Month
Kickoffs and Investment in Success scholarship interviews and awards conducted
in all seven areas.
Bringing Investment in Success and the Public Schools Advisory
Councils to fruition would not have been possible without the driving force of
Joyce Hahn and the Grand Lodge staff that supports her. The Board recognizes
her for her incalculable contribution to the Foundation and its objective of making
a profound impact on student lives.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

277

Other Programs
The Foundation continued to underwrite our existing leadership
development, Lodge growth and Masonic education programs; including
the Wardens’ Leadership Retreats, Lodge Certification Program, Inspector’s
Development Academy, Masonic Formation, the Institute for Masonic Studies
and this year’s successful Masonic Symposium. In addition, our Heritage sites,
historic article preservation, Library and Museum, and CMMT maintenance
were funded.
Based on feedback from the brethren, the Child ID program continues
to be successful in many of our districts. This year, Vice President, Mark Pressey,
began transitioning future software support to involved brethren within the
jurisdiction to allow the software to keep pace with technology and be available
to interested Lodges.
Board Governance
The Board continued to evaluate and modify processes this year to more
efficiently execute the business of the Foundation. The annual strategic planning
retreat was held in June and a thorough review of the current AAA operating
philosophy, roles and responsibilities, and time commitments was conducted. The
Trustees unanimously agreed to remain committed to the operating model and to
further promote understanding of the purpose and initiatives of the Foundation
to the brethren. Thus, I am pleased to report that your Foundation is being well
managed by strong and committed leadership.
Once again, quarterly meetings were held by teleconference or in the
Masonic Home in Covina to reduce expenses. Monthly telephone calls were
held to status progress and address specific items, such as finalizing scholarship
recommendations, completing budget planning for the ensuing year, or reviewing
quarterly financials.
To improve member understanding of the purposes and programs of the
Foundation, an update to the Grand Lodge website was initiated to modify and
improve access to Foundation communications and activities.
Looking Forward to 2012
The Foundation is poised to enter 2012 with an increasing level of
activity throughout the jurisdiction. The establishment of four more Public Schools
Advisory Councils will more than double the number of brethren actively working
to make an impact on public education in their communities. Conducting seven
simultaneous Public Schools Month Kickoff events will increase the fraternity’s

278

Proceedings of the

visibility and continue to establish the Masons of California as a major force
behind the improvement of education in this state. The Board plans to increase the
number of Investment in Success scholarships and continue to revamp the overall
scholarship program.
The Foundation will also begin its campaign to double our financial
resources by the 50th anniversary of the Foundation in 2019. With increased
resources, we will be able to substantially increase our presence and impact in our
communities. That way we will be able to fulfill our vision of making a profound
difference in students’ lives and in our society.
Acknowledgements
The Trustees wish to thank Most Worshipful Bray for our appointments
and the opportunity to serve this Grand lodge. Special thanks in particular go
to Doug Ismail, Executive Vice President and Chief Philanthropy Officer, Brad
Colby, Director of Board Governance, Mark Pressey, Vice President, and the
Grand Lodge staff led by Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, Grand Secretary, for
their outstanding leadership, guidance and support to this Foundation Board.
Respectfully submitted,
Arthur H. Weiss, President
Mark E. Pressey, Vice-President
Douglas D. Ismail, Executive Vice-President
Saul Alvarado
Wesley W. Daniels
H. John Fletcher
Edmond M. Lim
Frank Loui

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

279

Report of the Board of Trustees

of the California Masonic Memorial Temple

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
This afternoon I am pleased to make the annual report of the Board of
Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The CMMT owns this great edifice in which we meet today and derives
tax-exempt revenue by leasing space to the Grand Lodge of California whose
offices are on the third floor; to the Nob Hill Masonic Center that operates the
garage; the telecommunications facility on the roof and to other third parties
who lease space in the building. We also receive tax-exempt contributions from
candidates who are initiated into our California lodges. We are very happy that
this number continues to grow each year. In spite of the continued low return
on investments this year, the CMMT experienced a very healthy cash flow. This
Board was most prudent in the expenses for operating and maintaining this
building and we look to an increase in building use in order to fund necessary
improvements in the future.
Our efforts continue to be devoted to implementing our vision to keep
your facility viable for the future and competitive in the ever changing market in
which we operate.
The plans to optimize the utilization of this building, enabling us to meet
our current and future operating needs, and provide the means for the increasing
costs of maintenance, repair, and restoration continues to be long and arduous.
Approval for the current use of the building has been granted by the courts and
the permit process continues but at a slow pace. With patience the result will be
to create this auditorium into the premiere performance venue in San Francisco,
make the California Room a viable and welcome respite while transforming
the Exhibit Hall and kitchen into a world class restaurant, all while maintaining
our beautiful War Memorial for all time; still serve the needs for our Annual
Communication and Grand Lodge while maintaining a positive relationship with
our neighbors on Nob Hill.
Our agreement with Live Nation extends their use portions of the building
through December 2013. This contract results in significant revenue to CMMT
as well as the Nob Hill Masonic Center, all for the betterment of Freemasonry
in California.
Building maintenance continues to be the highest priority. This year
the air handling system in the Grand Lodge Server Room was upgraded and fire
prevention equipment improved.

Report of the Board of Directors

of the Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is the for profit, income tax paying entity
which oversees the parking garage at the Nob Hill Masonic Center and until
January 1, 2009, also managed the operations of the Auditorium and Exhibit
Hall. On January 1, 2009 Nob Hill relinquished management of the Auditorium
and Exhibit hall back to C.M.M.T., who at the same time entered into a lease
agreement with Live Nation to operate the Auditorium and Exhibit Hall.
As reported by CMMT, efforts are still underway to make improvements
to the auditorium and food service areas of the building. Once that is completed,
we anticipate greater event revenue which has been lagging in recent years
while CMMT has worked through the legal and legislative process to bring the
improvements about.
In addition, garage revenues for the year ending October 31, 2011
will continue to be lower than originally anticipated due to a drop in monthly
parking primarily resulting from the economic downturn and increased
apartment vacancies.
In order to improve operating efficiencies, Nob Hill undertook a
garage automation project in 2010. As a part of this project the longed planned
improvements to the garage entrance were also completed. The entrance, exiting
and payment operations were all automated. This will allow Nob Hill to reduce its
labor costs by approximately 50% or $170,000 per year. The cost of the project
was approximately $250,000.

income and expenses through October 31, 2011, are as follows:

Report of the Committee
On Finance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code requires the Committee on Finance to
review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to be considered at
the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact these items may
have on the Grand Lodge budget.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Grand Master’s
Recommendations and the Carry-Over and new Resolutions as provided by the
Grand Secretary. On July 20, we finalized our report on the cost impact of each
item and it was mailed to the lodges by the Grand Secretary on July 26 with
the legislation.
Only three items have any financial impact on the Grand Lodge, and in
as much as our written report has been distributed, I will report on them now and
not later during the session.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 1: Increases the
Representation on the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee: The
Grand Lodge reimburses the committee members for their necessary expenses to
attend the Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee meeting. The average
reimbursement for the most recent meeting was approximately $200 per person.
There are currently nine divisions so there would be six additional committee
members. Using these figures, the impact to the Grand Lodge budget would be
approximately $1,200.
Grand Master Nagel’s Recommendation No. 3: Modifies Masonic Trial
Procedures: According to the Grand Secretary, the Grand Lodge currently spends
approximately $15,500 in administrative support of Masonic trials. It is expected
that the administrative responsibilities of the Grand Lodge will increase with
this new procedure by approximately one-third which could result in additional
expenses of approximately $5,100. This expense has been considered in the
preparation of the 2010/2011 Grand Lodge budget.
Carry-Over Resolution No. 09-01: Creates the Hiram’s Pillar Award:
The certificates will cost the Grand Lodge approximately %500. The resolution
stipulates that the medallion and pin will be made available by Grand Lodge for
purchase, but the potentical cost to Grand Lodge is the expense of any unsold,
returned, or damaged medallions and pins.
Again, in the view of the Committee on Finance, none of the other
legislation will have an impact on the Grand Lodge budget.

Report of the Committee

on Institute for Masonic Studies

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
This report provides information as to the activities of the Institute
for Masonic Studies for the year 2010–2011. The Institute is an agency of the
Grand Lodge of California that seeks to educate the Freemasons and the general
community about the philosophy, values and tenets of Freemasonry and enrich our
understanding of its symbolism and rituals. Regular meetings are held quarterly
during the fiscal year.
The Institute is charged with providing resources to encourage the study
of Freemasonry and oversees programs the Grand Lodge created to accomplish
these activities.
These responsibilities include the development and implementation of
Masonic Formation programs, including Masonic symposiums, membership and
candidate education materials and lodge Masonic education training programs
and stewardship over the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum.
During this year the following actions were accomplished after aligning
the IMS with the priorities in the 2011 Strategic Plan for the Masons of California
and establishing goals and tasks that would support achieving the goals of the five
year strategic plan:
•

The Henry W. Coil Library & Museum continues to be the little
museum that could. In 2011, the HWC participated in the San
Francisco History Expo, where a small display, including the Old
Mint trowel and the Builders of the Dream video, accompanied
by a personal guide, told the story of Freemasonry in California.
For this weekend event, over 3,000 people were in attendance.
Additionally, as a result of the increased visibility, the United
Grand Lodge of England’s library and museum included
photographs and artifacts from the HWC collection for their
July-December 2011 exhibit, The Patriot Mason: Freemasonry
in American Society.

•

In order to bring our collection to an even wider audience, the
HWC’s Website began featuring online exhibits, and as a result,
Adam Kendall, P.M., the Collections Manager, has noticed a
marked increase in attention by way of inquiries about Masonic
history from the public and scholars alike. The HWC has also
consulted with several lodges, notably Humboldt #79 and San
Diego #35, that have embarked upon a plan to preserve their
heritage. Further outreach has included several published essays
in academic journals and public lectures by the Collections

288

Proceedings of the
Manager - - most notably for the second time at the International
Conference on the History of Freemasonry. This research was
based on materials found in the HWC archive.
•

In April, the museum acquired the beautiful and very rare 1872
ceremonial trowel for the San Francisco City Hall and Law
Courts (destroyed in 1906). This trowel was used by M.W.
Bro. Leonidas Pratt, who also consecrated the cornerstone of
the U.S. Mint in San Francisco. Spurred by this acquisition,
a re-assessment of our collection of historic trowels has been
undertaken for a future in-house and on-line display. Similarly,
the inventory of the historic aprons has continued with many
important discoveries. Other “finds” have included unregistered
and rare mid-18th century copies of Anderson’s Constitutions
from Germany and Ireland.

•

The 2011 California Masonic Symposium, “The Morgan
Affair: The Kidnapping that Changed American Freemasonry,”
was held on June 25, 2011 at the Pasadena Scottish Rite.
There were approximately 150 persons in attendance. The first
presenter was Arthur H. Weiss, the President of the Board of
Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation, whose paper
explored the events leading up to and surrounding Captain
Morgan’s disappearance and the investigation which followed.
The title of Art’s paper was “William Morgan’s Disappearance:
Prelude and Aftermath.” The second presenter was Past Grand
Master R. Stephen Doan, whose presentation was entitled
“The Morgan Affair: The Second Great Religious Awakening
and the American Anti-Masonic Movement,” in which Steve
addressed the social, economic and political climate at the
time to explain America’s reaction to Morgan’s disappearance.
The final presenter was the 2011 Henry Wilson Coil Lecturer,
Mark A. Tabbert, Director of Collections at the George
Washington Masonic Memorial in Alexandria, Virginia, the
author of “American Freemasons: Three Centuries of Building
Communities.” The title of Mark’s lecture and paper was “New
England Masonic Grand Lodge Reaction, Recovery and Reform
during the Anti-Masonic Period, 1826-1845.” The symposium
concluded with a panel discussion on the symposium topic. The
panel included the three symposium speakers as well as Dr.
John L. Cooper, the Junior Grand Warden, and Dr. Matthew E.
Crow, the panel moderator, who had just received his Ph.D. in
American history at UCLA.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

•

The Institute for Masonic Studies continues its role of
overseeing our Grand Lodge’s Partnership to Advance the
Study and Understanding of Freemasonry with UCLA. This
project demonstrates our fraternity’s commitment to improving
Masonic education by expanding the learning opportunities for
college students, academic scholars, the public and members
of our craft. This past year, seventy-one undergraduate
students enrolled and completed four courses on the history
of Freemasonry and its impact on civil society in Europe, the
United States, and Latin America. The classes were taught by
Dr. Emiliano da Costa, of University of Ghent; Jesse Sadler,
Ph.D., candidate at UCLA; and Dr. Maria Eugenia Vazquez
Semadeni, Post-Doctoral Fellow at UCLA. The courses were
also added to the University’s extension course offerings for
the first time. Again this summer, abbreviated courses based
upon the university’s offerings were also made available to
Masons and non-Masons in Anaheim, Pasadena, San Diego,
and San Francisco. These classes were attended by fifty-seven
students. The partnership will continue next year, highlighted
by our first jointly sponsored academic conference addressing
Freemasonry in Latin America and will feature a distinguished
list of scholars, including Margaret Jacob of UCLA, Jose
Antonio Ferrer Benimeli of Universidad de Zaragosa, Miguel
Guzman-Stein of Universidad de Costa Rica, Maria Eugenia
Vazquez Semadeni of UCLA, and Guillermo de los Reyes
Heredia of the University of Houston.

Report of the Committee
on Insurance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Overview
The Insurance Committee is tasked with the responsibility of reviewing
the Grand Lodge property and casualty insurance program, working with the
broker selected by Grand Lodge and making recommendations regarding the
coverages. The Insurance Committee reports directly to the Grand Secretary on
all insurance matters (except Life and Medical Coverage and other benefits for
employees) who then makes the final decision regarding the different coverages
and limits to purchase or renew. The Committee also works closely with the Chief
Financial Officer on an ongoing basis.
Currently there are three meetings a Masonic year of the full Committee
and, an additional meeting late in the calendar year of just the Chairman, ViceChairman and CFO with the Grand Lodge’s insurance broker. This purpose of
this meeting to advise the broker of changes in Grand Lodge activities or new
programs being contemplated or under way. The Grand Lodge staff updates
the broker on the current status of the different Grand Lodge programs and any
changes that will be taking place and receives any information back from the
broker on changes in the insurance market place regarding costs and coverages.
The date for the renewal quotes for the following policy year is also set at
this meeting.
Review of Committee Meetings
The three full Committee meetings are as follows:
1.

The first meeting of the full Committee takes place in January. At this
meeting the broker reviews all of the current coverages presently in
effect and advises the Committee and Grand Lodge personnel on the
status of the insurance markets as to the availability of coverages and
current pricing. The broker also presents recommendations for changes
that could be made with the current coverages or the limits of coverage.
The Grand Lodge staff updates the broker and the Committee on any
changes in operations being made or that will be made that would affect
the coverages that are needed for the upcoming policy year.

2.

The second meeting of the full Committee takes place on the date set for
the renewal proposals (normally in mid-March) from the broker to be
presented. In addition to presenting the premium quotes for each policy
to be renewed the broker also presents alternative proposals for changes
in limits of coverage or specific coverages themselves. The Committee

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

291

then makes recommendations to the Grand Secretary as to how each
policy should be renewed and at what limits of coverage. Once the Grand
Secretary has these recommendations from the Insurance Committee he
makes the final decision on the recommendations of the Committee. The
renewal policies are then ordered.
3.

The third and final regular meeting of the Committee takes place in
June. By this date all of the renewal policies should have been received
from the broker. The Committee reviews all of the policies to be certain
that they contain the coverages and limits of coverages as ordered and
that there are no new or unusual restrictions or limitations added to the
policies. The Committee also reminds the Grand Lodge staff to be certain
that each policy names as an insured each of the Grand Lodge entities to
which a particular coverage is to apply.
Key Initiatives

The most significant event, from the standpoint of the Insurance
Committee, to take place during the past year was the opening of the Masonic
Center for Youth and Families. This new facility expands the Masonic Homes
outreach programs and presented its own special set of exposures to be addressed
by the Committee and the Broker. The decision was made to have separate
liability (primary and excess) policies issued to cover the MCYAF exposures.
The remaining coverages needed for MCYAF were incorporated into existing
Grand Lodge Insurance Policies.
The insurance coverages for Acacia Creek were also finalized. A
separate general liability and professional liability policy, along with a separate
excess liability policy, were issued for Acacia Creek. Also, a separate Difference
in Conditions policy was issued covering Acacia Creek to provide earthquake
coverage solely for this facility. It should be noted that the earthquake coverage
limits for Acacia Creek, the Masonic Homes and for the Grand Lodge location (the
SF Temple) are less than the estimated replacement cost of the buildings insured.
The remaining coverages for Acacia Creek were incorporated into existing Grand
Lodge policies.
The sample premise lease for Hall Associations is now available on the
Masonic Website (www.freemason.org). The Insurance Committee recommends
that all Hall Associations use this lease with anyone renting their facilities.

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The
Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Bray’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
In the Committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on July 18th of this year is sufficient to carry out the
intent of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Bray’s
recommendations which he will present in his message is sufficient to carry out
his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set
forth in it.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website
on July 18th of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Bray’s
recommendations require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman
